items.title: Meet Cloudflare Clef-omni: A 30B-A3B Multimodal Decision Model for Audio, Video, Image and Text
items.summary: Cloudflare has released Clef-omni , a new open-weight member of its Clef decision model family. Clef-omni is a Cloudflare decision model that scores text, images, audio and video in 1 call. It arrived on October 9, 2026, 8 days after the original Clef and Clef-flash launch . The same update cut Clef-flash pricing below TypeSafe’s Jev and made hosted Clef roughly 2x faster. For developers, this removes the transcription and captioning steps that multimodal agent pipelines usually need. TL;DR Size: 30B total, 3B active parameters (MoE); 64,000-token context on Workers AI Runs on: Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clef-omni ; self-hosting tested on a single H200, about 64 GB GPU memory in bfloat16 Performance: Close to Clef on routing and intent tasks, behind it on most reasoning and workflow evals Best: 97.7 macro-F1 on CLINC150+OOS, top of the 4 Clef and Jev models Worst: 2.6 accuracy on POP909-CL, and 47.4 on GPQA Diamond versus Jev’s 78.3 Bottom line: Best: one call decides across 4 modalities. Worst: weaker accuracy than text-focused Clef on hard reasoning. What is a decision model? A decision model returns typed answers with probabilities instead of generated text. You send a state and a schema of questions. The model returns a probability for every allowed option. Clef supports 3 question types : noul (true or false), choice and score . The format follows the Jev and SystemOne API from TypeSafe AI . How does Clef-omni work? Clef-omni is post-trained from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct . Cloudflare keeps the comprehension backbone and drops the text-to-speech output path. The model runs a single prefill pass over the full payload. Video frames and audio are synced into 1 sequence for joint processing. A small joint schema head then scores the options. Each valid option first gathers evidence from the input. Field vectors then cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. Cloudflare froze the Qwen3 backbone and trained LoRA adapters. Training combined label-smoothed cross-entropy with Brier score calibration. Supported inputs on Workers AI, per the developer docs : Images: up to 4, PNG, JPEG or WebP, 64 to 1,024 tokens each Audio: up to 4 clips, WAV or MP3, 300 seconds each, about 780 tokens per minute Video: up to 2 clips, MP4 or WebM, 60 seconds each, sampled at 2 frames per second Questions: 1 to 64 per request Cloudflare reports text decisions in about 130 ms at the median and images in about 150 ms. A 21-second video with sound scores in about 1.5 seconds. How does Clef-omni perform on benchmarks? Cloudflare compared Clef-omni against Clef, Clef-flash and Jev on its Decision Index run. Clef-omni leads on intent classification: 94.8 macro-F1 on BANKING77 and 97.7 on CLINC150+OOS. It also tops Amazon ESCI at 57.8. It trails elsewhere. Home appliances case-exact accuracy is 69.3, versus 97.73 for Clef-flash. When2Call accuracy is 63.3, versus 80.97 for Jev. On TypeSafe’s workflow evals , Clef-omni scores below Clef in all 5 reported metrics. && Clef-omni vs Clef vs Clef-flash vs Jev Feature Clef-omni Clef Clef-flash Jev Developer Cloudflare Cloudflare Cloudflare TypeSafe AI Parameters 30B total, 3B active (MoE) 27B dense 9B dense Not disclosed Base model Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct Qwen3.8-27B Qwen3.5-9B Not disclosed Inputs Text, image, audio, video Text, image, video frames Text, image, video frames Text (per Cloudflare ) Hosted context 64,000 tokens 64k 24k (256k self-hosted) Not disclosed by TypeSafe (Cloudflare cites 32k) Input price per M tokens $0.15 $0.24 $0.038 $0.042 License Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 Apache-2.0 API only, early access BANKING77 (macro-F1) 94.8 94.20 90.93 79.74 CLINC150+OOS (macro-F1) 97.7 97.43 66.77 89.27 When2Call (accuracy) 63.3 72.37 65.58 80.97 BRIGHT (nDCG@10) 42.0 45.91 39.26 47.52 Invoice processing, primary action 82.0 86.2 73.3 83.1 Benchmark scores are from Cloudflare’s announcement and were not independently verified. How much faster is Clef? Cloudflare moved hosted Clef to SGLang and tuned its serving stack. No new weights were released. Median latency fell from 262 ms to 152 ms at about 800 tokens, a 1.7x gain. At about 3,400 tokens it fell from 616 ms to 305 ms, a 2.0x gain. At about 16,000 tokens it dropped from 2,721 ms to 1,635 ms. Clef support lands in SGLang 0.5.22. Key Takeaways Clef-omni scores text, images, audio and video in 1 decision call. It is a 30B-A3B MoE on Qwen3-Omni, Apache-2.0, at $0.15 per million tokens. Clef-flash now costs $0.038, under Jev’s $0.042, with 24k hosted context. Hosted Clef is 1.7x to 2.0x faster at the median after moving to SGLang. Clef-omni wins intent tasks but trails Clef on reasoning and workflow evals. Check out the Cloudflare announcement , model weights and Workers AI docs . items.summary_html:
Cloudflare has released Clef-omni, a new open-weight member of its Clef decision model family. Clef-omni is a Cloudflare decision model that scores text, images, audio and video in 1 call. It arrived on October 9, 2026, 8 days after the original Clef and Clef-flash launch. The same update cut Clef-flash pricing below TypeSafe’s Jev and made hosted Clef roughly 2x faster. For developers, this removes the transcription and captioning steps that multimodal agent pipelines usually need.

TL;DR
  • Size: 30B total, 3B active parameters (MoE); 64,000-token context on Workers AI
  • Runs on: Workers AI as @cf/cloudflare/clef-omni; self-hosting tested on a single H200, about 64 GB GPU memory in bfloat16
  • Performance: Close to Clef on routing and intent tasks, behind it on most reasoning and workflow evals
  • Best: 97.7 macro-F1 on CLINC150+OOS, top of the 4 Clef and Jev models
  • Worst: 2.6 accuracy on POP909-CL, and 47.4 on GPQA Diamond versus Jev’s 78.3
  • Bottom line:
    • Best: one call decides across 4 modalities.
    • Worst: weaker accuracy than text-focused Clef on hard reasoning.
What is a decision model?

A decision model returns typed answers with probabilities instead of generated text. You send a state and a schema of questions. The model returns a probability for every allowed option. Clef supports 3 question types: noul (true or false), choice and score. The format follows the Jev and SystemOne API from TypeSafe AI.

How does Clef-omni work?

Clef-omni is post-trained from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. Cloudflare keeps the comprehension backbone and drops the text-to-speech output path. The model runs a single prefill pass over the full payload. Video frames and audio are synced into 1 sequence for joint processing.

A small joint schema head then scores the options. Each valid option first gathers evidence from the input. Field vectors then cross-attend across the full context to compute confidence scores. Cloudflare froze the Qwen3 backbone and trained LoRA adapters. Training combined label-smoothed cross-entropy with Brier score calibration.

Supported inputs on Workers AI, per the developer docs:

  • Images: up to 4, PNG, JPEG or WebP, 64 to 1,024 tokens each
  • Audio: up to 4 clips, WAV or MP3, 300 seconds each, about 780 tokens per minute
  • Video: up to 2 clips, MP4 or WebM, 60 seconds each, sampled at 2 frames per second
  • Questions: 1 to 64 per request

Cloudflare reports text decisions in about 130 ms at the median and images in about 150 ms. A 21-second video with sound scores in about 1.5 seconds.

How does Clef-omni perform on benchmarks?

Cloudflare compared Clef-omni against Clef, Clef-flash and Jev on its Decision Index run. Clef-omni leads on intent classification: 94.8 macro-F1 on BANKING77 and 97.7 on CLINC150+OOS. It also tops Amazon ESCI at 57.8.

It trails elsewhere. Home appliances case-exact accuracy is 69.3, versus 97.73 for Clef-flash. When2Call accuracy is 63.3, versus 80.97 for Jev. On TypeSafe’s workflow evals, Clef-omni scores below Clef in all 5 reported metrics.

&&

Clef-omni vs Clef vs Clef-flash vs Jev FeatureClef-omniClefClef-flashJevDeveloperCloudflareCloudflareCloudflareTypeSafe AIParameters30B total, 3B active (MoE)27B dense9B denseNot disclosedBase modelQwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-InstructQwen3.8-27BQwen3.5-9BNot disclosedInputsText, image, audio, videoText, image, video framesText, image, video framesText (per Cloudflare)Hosted context64,000 tokens64k24k (256k self-hosted)Not disclosed by TypeSafe (Cloudflare cites 32k)Input price per M tokens$0.15$0.24$0.038$0.042LicenseApache-2.0Apache-2.0Apache-2.0API only, early accessBANKING77 (macro-F1)94.894.2090.9379.74CLINC150+OOS (macro-F1)97.797.4366.7789.27When2Call (accuracy)63.372.3765.5880.97BRIGHT (nDCG@10)42.045.9139.2647.52Invoice processing, primary action82.086.273.383.1

Benchmark scores are from Cloudflare’s announcement and were not independently verified.

How much faster is Clef?

Cloudflare moved hosted Clef to SGLang and tuned its serving stack. No new weights were released. Median latency fell from 262 ms to 152 ms at about 800 tokens, a 1.7x gain. At about 3,400 tokens it fell from 616 ms to 305 ms, a 2.0x gain. At about 16,000 tokens it dropped from 2,721 ms to 1,635 ms. Clef support lands in SGLang 0.5.22.

Key Takeaways
  • Clef-omni scores text, images, audio and video in 1 decision call.
  • It is a 30B-A3B MoE on Qwen3-Omni, Apache-2.0, at $0.15 per million tokens.
  • Clef-flash now costs $0.038, under Jev’s $0.042, with 24k hosted context.
  • Hosted Clef is 1.7x to 2.0x faster at the median after moving to SGLang.
  • Clef-omni wins intent tasks but trails Clef on reasoning and workflow evals.

Check out the Cloudflare announcement, model weights and Workers AI docs. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well.

items.title: Amazon’s Bargains Include Its Stock
items.summary: It’s the quiet before the storm of earnings season, which starts in a week or two. While we wait for the third-quarter updates, here’s a thought: Investor enthusiasm for semiconductor stocks and blue-sky vision companies like SpaceX appears to have sucked money out of stocks of long-established tech companies. Some are now trading at bargain-basement prices. We’re thinking specifically of Amazon, whose stock really deserves a bit more love. We know the gripes: Like Alphabet and Meta, Amazon is spending an absolute ton—$220 billion this year alone—on capital expenditures to build out its AI data center capacity. That’s not without risk, for sure: The investment depends on business demand for AI services taking off. Even so, that can’t justify Amazon trading at a discount to Walmart, as it has done for the last 18 months or so. Walmart is expected to grow revenue this year by about 5.6%—about a third of Amazon’s estimated growth rate. And yet Amazon is trading at about 29 times forward earnings, compared with 37 times for Walmart, according to Koyfin data.

items.title: Ordered set partitions and formulas in permute
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on From the bottom of the heap — R posts, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

I’ve been giving permute a bit of attention recently. Two additions should make it easier to set up permutation tests: an option for ordered set partitions, and formulas for specifying plots and blocks. That’s a rather grand name for the first addition, so let’s start with what it does.

These changes are in the development version. To follow along, install it from my R-universe:

install.packages("permute", repos = c(
  "https://gavinsimpson.r-universe.dev",
  "https://cloud.r-project.org"
))
Same groups, fewer permutations

The jackal data that come with permute contain mandible lengths, in millimetres, for male and female golden jackals. They’re also used in the package vignette. Let’s ask whether mean mandible length differs between the sexes.

library("permute")
data(jackal, package = "permute")

table(jackal$Sex)
  Male Female 
    10     10

We could shuffle all the observation indices and use them to rearrange the sex labels. With the default Within(type = "free") design, the number of possible index permutations is:

numPerms(nrow(jackal), control = how(within = Within(type = "free")))
[1] 2.432902e+18

But swapping a pair of males, or a pair of females, leaves the group labels unchanged. If our statistic is a difference of means, we haven’t created a different result by doing that.

What we need are the distinct ways of assigning the observations to two labelled groups, keeping the group sizes fixed. That’s the ordered set partition. Here, ordered means the groups are distinguishable — male and female have different roles — rather than that observations have to be sorted inside each group.

The new option is type = "partition" which belongs in Plots(). I’ll use the new formula interface here too; ~ Sex says to get the grouping variable from data, to which we pass jackal:

ctrl <- how(
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ Sex, type = "partition"),
  data = jackal
)

numPerms(nrow(jackal), control = ctrl)
[1] 184756

That’s quite a reduction from all the possible permutations of the observation indices! In general, if the group sizes are , the number of distinct assignments is

The group sizes come from the data; they don’t have to be equal.

We still get observation indices back from permute, so the usual indexing workflow works:

set.seed(42)
p <- shuffle(nrow(jackal), control = ctrl)

table(jackal$Sex[p])
  Male Female 
    10     10

The labels have been shuffled, but their counts haven’t changed. Within the returned index vector, observations that originally had the same label retain their relative order. This gives us one representative for each distinct arrangement of the labels, instead of all the index permutations that would produce it.

There’s an important difference from Plots(type = "free"): that option moves whole plots as intact units. The partition option rearranges group membership. how() also selects Within(type = "none") automatically for a partition design. Asking to shuffle within these groups as well would put back the redundant orderings we’re trying to leave out, so other within-plot types aren’t allowed.

A permutation test with lm()

permute isn’t just for use with the vegan package — it was designed to be agnostic to the underlying model or test statistic. As an illustration, let’s fit a linear model to the jackal data:

fit <- lm(Length ~ Sex, data = jackal)
coef(fit)
(Intercept)   SexFemale 
      113.4        -4.8

The intercept is the mean for males, the reference level. The second coefficient is the female mean minus the male mean: females have mandibles that are, on average, 4.8 mm shorter in these data.

For a permutation test, we’ll keep the lengths where they are and shuffle the sex labels. We then refit the model for each assignment and save that same coefficient. Under the null hypothesis, we’re treating the labels as exchangeable among observations; this needs to be a reasonable assumption for the data we’re analysing.

set.seed(42)
perms <- shuffleSet(nrow(jackal), nset = 999, control = ctrl)

observed <- unname(coef(fit)[2])
null <- apply(perms, 1, function(i) {
  permuted <- jackal
  permuted$Sex <- jackal$Sex[i]
  unname(coef(lm(Length ~ Sex, data = permuted))[2])
})

shuffleSet() gives us a matrix with one assignment per row. We’re sampling a manageable set here, rather than fitting a model for every possible assignment.

Here’s what those coefficients look like, with the observed difference marked in red:

hist(null, breaks = "FD", main = "",
     xlab = "Female minus male mean mandible length (mm)",
     col = "grey85", border = "white")
abline(v = observed, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

Permutation distribution of the female-minus-male mean mandible length. The red line marks the observed difference.

For a two-sided test, we count differences at least as large as the observed one in absolute value:

tol <- sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)
p_value <- (1 + sum(abs(null) >= abs(observed) - tol)) /
  (nrow(perms) + 1)

c(difference_mm = observed, p_value = p_value)
difference_mm       p_value 
       -4.800         0.005

The small tolerance includes ties that might otherwise be missed because of floating-point arithmetic in the model fits. Adding one to the numerator and denominator includes the observed result in this Monte Carlo test. The p-value is an estimate based on the sampled assignments, so it will vary with the random seed and the number requested.

If you don’t need to build a design explicitly, shufflePartition(jackal$Sex) and shufflePartitionSet(jackal$Sex, nset = 999) are handy shortcuts. There’s also allPartitions() for complete enumeration when the assignment space is small enough. As with allPerms(), it leaves out the observed assignment by default; use control = how(observed = TRUE) to include it.

Less typing with formulas

The formula interface works for both plot strata and blocks. To show the two together, let’s use the dune meadow data from vegan. dune contains the species data and dune.env contains the matching environmental variables.

Suppose we want to look at the association between vegetation and soil A1 horizon thickness, allowing comparisons only among sites with the same management and land use. We can express that restriction directly:

library("vegan")
data(dune, package = "vegan")
data(dune.env, package = "vegan")

formula_ctrl <- how(
  plots = Plots(strata = ~ Management / Use),
  blocks = ~ Management,
  data = dune.env
)

~ Management / Use creates a grouping factor for the observed combinations of management and land use. Plots() defaults to type = "none", while Within() defaults to "free", so sites are shuffled within those combinations. The blocks say that sites must also stay within their management category. The plot restriction already implies that here, but writing out both makes the hierarchy clear.

These restrictions assume sites are exchangeable within each management–use combination; grouping them this way doesn’t account for any remaining spatial dependence.

We can check where an actual shuffle sends the observations:

set.seed(42)
i <- shuffle(nrow(dune.env), control = formula_ctrl)

all(getBlocks(formula_ctrl)[i] == getBlocks(formula_ctrl))
[1] TRUE
all(getStrata(formula_ctrl)[i] == getStrata(formula_ctrl))
[1] TRUE

Both the blocks and plot groups are respected. We can use the design directly in a vegan analysis. Here I partial out the management–use groups in an RDA, then test the additional association with A1 horizon thickness:

env <- dune.env
env$group <- getStrata(formula_ctrl)
ord <- rda(dune ~ A1 + Condition(group), data = env)

set.seed(42)
anova(ord, permutations = formula_ctrl)
Permutation test for rda under reduced model
Blocks:  Management 
Plots: Management/Use, plot permutation: none
Permutation: free
Number of permutations: 199

Model: rda(formula = dune ~ A1 + Condition(group), data = env)
         Df Variance      F Pr(>F)
Model     1   4.3492 1.3265  0.225
Residual  8  26.2298

There’s little evidence of an additional association in this particular analysis. Some of the groups contain only one site, so those sites can’t move at all under this design. Restrictions matter, both for what question we’re asking and for how much information is available to answer it.

A couple of details are worth keeping in mind when writing these formulas. They describe grouping factors, not model terms: ~ Management + Use, ~ Management:Use, and ~ Management / Use all produce groups from the combinations of those variables. The slash doesn’t create an extra level in permute’s hierarchy.

Also, when Plots() is inside how(), supply data to how(), as above. If you’re constructing Plots() on its own, it can take its own data argument:

plot_groups <- Plots(strata = ~ Management / Use, data = dune.env)

The existing factor interface still works, so there’s no need to rewrite old code. But I find the formulas easier to read, especially when grouping variables need to be combined. You can find the details in the design documentation, and I’d welcome feedback on either addition through the issue tracker.

There are also new helpers for working with the resulting permutations: permutations() returns shuffled values directly, while permutator() lets you step through a set of permutations. I’ll show those in a follow-up post.

items.title: What is Decision 3.0? vLLM Semantic Router’s New Open Decision Models
items.summary: The vLLM Semantic Router team has released Decision 3.0 , a family of multimodal decision models. Decision 3.0 multimodal decision models read text, JSON and images, then answer typed questions about them. There are 5 sizes, from 0.8B to 27B, all under Apache-2.0. For developers, this is a fast way to classify, route and gate requests without parsing generated text. TL;DR Size: 5 models: d3-lite (0.85B), d3-nano (2.21B), d3-mini (4.54B), d3-flash (8.39B), d3 (26.09B). Context length: not disclosed. Runs on: latency measured on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X GPU. BF16 weights; no official quantized variants listed. Performance: the 27B d3 leads both the text and vision tables in its card, but on internal evaluation. Best: 97.7 on KIE (CORD+FUNSD) document extraction (d3). Worst: 34.1 on R-Bench-M (d3). Bottom line: Best: a 9B model now beats last generation’s 27B. Worst: scores are self-reported against live board data. What is Decision 3.0? Decision 3.0 is a set of open decision models from vLLM Semantic Router that return probabilities instead of text. You pass a state (text or JSON), optional images, and named questions. Each question is a Choice, a Yes/No, or a Score on a scale. The model answers all questions in one call and returns a probability for every answer. This is the ‘system one’ pattern for routers and guardrails. Instead of prompting an LLM and parsing its output, you get calibrated scores you can threshold. How does d3 work? Each model is a fine-tune of a Qwen base. The 27B d3 is built on Qwen3.8-27B . The smaller 4 build on Qwen3.5 checkpoints at 0.8B, 2B, 4B and 9B. Every size carries a vision encoder: 0.10B in d3-lite, 0.33B in d3-nano and d3-mini, and 0.46B in d3-flash and d3. Requests accept several PNG, JPEG or WebP images, each read at up to 1.6 megapixels. Every question sees all images. Each question gets its own forward pass over the input. Install targets transformers==5.17.0 , and the optional flash-linear-attention package speeds up the linear-attention layers. Loading needs trust_remote_code=True . How does Decision 3.0 perform on benchmarks? Through the model card, the research team state the Jev Decision Index 0.3.1, a board that ranks open reproductions of TypeSafe’s Jev decision system. d3 numbers are the team’s internal evaluation. On text, d3 scores 64.1, ahead of Perplexity Decider v1.1 (62.8) and Jev (60.1). One caveat: Torchcast Decision 27B posts a higher public-suite score (65.1 vs 64.9). On the vision board, d3 scores 71.6 against 70.6 for Perplexity Decider v1.1. The size story is the strongest part. d3-flash (9B) scores 59.0, above Decision 2.0’s 27B at 55.9. On the public suite, gains over Decision 2.0 range from +8.0 (27B) to +15.1 (0.8B). Class leadership is not uniform, though: d3-mini (4B) and d3-flash (9B) lead both their text and vision tables. d3-lite (0.8B) leads on text but ranks 3rd on vision (41.1, behind JPT-0.8B at 42.1). d3-nano (2B) leads its vision table but trails LiquidAI d1-3B on text (35.8 vs 40.1). On public vision tasks, d3 scores 97.3 on InfographicVQA and 89.9 on Mind2Web, both approximate rebuilds. It is weaker on MMMU-Pro vision (46.2) and Hateful Memes moderation (44.6). && How fast are the models? items.summary_html:
The vLLM Semantic Router team has released Decision 3.0, a family of multimodal decision models. Decision 3.0 multimodal decision models read text, JSON and images, then answer typed questions about them. There are 5 sizes, from 0.8B to 27B, all under Apache-2.0. For developers, this is a fast way to classify, route and gate requests without parsing generated text.

TL;DR
  • Size: 5 models: d3-lite (0.85B), d3-nano (2.21B), d3-mini (4.54B), d3-flash (8.39B), d3 (26.09B). Context length: not disclosed.
  • Runs on: latency measured on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X GPU. BF16 weights; no official quantized variants listed.
  • Performance: the 27B d3 leads both the text and vision tables in its card, but on internal evaluation.
  • Best: 97.7 on KIE (CORD+FUNSD) document extraction (d3).
  • Worst: 34.1 on R-Bench-M (d3).
  • Bottom line:
    • Best: a 9B model now beats last generation’s 27B.
    • Worst: scores are self-reported against live board data.
What is Decision 3.0?

Decision 3.0 is a set of open decision models from vLLM Semantic Router that return probabilities instead of text. You pass a state (text or JSON), optional images, and named questions. Each question is a Choice, a Yes/No, or a Score on a scale. The model answers all questions in one call and returns a probability for every answer.

This is the ‘system one’ pattern for routers and guardrails. Instead of prompting an LLM and parsing its output, you get calibrated scores you can threshold.

How does d3 work?

Each model is a fine-tune of a Qwen base. The 27B d3 is built on Qwen3.8-27B. The smaller 4 build on Qwen3.5 checkpoints at 0.8B, 2B, 4B and 9B.

Every size carries a vision encoder: 0.10B in d3-lite, 0.33B in d3-nano and d3-mini, and 0.46B in d3-flash and d3. Requests accept several PNG, JPEG or WebP images, each read at up to 1.6 megapixels. Every question sees all images.

Each question gets its own forward pass over the input. Install targets transformers==5.17.0, and the optional flash-linear-attention package speeds up the linear-attention layers. Loading needs trust_remote_code=True.

How does Decision 3.0 perform on benchmarks?

Through the model card, the research team state the Jev Decision Index 0.3.1, a board that ranks open reproductions of TypeSafe’s Jev decision system. d3 numbers are the team’s internal evaluation.

On text, d3 scores 64.1, ahead of Perplexity Decider v1.1 (62.8) and Jev (60.1). One caveat: Torchcast Decision 27B posts a higher public-suite score (65.1 vs 64.9). On the vision board, d3 scores 71.6 against 70.6 for Perplexity Decider v1.1.

The size story is the strongest part. d3-flash (9B) scores 59.0, above Decision 2.0’s 27B at 55.9. On the public suite, gains over Decision 2.0 range from +8.0 (27B) to +15.1 (0.8B).

Class leadership is not uniform, though:

  • d3-mini (4B) and d3-flash (9B) lead both their text and vision tables.
  • d3-lite (0.8B) leads on text but ranks 3rd on vision (41.1, behind JPT-0.8B at 42.1).
  • d3-nano (2B) leads its vision table but trails LiquidAI d1-3B on text (35.8 vs 40.1).

On public vision tasks, d3 scores 97.3 on InfographicVQA and 89.9 on Mind2Web, both approximate rebuilds. It is weaker on MMMU-Pro vision (46.2) and Hateful Memes moderation (44.6).

&&

How fast are the models?

Medians below are for 1 request at a time on 1 AMD Instinct MI325X, per each card:

  • d3-nano: 21.7 ms text, 92.0 ms with an image
  • d3-lite: 23.5 ms text, 60.7 ms with an image
  • d3-mini: 28.5 ms text, 115.0 ms with an image
  • d3-flash: 29.7 ms text, 171.8 ms with an image
  • d3: 84 ms text, 342 ms with an image

All models were trained on AMD Instinct MI325X GPUs.

How does d3 compare with other decision models?   • 5 Apache-2.0 decision models, 0.8B to 27B, all with image input.
  • d3 (27B) tops its text (64.1) and vision (71.6) tables, on internal evals.
  • The 9B d3-flash (59.0) beats Decision 2.0’s 27B (55.9).
  • The 0.8B and 2B models do not lead every board.
  • Median text latency runs 21.7 to 84 ms on 1 MI325X.

items.summary: You open the take-home on a Thursday night. The README is smooth. A demo script prints three green lines, and a note at the bottom says a model "handled the edge cases." You close the pasted chat, stop the process, and start it again. The third request returns 200. The spec you wrote on Monday said 429. The polish was never the contract. It was a scratch pad that remembered the prompt better than the program did. That is the failure mode showing up in AI-assisted submissions right now. Fluency got cheap. A restart did not. If you hire people who will ship code a model helped draft, the take-home has to separate those two facts before a live interview is spent on a demo that only works inside one session. Buy a contract, not a tour You are not buying a tour of a free model. You are buying a small program you can re-check without the author's laptop, the author's transcript, or the author's confidence. A submission that only runs while the chat is open is a demo. A submission whose tests still mean the same thing after a new process is a candidate. You are not asking them to rebuild a machine from a blank image. You are asking whether the number 2 still means 2 when the chat window is closed. Write the prompt so the spec is a file in the repo. Tell them a model may draft the implementation. Tell them the draft is untrusted until a test they also commit fails for the right reason and then passes for the right reason. If they cannot explain a red assertion without scrolling a transcript, they do not own the work yet. Order matters more than tone. Ask for the tests before the implementation, and ask the README to name one case the tests do not cover. People who only steered a model often cannot name a hole. People who wrote the spec usually can, and the hole they name tells you how they think once the happy path is already green. Here is a prompt you can send. Treat it as a proposal you still need to edit for your stack, not as a record of a live loop. Build a tiny retry gate. POST /retry?key=... may succeed at most 2 times for a given key. The third call returns 429 and must not increment the counter. GET /retry?key=... returns the number already used. State lives on disk. Stopping the process and starting it again must not reset the count. Do not commit secrets, tokens, or a model transcript. You may draft with a model. Commit the tests first. In the README, name one case the tests do not cover, and narrate the red-green sequence in your own words. Commit timestamps are not evidence. They can be rewritten. The narration line is doing quiet work. Git history looks like proof until someone rebases. A short paragraph in the candidate's own words is harder to fake with a paste, and it gives you something concrete to ask about on the call. A sample you can fail on purpose The Python below is an unexecuted sample, not a benchmark and not a hiring key. It shows the shape of a pass so your rubric has a concrete object. Run it, break it, and only then decide whether it belongs in your packet. # gate.py — sample solution, not measured on a hosted box import json from pathlib import Path class RetryGate : def __init__ ( self , root : Path , limit : int = 2 ): self . root = root self . limit = limit self . root . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) def _path ( self , key : str ) -> Path : safe = "" . join ( ch for ch in key if ch . isalnum () or ch in " -_ " )[: 64 ] if not safe : raise ValueError ( " empty key " ) return self . root / f " { safe } .json " def used ( self , key : str ) -> int : path = self . _path ( key ) if not path . exists (): return 0 data = json . loads ( path . read_text ()) return int ( data [ " used " ]) def allow ( self , key : str ) -> bool : path = self . _path ( key ) used = self . used ( key ) if used >= self . limit : return False # Teaching stand-in, not a database. Two writers can still race. path . write_text ( json . dumps ({ " used " : used + 1 })) return True A new object pointed at the same directory is the restart. You do not need a cluster to teach that idea. You need a file that outlives the process, and a test that constructs a second object instead of reusing the first. # test_gate.py — unexecuted example from gate import RetryGate def test_third_call_sticks_after_new_object ( tmp_path ): first = RetryGate ( tmp_path , limit = 2 ) assert first . allow ( " job-9 " ) is True assert first . allow ( " job-9 " ) is True assert first . used ( " job-9 " ) == 2 restarted = RetryGate ( tmp_path , limit = 2 ) assert restarted . allow ( " job-9 " ) is False assert restarted . used ( " job-9 " ) == 2 def test_rejected_key_does_not_create_a_file ( tmp_path ): gate = RetryGate ( tmp_path , limit = 2 ) try : gate . allow ( " *** " ) except ValueError : pass assert list ( tmp_path . glob ( " *.json " )) == [] The second test is the one hurried drafts skip. A model that only heard "store the count" will happily write a file from raw user input, or it will swallow a bad key and return false without saying why. You want the exception, and you want the directory empty afterward. That is a small contract, and it is enough for this exercise. python -m pytest test_gate.py -q # on the box, after the process is listening: curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} \n " -X POST "http://127.0.0.1:8080/retry?key=job-9" curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8080/retry?key=job-9" # stop the process, start it again, POST until you expect 429 If the count returns to zero after the stop, the green demo was session memory. Fail that behavior even if the README is kind. If the third call stays at 429 and the stored count stays at 2, you have a pass on the only state claim this task makes. A reviewer script keeps you from grading by vibe. This one is also unexecuted proposal code. Point it at the key file after your restart, and let the exit code be the note you keep. # review_check.py — proposal, unexecuted import json , sys from pathlib import Path def main () -> None : used = int ( json . loads ( Path ( sys . argv [ 1 ]). read_text ())[ " used " ]) if used != 2 : raise SystemExit ( f " expected used=2 after restart, got { used } " ) print ( " restart count held " ) if __name__ == " __main__ " : main () python review_check.py /var/lib/retry-gate/job-9.json Do not treat a missing file as a clever zero. A missing file after two successful posts means the gate wrote somewhere you are not looking, which is a fail with a different name. Use the free door for the draft, not for the spec You can run this exercise on a laptop. The reason to involve a hosted box is narrower than a launch post implies. Candidates should not have to open a cloud account, pick a region, and wait on a billing ticket before they can show you a restart. A free server option removes that toll booth. Free model access lets them draft without you pretending the draft is the submission. Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode fits this workflow only as that pair of conveniences: free model access for the scratch pad, and a free server so the restart is not "trust my laptop." Repeat those two availability claims and stop. They are not a chip count, a model menu, a token cap, or a promise that the free tier will look the same next quarter. This article does not freeze any of those. Before you send the prompt, open the current limits page and copy only the constraints you just read. If the page is vague, say that in the task. Inventing a machine size to sound precise is how take-homes become unfair. Use the model the way you would use a whiteboard that talks. Sketch RetryGate if you want. Then throw the sketch at the test that already existed. If the test was written after the model was already green, you graded a memory. The README narration is where that slip shows up. A candidate who says "I asserted 429 because the chat said the third call should fail" has described a scratch pad. A candidate who says "I asserted 429 because the prompt defined a budget of 2, and I checked the file after a new object" has described a spec. If you want a single next step, read MonkeyCode's current notes on free model access and the free server, paste the limits you actually see into the prompt, and send the task to one person before you standardize it. Score the restart, then stop Read the test file before the README. Assertions that restate the prompt in code mean the candidate understood the contract. Assertions that only check for a dict key named ok mean they tested a shape the scratch pad likes. You can feel the difference quickly, which is the point of keeping the task small. Then restart, once, on the box named in the prompt. A pass that exists only inside one process is a partial. You may still talk to a partial if the role is early-career and the writing is honest. Do not relabel it as a pass on state. Honesty looks like a README that says "two processes can race on the same key, and I did not take a lock." Evasion looks like a transcript dropped under docs/ and a sentence that says the model verified the edges. Keep your own review inside the prompt. A clever extra endpoint is not credit if /retry forgets its count. A plain function that survives the restart is a pass. You are hiring for ownership of a contract, not for taste. The failures repeat, and they are boring, which is useful. One candidate commits the transcript and calls it design notes. Another keeps the count in a global, so the restart check fails immediately. Another builds the storage path with string concatenation aimed at a shell, so the key is no longer just data. Another mocks allow() and asserts the mock was called, which proves the test runner, not the disk. Any one of those earns a short note. You do not owe a novel, and you should not soften the note because the prose around the bug was confident. There is a subtler miss. The implementation writes the JSON through a temp file and os.replace , which is a fair durability improvement, but the tests never stop the process mid-write. If the README claims crash safety you did not ask for, ask them to show the test or withdraw the claim. Extra claims without extra checks are the same scratch-pad habit in a nicer coat. Who should leave this on the shelf Skip the task when the role is a pure algorithm screen. A restart file adds noise when you only wanted to watch someone reason about a graph. Skip it when policy forbids sending exercise text to a third-party model, including a free one. Skip it when you need a named uptime target, a specific machine, or a frozen token budget. None of those are established here, and a free box that shifts under the candidate will punish them for a reason that is not theirs. The filter also misses collaboration, deletion, and design depth. A person can pass test_third_call_sticks_after_new_object and still be a poor teammate. Use the hour to see whether they can keep a spec off the scratch pad. Then interview the human. Free access is a door, not a measurement. If the door is closed on review day, reschedule. Do not lower the rubric because the box was slow, and do not raise it because the draft sounded sure. The spec you froze before the draft is the only sentence that should still be true after the reboot.

# gate.py — sample solution, not measured on a hosted box
import json
from pathlib import Path

class RetryGate:
    def __init__(self, root: Path, limit: int = 2):
        self.root = root
        self.limit = limit
        self.root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    def _path(self, key: str) -> Path:
        safe = "".join(ch for ch in key if ch.isalnum() or ch in "-_")[:64]
        if not safe:
            raise ValueError("empty key")
        return self.root / f"{safe}.json"

    def used(self, key: str) -> int:
        path = self._path(key)
        if not path.exists():
            return 0
        data = json.loads(path.read_text())
        return int(data["used"])

    def allow(self, key: str) -> bool:
        path = self._path(key)
        used = self.used(key)
        if used >= self.limit:
            return False
        # Teaching stand-in, not a database. Two writers can still race.
        path.write_text(json.dumps({"used": used + 1}))

    assert first.used("job-9") == 2
    restarted = RetryGate(tmp_path, limit=2)
    assert restarted.allow("job-9") is False
    assert restarted.used("job-9") == 2

    gate = RetryGate(tmp_path, limit=2)
    try:
        gate.allow("***")
    except ValueError:

    assert list(tmp_path.glob("*.json")) == []

The README narration is where that slip shows up. A candidate who says "I asserted 429 because the chat said the third call should fail" has described a scratch pad. A candidate who says "I asserted 429 because the prompt defined a budget of 2, and I checked the file after a new object" has described a spec.

If you want a single next step, read MonkeyCode's current notes on free model access and the free server, paste the limits you actually see into the prompt, and send the task to one person before you standardize it.

Score the restart, then stop

Read the test file before the README. Assertions that restate the prompt in code mean the candidate understood the contract. Assertions that only check for a dict key named ok mean they tested a shape the scratch pad likes. You can feel the difference quickly, which is the point of keeping the task small.

Then restart, once, on the box named in the prompt. A pass that exists only inside one process is a partial. You may still talk to a partial if the role is early-career and the writing is honest. Do not relabel it as a pass on state.

Honesty looks like a README that says "two processes can race on the same key, and I did not take a lock." Evasion looks like a transcript dropped under docs/ and a sentence that says the model verified the edges.

Keep your own review inside the prompt. A clever extra endpoint is not credit if /retry forgets its count. A plain function that survives the restart is a pass. You are hiring for ownership of a contract, not for taste.

The failures repeat, and they are boring, which is useful. One candidate commits the transcript and calls it design notes. Another keeps the count in a global, so the restart check fails immediately. Another builds the storage path with string concatenation aimed at a shell, so the key is no longer just data.

Another mocks allow() and asserts the mock was called, which proves the test runner, not the disk. Any one of those earns a short note. You do not owe a novel, and you should not soften the note because the prose around the bug was confident.

There is a subtler miss. The implementation writes the JSON through a temp file and os.replace, which is a fair durability improvement, but the tests never stop the process mid-write. If the README claims crash safety you did not ask for, ask them to show the test or withdraw the claim. Extra claims without extra checks are the same scratch-pad habit in a nicer coat.

Who should leave this on the shelf

Skip the task when the role is a pure algorithm screen. A restart file adds noise when you only wanted to watch someone reason about a graph. Skip it when policy forbids sending exercise text to a third-party model, including a free one.

Skip it when you need a named uptime target, a specific machine, or a frozen token budget. None of those are established here, and a free box that shifts under the candidate will punish them for a reason that is not theirs.

The filter also misses collaboration, deletion, and design depth. A person can pass test_third_call_sticks_after_new_object and still be a poor teammate. Use the hour to see whether they can keep a spec off the scratch pad. Then interview the human.

Free access is a door, not a measurement. If the door is closed on review day, reschedule. Do not lower the rubric because the box was slow, and do not raise it because the draft sounded sure. The spec you froze before the draft is the only sentence that should still be true after the reboot.

items.title: Grass Pass: Photograph to Unlock Reddit
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Grass Pass is a Chromium extension (Chrome, Edge, Brave) that blocks the sites you doomscroll on. To get them back, you have to go outside and prove it You maintain a block list (by default, X, Reddit, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, YouTube). Opening one of such websites takes you to a blocked page with a "Go touch grass" button. A task like "photograph three leaves that look different from each other" is initiated. You can upload a picture from your phone or use your webcam to take each one. Every picture is examined by a vision model that runs on your own computer Demo The following application is deployed on Vercel Grass Pass - Demo Code Github-Link How I Built It The default model is SmolVLM-500M-Instruct, which uses Transformers.js v3 on WebGPU to operate in the browser. For models like Moondream without a browser build, there is an optional Ollama backend on localhost and an experimental "accurate" tier utilizing Qwen2-VL-2B. They are all hidden behind a single, tiny VisionBackend interface (init, askYesNo, dispose); thus the remainder of the program is unaware of which one is active. Small vision models are good at responding to a single yes/no inquiry concerning a single image, but they struggle with counting and reasoning across multiple images. Thus, every image is independently validated in order. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Grass Pass's primary design limitation is privacy, since it requires you to point a camera at your surroundings. Every picture of your garden, your street would need to be uploaded to someone's server, linked to an account and an API key, and charged for each call if you used a closed vision API. It's hardly much of a barrier if it stops functioning when the network goes down or your API credits run out. Open-weight models changed what I could build: Photos never leave the device. The only network traffic is a one-time download of model weights from Hugging Face. No server, accounts, or keys. There’s no Grass Pass backend to run or pay for, and nothing to shut down later. Swappable models. Because the weights are open, the same app can run SmolVLM in the browser, Qwen2-VL on WebGPU, or Moondream through Ollama The trade-off is that 500M-parameter model is less accurate than frontier model, which is why the design leans on narrow yes/no questions and doesn’t try to defend against a determined cheater.
items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

Grass Pass is a Chromium extension (Chrome, Edge, Brave) that blocks the sites you doomscroll on. To get them back, you have to go outside and prove it

You maintain a block list (by default, X, Reddit, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, YouTube). Opening one of such websites takes you to a blocked page with a "Go touch grass" button.

A task like "photograph three leaves that look different from each other" is initiated.

You can upload a picture from your phone or use your webcam to take each one.

Every picture is examined by a vision model that runs on your own computer

Demo

The following application is deployed on Vercel
Grass Pass - Demo

Code

Github-Link

How I Built It

The default model is SmolVLM-500M-Instruct, which uses Transformers.js v3 on WebGPU to operate in the browser.

For models like Moondream without a browser build, there is an optional Ollama backend on localhost and an experimental "accurate" tier utilizing Qwen2-VL-2B.

They are all hidden behind a single, tiny VisionBackend interface (init, askYesNo, dispose); thus the remainder of the program is unaware of which one is active.

Small vision models are good at responding to a single yes/no inquiry concerning a single image, but they struggle with counting and reasoning across multiple images. Thus, every image is independently validated in order.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Grass Pass's primary design limitation is privacy, since it requires you to point a camera at your surroundings.

Every picture of your garden, your street would need to be uploaded to someone's server, linked to an account and an API key, and charged for each call if you used a closed vision API.

It's hardly much of a barrier if it stops functioning when the network goes down or your API credits run out.

Open-weight models changed what I could build:

  • Photos never leave the device. The only network traffic is a one-time download of model weights from Hugging Face.
  • No server, accounts, or keys. There’s no Grass Pass backend to run or pay for, and nothing to shut down later.
  • Swappable models. Because the weights are open, the same app can run SmolVLM in the browser, Qwen2-VL on WebGPU, or Moondream through Ollama

The trade-off is that 500M-parameter model is less accurate than frontier model, which is why the design leans on narrow yes/no questions and doesn’t try to defend against a determined cheater.

items.title: DuckDuckGo CI/CD RCE: How a Single GitHub Workflow Could Have Backdoored Every DuckDuckGo Browser — Writeup Analysis
items.summary: Some vulnerabilities are interesting because of their complexity. Others are terrifying because of their simplicity. The GitHub Actions RCE reported against DuckDuckGo in 2026 falls firmly in the second category: one misconfigured workflow file, zero required privileges beyond a free GitHub account, and a straight path from a forked pull request to a poisoned release shipped inside every DuckDuckGo browser on the planet. This is my original analysis of a disclosed finding by independent researcher 6r1ff1n , reported through DuckDuckGo's HackerOne program (report #3619287 — full disclosure: https://hackerone.com/reports/3619287 ). What follows is my own breakdown of the technique, the attack chain, and the lessons for hunters and defenders. Analysis by Faizan Akhtar. The Discovery at a Glance In early 2026, 6r1ff1n was reviewing DuckDuckGo's public GitHub repositories when one workflow file stood out: .github/workflows/semver-label.yml in duckduckgo/content-scope-scripts — described in its own README as "shared JavaScript used within ALL DuckDuckGo browsers": Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, the Chrome and Firefox extensions, and autofill. Tens of millions of users. The workflow's job was mundane — auto-applying semantic-version labels to PRs. Its configuration was not: it triggered on pull_request_target with no access controls, no fork detection, and no approval gate, then checked out the PR's code and executed it. Any GitHub user could open a fork PR and get arbitrary code execution on DuckDuckGo's CI runner, with the workflow's secrets in the environment. The report contained four related findings, including secret exposure via sibling workflows and ten workflows across the org using the same trigger. But the headline — RCE plus a direct road into the release pipeline — is what makes this a case study. Background: Why pull_request_target Is a Loaded Gun GitHub has two pull request triggers, and confusing them is one of the most common CI/CD security mistakes in existence. The pull_request trigger runs in the context of the fork — the attacker's copy — with no access to the base repository's secrets. Safe by default. The pull_request_target trigger runs in the context of the base repository, which means it does get secrets. It exists for workflows that need secrets while handling PRs, like posting comments or applying labels. GitHub's own documented rule: never check out and execute untrusted code under this trigger, because the code comes from the attacker while the secrets come from you. The classic exploitation pattern even has a name: the "pwn request." Attacker forks the repo, plants malicious code, opens a PR, and the privileged workflow obediently runs it. DuckDuckGo's workflow was a textbook instance — except the blast radius was extraordinary. The Vulnerable Workflow The semver-label.yml workflow fired automatically on pull request events — opened, synchronized, reopened — with no conditions: no fork check, no required maintainer label, no author verification. The fatal step was the checkout: instead of the trusted base branch, the workflow checked out the PR's merge ref — the attacker's fork code merged with the base — then ran dependency installation and a build inside that directory. In Node.js, that is game over by itself: package installation executes lifecycle scripts from the checked-out code. Whoever controls package.json controls the machine. The runner operated with the base repository's privileges, with sensitive values in its environment — including an Anthropic API key and the automatic GITHUB_TOKEN , which carried pull-requests: write permission. The Attack Chain, Step by Step The full chain, reconstructed from the disclosed report: Step 1 — Fork and plant. The attacker forks content-scope-scripts and edits package.json to add a lifecycle script (auto-executed by npm during installation). A single file, a single commit. Step 2 — Open a pull request. Any trivial change justifies the PR. The pull_request_target trigger fires immediately and automatically. No maintainer approval, no label, no review needed. Step 3 — The runner checks out attacker code. The workflow checks out the PR merge ref, pulling the attacker's modified files onto the runner. Step 4 — Installation executes the payload. When the workflow runs the install step, npm executes the planted script. Attacker commands now run on the runner with the workflow's full environment — including every configured secret. Step 5 — Secret exfiltration. The script reads secrets from the environment and sends them to attacker-controlled infrastructure. Two prizes: the Anthropic API key and the GITHUB_TOKEN . Step 6 — From RCE to supply chain. This is where the finding graduates from "CI compromise" to "supply chain catastrophe." The stolen token could write pull-request metadata, so the attacker applies a semantic-version label to their own PR. On merge, the automated release pipeline — driven by those very labels — cuts a new release, producing artifacts with no code signing and no integrity verification. Step 7 — Poisoned fleet. Attacker-controlled JavaScript ships to every platform DuckDuckGo supports. The researcher later validated the finding with a safe, minimal live proof-of-concept — a non-destructive callback received from a GitHub Actions runner on the same day DuckDuckGo pushed its fix — without exfiltrating any real secrets. But the pipeline path was real, the permissions were real, and with no signing there was no safety net. An alternative path noted in the report: instead of exfiltrating during installation, the payload could have modified the trusted analysis script the workflow runs afterward — persisting the attack into the build phase. Why This One Deserves Study Three things elevate this above a routine misconfiguration report. First, the blast radius math . Most CI RCEs end at "attacker gets a cloud runner and some secrets." Here, the runner was a stepping stone into an automated release pipeline for code embedded in tens of millions of browsers. The vulnerability's severity is a function of what the pipeline publishes , not just what the runner touches . Second, the missing safety nets compounded . Unsigned releases. Broad token permissions. Ten workflows sharing the dangerous trigger across the organization. Each a small, defensible-in-isolation decision; together, a chain with every link already open. Third, the fix was one line . A fork-detection condition on the job — only running when the PR's head repository matches the base — eliminates the entire attack class while preserving function for internal PRs. Thirty seconds of configuration versus a potential compromise of an entire browser fleet. Remediation: Defense in Depth for pull_request_target Any one of these mitigations breaks the chain; mature organizations apply several: Prefer the pull_request trigger when the workflow does not strictly need secrets. No secrets, no exfiltration target. Add an explicit fork check before any checkout of PR code. Gate on a maintainer-applied label ("safe to test"), ensuring a human reviews code before the privileged workflow runs it — and ensure the label check itself can't be manipulated by the PR author. Use GitHub Environments with required reviewers for secret-handling jobs. Minimize token permissions — this token never needed pull-request write access. Sign releases and verify signatures downstream , so a compromised pipeline can't silently ship tampered artifacts. Hunting Methodology: Finding This Bug Class Yourself The methodology here is cheap, fast, and repeatable — the most valuable part for working hunters: Enumerate workflow files. For any target with a public GitHub organization, list every .github/workflows/*.yml file across every repository. This is pure reconnaissance — no interaction with the target's infrastructure. Grep for the dangerous trigger. Search for pull_request_target (and its cousin workflow_run , which has similar trust implications). Most organizations have a handful; each is a candidate. Read what gets checked out. The critical question: does the workflow check out the PR head, the merge ref, or any attacker-influenced ref? A checkout of ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} or the merge ref under a privileged trigger is the core signal. Check what executes. Look for package manager installs, build scripts, test runners, or any step that runs code from the checkout. In Node.js repos, npm install alone is sufficient. Map the secrets. Which secrets are present in the job's environment? What permissions does the token carry? The finding's severity scales with both. Trace the downstream. Does the workflow feed a release pipeline, publish packages, or deploy? A CI bug that ends at the runner is a finding; one that ends at the release artifact is a headline. The researcher also demonstrated tradecraft worth emulating: careful static analysis, a safe non-destructive live PoC (a minimal callback proving code execution on the runner, no secrets touched), contrast with a correctly-guarded workflow elsewhere, and concrete remediations. That is the anatomy of a report that gets taken seriously. Key Takeaways pull_request_target plus checkout of PR code plus execution equals remote code execution. This pattern is years old and still everywhere. Assess CI findings by what the pipeline publishes , not just what the runner exposes. Supply-chain impact is where critical severity lives. Unsigned release artifacts turn a CI compromise into a fleet compromise. Signing is the cheapest catastrophic-failure insurance in software distribution. The fix is often one line — but only if someone is reading the workflow files. Continuous, boring static review of CI configuration catches what scanners miss. For hunters: workflow enumeration is high-signal, low-noise reconnaissance. Add it to your standard checklist for any target with public repositories. Credit Full credit for the discovery goes to 6r1ff1n (HackerOne: https://hackerone.com/6r1ff1n ), who reported this through DuckDuckGo's bounty program. Original disclosed report: https://hackerone.com/reports/3619287 . This post is my own independent analysis of the technique and its lessons. Report by Faizan Akhtar — The Cyber Security Researcher

Third, the fix was one line. items.title: Trailtale: A Pocket-Sized Audio Story That Gets You Off Your Screen and Back on the Trail
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Trailtale is a local, offline walking app that turns a walk into an immersive audio story. While you move, the app plays a short story segment; when you stop, the audio pauses automatically. It also surfaces weekly nature quests and lets you confirm interesting finds with a photo, all without pulling you back to a screen. It’s built for people who want to spend more time outside without getting stuck in their phone. The idea is simple: make the walk the main experience, not a distraction from it. Code Repository: HarshitAnand1 / trailtale-touch-grass Trailtale An audio story that plays only while you walk, plus weekly nature quests. Every model runs locally — no cloud, no account, works offline. Quick Start 1. Install Python dependencies cd server pip install -r requirements.txt 2. Start the server # From the project root uvicorn server.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload 3. Open the app Visit http://localhost:8000 on your phone (or laptop browser). 4. (Optional) Set up llama.cpp for story generation # Download a Gemma model and start the llama.cpp server ./llama-server -m gemma-2b.gguf --port 8080 Without llama.cpp, the story engine returns fallback text so you can still test the full walk flow. 5. (Optional) Install Piper for TTS # See https://github.com/rhasspy/piper for installation piper --model en_US-lessac-medium --output_file test.wav <<< " Hello from the trail " Without Piper, the TTS engine generates silent placeholder audio. Architecture Phone (PWA) Host (FastAPI) ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │ Walk Gate │──────▶ │ Orchestrator … View on GitHub Project source: this includes the PWA client, FastAPI backend, quest data, and local AI pipeline. How I Built It I built Trailtale as a combination of a mobile-first PWA and a local AI backend: Frontend: a lightweight browser app in the client/ folder using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript Sensors: phone motion and GPS data are used to detect whether the user is walking or stopped Backend: FastAPI in the server/ folder orchestrates the walk flow, story queue, quests, and logs Story generation: a local model runs through llama.cpp using Gemma Voice: Piper generates spoken audio from the generated story text Quest system: weekly nature quests are stored as local JSON packs and tracked in SQLite Optional vision check: a local multimodal model can verify that a photo matches a quest item Offline-first design: the app is intended to work with no cloud service, no account, and no internet dependency This stack makes the app feel like a real walk companion rather than a web app that happens to use AI. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation mattered here because the whole product depends on privacy, local control, and flexibility. A closed API would have forced: cloud-based story generation for every segment network calls for TTS and photo verification higher cost per walk user data leaving the device With open-source tools and open-weight models, Trailtale can run locally on a phone, laptop, or a backpack setup. That means: no cloud dependency no account required no pay-per-token barrier the prompt, model, and voice can all be tuned or swapped easily For an app designed to get people to step away from screens, local open tech is not just a technical choice—it’s the product requirement. Prize Categories Gemma

Repository:

HarshitAnand1 / trailtale-touch-grass
Trailtale

Quick Start
1. Install Python dependencies 
cd server
pip install -r requirements.txt
2. Start the server 
# From the project root
uvicorn server.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload
3. Open the app

# Download a Gemma model and start the llama.cpp server

# See https://github.com/rhasspy/piper for installation
piper --model en_US-lessac-medium --output_file test.wav <<< "Hello from the trail"

How I Built It

I built Trailtale as a combination of a mobile-first PWA and a local AI backend:

  • Frontend: a lightweight browser app in the client/ folder using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
  • Sensors: phone motion and GPS data are used to detect whether the user is walking or stopped
  • Backend: FastAPI in the server/ folder orchestrates the walk flow, story queue, quests, and logs
  • Story generation: a local model runs through llama.cpp using Gemma
  • Voice: Piper generates spoken audio from the generated story text
  • Quest system: weekly nature quests are stored as local JSON packs and tracked in SQLite
  • Optional vision check: a local multimodal model can verify that a photo matches a quest item
  • Offline-first design: the app is intended to work with no cloud service, no account, and no internet dependency

This stack makes the app feel like a real walk companion rather than a web app that happens to use AI.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation mattered here because the whole product depends on privacy, local control, and flexibility.

A closed API would have forced:

  • cloud-based story generation for every segment
  • network calls for TTS and photo verification
  • higher cost per walk
  • user data leaving the device

With open-source tools and open-weight models, Trailtale can run locally on a phone, laptop, or a backpack setup. That means:

  • no cloud dependency
  • no account required
  • no pay-per-token barrier
  • the prompt, model, and voice can all be tuned or swapped easily

For an app designed to get people to step away from screens, local open tech is not just a technical choice—it’s the product requirement.
