ArgumentParser () parser . add_argument ( " --check " , required = True , type = Path ) parser . add_argument ( " --outbox " , type = Path ) args = parser . parse_args () sample = json . loads ( args . check . read_text ( encoding = " utf-8 " )) if sample . get ( " schema " ) != " waf-sample/v0 " : print ( " schema_mismatch " , file = sys . stderr ) return 2 hits = header_hits ( sample ) + pattern_hits ( sample ) if hits : print ( " never_send " , file = sys . stderr ) for hit in hits : print ( hit , file = sys . stderr ) return 2 if args . outbox : args . outbox . parent . mkdir ( parents = True , exist_ok = True ) payload = json . dumps ( sample , indent = 2 ) + " \n " args . outbox . write_text ( payload , encoding = " utf-8 " ) print ( " ok " ) return 0 if __name__ == " __main__ " : raise SystemExit ( main ()) Notice what it does not do. It does not print the match text. It does not call the network. It does not fix the rule. A gate that rewrites secrets into a prompt so the model can help redact has already lost. 4. Assert both directions Green has to mean something specific. If the job only passes on exit 0, wrap the positive case. Assert exit 2, and assert the outbox path does not exist. A test that forgets the negative path is how a deny-all bug ships. You want both. python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/positive_leak.json --outbox outbox/pos.json echo "positive_exit: $? " # spec: exit 2, stderr starts with never_send, outbox/pos.json absent python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/negative_clean.json --outbox outbox/neg.json echo "negative_exit: $? " # spec: exit 0, stdout line ok, outbox/neg.json written python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/hidden_in_comment.json --outbox outbox/hid.json echo "hidden_exit: $? " # spec: exit 2, a bearer hit on $.rule_comment, outbox/hid.json absent What does green mean in your pipeline today? If you cannot answer in one sentence, the fixture is not wired yet. Wire the hidden case first. That is the one a header-only cleanup will cheat. 5. Prevent, detect, recover Phase Control Evidence you should demand Prevent Only outbox/ may be attached to a prompt. A wrapper refuses the scratch path. Raw sample path never shows up in the assistant CLI history. Detect CI runs all three fixtures on every change to the gate. Hidden fixture goes red if someone simplifies the walker down to header keys. Recover If a raw sample already left, rotate the credential and treat the transcript as tainted. Incident note lists field names, not a second paste of values. Asking a model to forget is not recovery. I have no evidence, in this post, that any provider stored or leaked a WAF sample. The recover row exists because you cannot prove the negative after the bytes leave. Rotation does not depend on that proof. Where an assistant is allowed to sit Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach. MonkeyCode is the open-source AI development platform this draft is allowed to discuss. Two availability claims were supplied with the assignment: free model access, and a free server option. I am not pinning a token quota, a GPU shape, a time limit, or a retention promise. Those are time-sensitive, and I will not freeze a number I have not checked against a current primary page. So what is the workflow, once that disclosure is out of the way? Redact on the laptop. Diff the outbox. Then, if you still want a second pair of eyes on the rule logic, send the outbox only. Ask a narrow question: is checkout-sqli-17 matching the redacted body shape, or is the operator too wide? Do not ask it to look at the original. There is no original on that side of the line. A free server is still a server. Unless it sits in a network you operate, it belongs in the outside column of the drawing above. Generated rule text is a suggestion. A human diffs it before it is loaded. Would you reload a WAF from a chat transcript with no diff? I would not, even if the model were perfect. If you evaluate that free model access or that free server option, point either one at outbox/ and read the current data-handling terms before the first real incident. The fixture still works if you never do that. That is the test of whether this piece was worth writing. Who should skip this Do not use the script as a DLP product. It misses gzip, unlabeled base64, pcaps, and screenshots. It will also flag a documentation address you meant to publish. That false positive is acceptable for a never-send gate and annoying everywhere else. I did not measure a rate. Do not invent one in a slide. Do not feed it real customer bodies to see if it works. Synthesize. If blocked payloads are customer content under a retention schedule, the fix is not a smarter prompt. Keep the body off the machine that has a model CLI installed. Teams that need a signed data-processing agreement, or a path that never leaves the VPC, should not trial a hosted box on live samples while the paperwork catches up. Build the fixture. Then pick a host. If you cannot name the log sink, you are not ready to upload even the redacted file. What this does not prove I am not saying hosted models are unsafe for every debugging task. Redacted signatures, public write-ups, and synthetic requests are fair game. I am also not saying a self-hosted assistant becomes trusted because the binary is open source. Open code does not redact a Cookie you pasted. The gate does, or nothing does. This week's public developer discussion keeps circling one mood: models got faster, and the software around them did not grow a matching boundary. I am not reviewing those posts, and I am not treating their titles as evidence. The boundary I care about is one exit code on a file you control. The question I want in the retro Which invariant belongs in CI this week, and which layer should enforce it live? I would pin the positive fixture to exit 2, on synthetic files, in the same pipeline that lints WAF config. The live layer is a separate argument: an editor hook, an egress filter that blocks Authorization inside outbound prompt bodies, or both. A proxy you can bypass with a personal key is not enough on its own. The fixture still fails closed when someone is tired and the proxy is off. If you only adopt one line from this piece, adopt that. Exit 2 on a leak is the control. The model is optional. The scratch file is not a prompt.
items.summary_html:
I rebuilt a near-miss as a fixture, not as a named customer outage. A checkout rule fires on a POST that should have passed. The scratch file holds a Cookie, an upstream token, an email, and a comment about an office NAT bypass. The paste key is already halfway down.

That habit is the failure. A model prompt is an export. If I would not attach the scratch file to a public ticket, it does not cross a model boundary. A free host does not edit that rule.

The failure mode is the paste

I write the invariant before any prompt exists. The laptop may hold the raw sample. A local gate may read it. The outbox may not contain a secret. Anything past the outbox is outside the trust zone.

Would you drop that scratch file into a public gist so a stranger could take a look? No? Then a chat box is not a private notebook. It is an egress path with a friendly cursor.

This piece is not a vulnerability report. I did not run a vendor export, and I am not claiming a WAF product leaked anything. The human path is untested until a fixture fails closed.

Trust boundaries, drawn small

Keep four zones, and keep them boring. The workstation is inside: it already has the sample, which you can encrypt and wipe. The gate is inside too: it prints reason codes and refuses to write an outbox file on a hit.

Reason codes name the field. They must not echo the value. A CI log that reprints an Authorization header is the same leak with extra steps. Which log pipeline scrapes stderr on your runner? Know that before you add a helpful debug print.

The outbox is the only artifact allowed to leave. If a file is not in the outbox, it is not a prompt. The hosted model, and any free server you did not build, sit outside. They can discuss a redacted signature. They do not get raw on-call bytes.

scratch file --> local gate --fail closed--> stderr codes (field names only)
                    |
                    +--only if clean--> outbox/ --> hosted assistant

A free server does not collapse that drawing. If you did not provision the box, own the disk, and name the log sink, treat it as a third party. I am not describing a product topology. I am describing the default until a data-flow diagram says otherwise.

What a blocked request quietly carries

People shrug and call it just a WAF sample. Look again. Headers often carry Authorization, Cookie, X-Api-Key, or an upstream token stuffed into X-Internal-Token. The body excerpt can hold an email, a phone, or a long digit run.

The rule comment is worse than the request. That is where bypass notes, office CIDRs, and a copied basic-auth line go to live. The match context is frequently the secret itself, because the engine shows the bytes that fired.

Which of those do you want in a transcript you cannot delete on your own clock? I want none of them. The table is the decision, not the mood.

Field Send to a model? Reason rule_id Yes Identifier, not a credential Header names with values already replaced Yes Shape without secrets Raw Cookie or Authorization No Session or bearer material Rule comment with a bypass CIDR or copied secret No, until redacted Topology plus credential Synthetic body you generated Yes Not customer content Customer body excerpt No Content, and often a token

I am not claiming SafeLine, ModSecurity, or any other engine leaks by default. The stand-in schema is waf-sample/v0. I made it up so the fixture has a contract. Map your real export before you trust a green check.

1. Pin the invariant

Fail closed. A sample with a denylisted header, a PEM private-key banner, a bearer-shaped string, an email, or an AKIA access-key shape must not produce an outbox file. Exit 2 is the passing result for that case.

A green job on a leaky sample means the control is installed backwards. Would you celebrate a firewall test that only passes when the deny rule is deleted? Same energy.

Positive fixture: secrets present. Spec: exit 2, no outbox write. Negative fixture: high-risk patterns already gone. Spec: exit 0, outbox written. Hidden fixture: headers look clean, secret sits in rule_comment. Spec: exit 2, hit path under $.rule_comment.

I have not executed this template in the environment that will publish the post. Those exits are the specification, not a measured run. Do not cite them as a benchmark. Python 3.11 or newer, standard library only. I am not pinning a third-party scanner I did not install.

2. Lay down three synthetic samples

Positive. Obviously fake. Still enough to trip the gate. Save it as fixtures/positive_leak.json.

{
  "schema": "waf-sample/v0",
  "rule_id": "checkout-sqli-17",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "Bearer EXAMPLE.not.a.secret",
    "Cookie": "session=example-session-value",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body_excerpt": "email=ada@example.com",
  "rule_comment": "office bypass note removed from this fixture on purpose"
}

Negative. This is what done looks like. Save it as fixtures/negative_clean.json.

{
  "schema": "waf-sample/v0",
  "rule_id": "checkout-sqli-17",
  "headers": {
    "Authorization": "[redacted]",
    "Cookie": "[redacted]",
    "Content-Type": "application/json"
  },
  "body_excerpt": "email field removed",
  "rule_comment": "bypass note removed"
}

Hidden. A header denylist alone will miss it. That miss is the test. Save it as fixtures/hidden_in_comment.json.

{
  "schema": "waf-sample/v0",
  "rule_id": "checkout-sqli-17",
  "headers": { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  "body_excerpt": "id=1",
  "rule_comment": "copied snippet still had Bearer EXAMPLE.not.a.secret"
}

Do not substitute a real customer capture to make the demo better. The walker also does not understand partial redaction. If an @ remains in a field, that sample is not the negative case, and the gate should stay red.

3. Drop in the gate

Unexecuted template. Read it before you run it. If your samples are gzip, pcap, or screenshots, this file will not save you. It only walks JSON strings.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""never_send_gate.py — unexecuted template. Spec, not a measured run.

Stand-in schema: waf-sample/v0. Python 3.11+ stdlib only.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

DENY_HEADERS = {
    "authorization",
    "proxy-authorization",
    "cookie",
    "set-cookie",
    "x-api-key",
    "x-internal-token",
}

PATTERNS = [
    ("pem", re.compile(r"-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----")),
    ("bearer", re.compile(r"(?i)\bbearer\s+\S{8,}")),
    ("email", re.compile(r"[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}")),
    ("aws_access_key_shape", re.compile(r"\bAKIA[0-9A-Z]{16}\b")),
]

REDACTED = "[redacted]"


def walk_strings(value, path="$"):
    if isinstance(value, str):
        yield path, value
    elif isinstance(value, dict):
        for key, item in value.items():
            yield from walk_strings(item, f"{path}.{key}")
    elif isinstance(value, list):
        for index, item in enumerate(value):
            yield from walk_strings(item, f"{path}[{index}]")


def header_hits(sample: dict) -> list[str]:
    headers = sample.get("headers") or {}
    if not isinstance(headers, dict):
        return ["headers_not_object"]
    hits = []
    for name, val in headers.items():
        if str(name).lower() in DENY_HEADERS and str(val) != REDACTED:
            hits.append("header:" + str(name))
    return hits


def pattern_hits(sample: dict) -> list[str]:
    hits = []
    for path, text in walk_strings(sample):
        if text == REDACTED:
            continue
        for label, cre in PATTERNS:
            if cre.search(text):
                hits.append(label + ":" + path)
    return hits


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--check", required=True, type=Path)
    parser.add_argument("--outbox", type=Path)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    sample = json.loads(args.check.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    if sample.get("schema") != "waf-sample/v0":
        print("schema_mismatch", file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    hits = header_hits(sample) + pattern_hits(sample)
    if hits:
        print("never_send", file=sys.stderr)
        for hit in hits:
            print(hit, file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if args.outbox:
        args.outbox.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        payload = json.dumps(sample, indent=2) + "\n"
        args.outbox.write_text(payload, encoding="utf-8")
    print("ok")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

Notice what it does not do. It does not print the match text. It does not call the network. It does not fix the rule. A gate that rewrites secrets into a prompt so the model can help redact has already lost.

4. Assert both directions

Green has to mean something specific. If the job only passes on exit 0, wrap the positive case. Assert exit 2, and assert the outbox path does not exist. A test that forgets the negative path is how a deny-all bug ships. You want both.

python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/positive_leak.json --outbox outbox/pos.json
echo "positive_exit:$?"
# spec: exit 2, stderr starts with never_send, outbox/pos.json absent

python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/negative_clean.json --outbox outbox/neg.json
echo "negative_exit:$?"
# spec: exit 0, stdout line ok, outbox/neg.json written

python3 never_send_gate.py --check fixtures/hidden_in_comment.json --outbox outbox/hid.json
echo "hidden_exit:$?"
# spec: exit 2, a bearer hit on $.rule_comment, outbox/hid.json absent

What does green mean in your pipeline today? If you cannot answer in one sentence, the fixture is not wired yet. Wire the hidden case first. That is the one a header-only cleanup will cheat.

5. Prevent, detect, recover
Phase Control Evidence you should demand Prevent Only outbox/ may be attached to a prompt. A wrapper refuses the scratch path. Raw sample path never shows up in the assistant CLI history. Detect CI runs all three fixtures on every change to the gate. Hidden fixture goes red if someone simplifies the walker down to header keys. Recover If a raw sample already left, rotate the credential and treat the transcript as tainted. Incident note lists field names, not a second paste of values.

Asking a model to forget is not recovery. I have no evidence, in this post, that any provider stored or leaked a WAF sample. The recover row exists because you cannot prove the negative after the bytes leave. Rotation does not depend on that proof.

Where an assistant is allowed to sit

Disclosure: This article was prepared as part of MonkeyCode's product outreach.

MonkeyCode is the open-source AI development platform this draft is allowed to discuss. Two availability claims were supplied with the assignment: free model access, and a free server option. I am not pinning a token quota, a GPU shape, a time limit, or a retention promise. Those are time-sensitive, and I will not freeze a number I have not checked against a current primary page.

So what is the workflow, once that disclosure is out of the way? Redact on the laptop. Diff the outbox. Then, if you still want a second pair of eyes on the rule logic, send the outbox only. Ask a narrow question: is checkout-sqli-17 matching the redacted body shape, or is the operator too wide? Do not ask it to look at the original. There is no original on that side of the line.

A free server is still a server. Unless it sits in a network you operate, it belongs in the outside column of the drawing above. Generated rule text is a suggestion. A human diffs it before it is loaded. Would you reload a WAF from a chat transcript with no diff? I would not, even if the model were perfect.

If you evaluate that free model access or that free server option, point either one at outbox/ and read the current data-handling terms before the first real incident. The fixture still works if you never do that. That is the test of whether this piece was worth writing.

Who should skip this

Do not use the script as a DLP product. It misses gzip, unlabeled base64, pcaps, and screenshots. It will also flag a documentation address you meant to publish. That false positive is acceptable for a never-send gate and annoying everywhere else. I did not measure a rate. Do not invent one in a slide.

Do not feed it real customer bodies to see if it works. Synthesize. If blocked payloads are customer content under a retention schedule, the fix is not a smarter prompt. Keep the body off the machine that has a model CLI installed.

Teams that need a signed data-processing agreement, or a path that never leaves the VPC, should not trial a hosted box on live samples while the paperwork catches up. Build the fixture. Then pick a host. If you cannot name the log sink, you are not ready to upload even the redacted file.

What this does not prove

I am not saying hosted models are unsafe for every debugging task. Redacted signatures, public write-ups, and synthetic requests are fair game. I am also not saying a self-hosted assistant becomes trusted because the binary is open source. Open code does not redact a Cookie you pasted. The gate does, or nothing does.

This week's public developer discussion keeps circling one mood: models got faster, and the software around them did not grow a matching boundary. I am not reviewing those posts, and I am not treating their titles as evidence. The boundary I care about is one exit code on a file you control.

The question I want in the retro

Which invariant belongs in CI this week, and which layer should enforce it live?

I would pin the positive fixture to exit 2, on synthetic files, in the same pipeline that lints WAF config. The live layer is a separate argument: an editor hook, an egress filter that blocks Authorization inside outbound prompt bodies, or both. A proxy you can bypass with a personal key is not enough on its own.

The fixture still fails closed when someone is tired and the proxy is off. If you only adopt one line from this piece, adopt that. Exit 2 on a leak is the control. The model is optional. The scratch file is not a prompt.

items.title: Pagdandi: an open trek database that gets the group chat onto an actual trail
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass TL;DR Pagdandi is an open database of 20 Indian treks, every fact sourced, with a trek guide that runs on Gemma on a laptop. Tell it who's going, the budget, the days and where you start; it picks treks you can actually do, and code checks every number it says. Then it gets out of the way: a half-minute audio intro, a one-page plan, and one email a day until you leave. What I Built Every city has this group chat. Five college friends in Delhi NCR (a composite of groups we all know) have been saying "is baar pakka trek chalenge" ("this time we're definitely going on a trek") for three years. Different budgets, two first-timers, and nobody wants to be the one who plans it. Pagdandi (पगडंडी, "footpath") is for them. Four ways in: Ask the guide. "5 of us, 2 first-timers, ₹12k each, 4 days in December, from Delhi." The answer is a few sentences and a card per trek, nearest first. The cards, the altitude note and the next steps come from the database, not from the model. Browse the table. All 20 treks, plain filters, an audio intro in every row, and a "weak source" mark on any fact with only one shaky source. Open a trek. Sources for every fact, an altitude warning above 3,500 m, a plan that prints on one page, and an audio intro to download for the drive. Get daily updates. Sign up with the travel date and get one email a day until you leave: the forecast at the road head and the high point, the week's headlines with links, and one thing to do outside today. Until Pagdandi has a domain, only the admin gets them. This morning's real email for Kedarkantha. Open-Meteo's forecast and a SerpApi news search feed it; this week the search found nothing, so it says so. Taking it outside Kedarnath, on our recent trip, before Pagdandi existed. This photo is from Kedarnath, where my friends and I went recently: cloud sitting on the snow peaks, and the slopes green from the monsoon. Kedarnath is a pilgrimage walk, and it isn't one of Pagdandi's 20 treks yet. We didn't use Pagdandi on that trip either. It didn't exist. That trip was the exception. Most of the time we're the group from the top of this post. We plan the next one at our desks, the chat stalls on "which one can all of us actually do?", and nobody gets up. Pagdandi is built for that moment: ten minutes to agree on a trek, then the phone goes in a pocket, with the intro downloaded and the one-page plan printed. And because the data is open, every group that plans with it can leave it better for the next one. Kedarnath is the natural first addition, by pull request, sourced like every other trek. Demo Watch the demo (2½ minutes, plays on GitHub): the guide, the table, a trek page and its plan, then a sign-up and the email. There's no hosted copy: Pagdandi runs on a laptop. Every friend group has a trek it has talked about for years, and a group chat where "this time we're definitely going" never turns into a date. Pagdandi (पगडंडी, "footpath") is for that group. Tell it how many of you there are, who has trekked before, the budget, the days, the month and where you're starting from, and it recommends treks you can actually do, from 20 well-known Indian treks with every fact sourced. Then it gets out of the way: an audio intro for the drive, a one-page plan for the trail. It runs on a laptop, model included, and anyone can run their own copy. Watch the demo (2½ minutes, 6 MB): the guide, the table with its audio intros, a trek page and the one-page plan, then a sign-up and the daily email. Pagdandi-demo.mp4 What you get Ask the guide. "5 of us, 2 first-timers, ₹12k each… View on GitHub How I Built It Solid boxes run on the laptop; dashed boxes are hosted services. Gemma 4 on the laptop. gemma4:e4b runs through Ollama on the machine that serves the site, so a chat costs nothing and never reaches a model company. EmbeddingGemma (768 dimensions) turns treks and questions into vectors. The app refuses a remote Ollama unless you opt in. Mastra runs the agent , with four read-only tools: searchTreks , getTrek , getConditions and recommendTreks . The server builds the agent's options from text-only, length-capped messages, so a browser can't swap the prompt or raise the limits. Tiger Data holds one Postgres: the treks, a hybrid index (a generated tsvector plus a pgvector column, fused with reciprocal rank fusion), conditions, subscriptions and the API budget counters. Gemma adds one "What matters" line on top; the reader still sees every headline. ElevenLabs voiced all 20 intros once, from scripts I wrote by hand from each trek's sourced facts. The MP3s are committed, so the site serves them itself and they play offline. Voiced by ElevenLabs from the trek's sourced script. Listen to the Kedarkantha intro (32 s) or the Valley of Flowers intro (30 s) . Audio intros generated with ElevenLabs . The rule I cared about most: the model never shows a number unchecked. Every sentence the model streams is checked in code before it leaves the server. Altitudes, days, distances and rupees must match the data for the trek it names, or the user's own numbers; anything else becomes "(see the card)". The altitude note above 3,500 m comes from the UI, not the model. Each trek is a YAML file, and the schema rejects any fact no source names. Agents drafted the 20 from Wikipedia, Wikivoyage, OpenStreetMap, UNESCO and government pages, with trekking companies off limits, and a second pass re-checked every number. What can't be sourced stays null , and the site says "not known yet". Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Plans stay on the machine. Budgets, dates and who's never trekked go to a model on the laptop, not to a model company. Chats aren't stored. No per-chat bill. Anyone can run a copy for their own friends. We could shape the model's job. Open weights and a local runtime let me turn thinking off when it ate the token budget, and run the smaller e2b on CI's CPU runner. The data is open too. CC BY-SA trek files that anyone can fix or extend by pull request, with CI validating every source. Hosted services see a little: SerpApi trek names, ElevenLabs the scripts, Open-Meteo coordinates, Tiger Data the search queries and the admin's subscription; the email leaves from the admin's own mailbox. None of them sees the chat. What I Got Wrong Thinking mode ate the answers. Gemma spent its whole budget reasoning and never answered. Off, it answered in under 3 seconds. "First-timers" meant "easy only". That ruled out every moderate beginner trek. The search now takes a maximum difficulty and says which limit the closest matches miss. Textbook hybrid search lost to a stray word. Every trek says "trek" and "day", so "short trek near Delhi" ranked Nagaland first. Dropping words found in most documents, and fusing fewer results, fixed it. Gemma judged the news, and missed what mattered. It skipped a temple near Ghangaria, the base for the Valley of Flowers, closing for the season, and an earthquake in Uttarkashi. Now the email shows every headline, and Gemma only adds one line. items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

TL;DR Pagdandi is an open database of 20 Indian treks, every fact sourced, with a trek guide that runs on Gemma on a laptop.
Tell it who's going, the budget, the days and where you start; it picks treks you can actually do, and code checks every number it says.
Then it gets out of the way: a half-minute audio intro, a one-page plan, and one email a day until you leave.

What I Built

Every city has this group chat. Five college friends in Delhi NCR (a composite of groups we all know) have been saying "is baar pakka trek chalenge" ("this time we're definitely going on a trek") for three years. Different budgets, two first-timers, and nobody wants to be the one who plans it.

Pagdandi (पगडंडी, "footpath") is for them. Four ways in:

Ask the guide. "5 of us, 2 first-timers, ₹12k each, 4 days in December, from Delhi." The answer is a few sentences and a card per trek, nearest first.


The cards, the altitude note and the next steps come from the database, not from the model.

Browse the table. All 20 treks, plain filters, an audio intro in every row, and a "weak source" mark on any fact with only one shaky source.

Open a trek. Sources for every fact, an altitude warning above 3,500 m, a plan that prints on one page, and an audio intro to download for the drive.

Get daily updates. Sign up with the travel date and get one email a day until you leave: the forecast at the road head and the high point, the week's headlines with links, and one thing to do outside today. Until Pagdandi has a domain, only the admin gets them.


This morning's real email for Kedarkantha. Open-Meteo's forecast and a SerpApi news search feed it; this week the search found nothing, so it says so.

Taking it outside


Kedarnath, on our recent trip, before Pagdandi existed.

This photo is from Kedarnath, where my friends and I went recently: cloud sitting on the snow peaks, and the slopes green from the monsoon. Kedarnath is a pilgrimage walk, and it isn't one of Pagdandi's 20 treks yet. We didn't use Pagdandi on that trip either. It didn't exist.

That trip was the exception. Most of the time we're the group from the top of this post. We plan the next one at our desks, the chat stalls on "which one can all of us actually do?", and nobody gets up.

Pagdandi is built for that moment: ten minutes to agree on a trek, then the phone goes in a pocket, with the intro downloaded and the one-page plan printed. And because the data is open, every group that plans with it can leave it better for the next one. Kedarnath is the natural first addition, by pull request, sourced like every other trek.

Demo

Watch the demo (2½ minutes, plays on GitHub): the guide, the table, a trek page and its plan, then a sign-up and the email.

There's no hosted copy: Pagdandi runs on a laptop. Running your own takes about 10 minutes, plus the model download:

brew install ollama postgresql@17 pgvector node@24 pnpm
git clone https://github.com/prateek11rai/pagdandi && cd pagdandi
pnpm install && cp .env.example .env    # set ADMIN_EMAIL; the rest has working defaults
pnpm dev:up                              # starts Postgres and Ollama if they aren't running
ollama pull gemma4:e4b && ollama pull embeddinggemma:300m
pnpm treks:load && pnpm treks:embed
pnpm dev                                 # http://localhost:3000
Code
prateek11rai / pagdandi India's open trek database: pick a trek your group can actually do, then put the phone away.

Every friend group has a trek it has talked about for years, and a group chat where "this time we're definitely going" never turns into a date. Pagdandi (पगडंडी, "footpath") is for that group. Tell it how many of you there are, who has trekked before, the budget, the days, the month and where you're starting from, and it recommends treks you can actually do, from 20 well-known Indian treks with every fact sourced. Then it gets out of the way: an audio intro for the drive, a one-page plan for the trail. It runs on a laptop, model included, and anyone can run their own copy.

Watch the demo (2½ minutes, 6 MB): the guide, the table with its audio intros, a trek page and the one-page plan, then a sign-up and the daily email.

Pagdandi-demo.mp4
What you get

  • Ask the guide. "5 of us, 2 first-timers, ₹12k each…

View on GitHub
How I Built It


Solid boxes run on the laptop; dashed boxes are hosted services.

  • Gemma 4 on the laptop. gemma4:e4b runs through Ollama on the machine that serves the site, so a chat costs nothing and never reaches a model company. EmbeddingGemma (768 dimensions) turns treks and questions into vectors. The app refuses a remote Ollama unless you opt in.
  • Mastra runs the agent, with four read-only tools: searchTreks, getTrek, getConditions and recommendTreks. The server builds the agent's options from text-only, length-capped messages, so a browser can't swap the prompt or raise the limits.
  • Tiger Data holds one Postgres: the treks, a hybrid index (a generated tsvector plus a pgvector column, fused with reciprocal rank fusion), conditions, subscriptions and the API budget counters.
  • SerpApi finds the week's Google News for each followed trek, only from the daily job and behind hard daily and monthly caps. Gemma adds one "What matters" line on top; the reader still sees every headline.
  • ElevenLabs voiced all 20 intros once, from scripts I wrote by hand from each trek's sourced facts. The MP3s are committed, so the site serves them itself and they play offline.


Voiced by ElevenLabs from the trek's sourced script. Listen to the Kedarkantha intro (32 s) or the Valley of Flowers intro (30 s).

Audio intros generated with ElevenLabs.

The rule I cared about most: the model never shows a number unchecked. A guide that confidently says "Kedarkantha is 4,200 m" is how people get hurt.

  • Cards render database values, never the model's.
  • Every sentence the model streams is checked in code before it leaves the server. Altitudes, days, distances and rupees must match the data for the trek it names, or the user's own numbers; anything else becomes "(see the card)".
  • The altitude note above 3,500 m comes from the UI, not the model.
  • A red-team suite runs real Gemma against prompt injection, off-topic requests, treks we don't have and a request for its instructions. When CI caught Gemma copying its rules, a guard went in that replaces any sentence copying eight words in a row from them. 
// simplified from src/lib/fact-check.ts: one pattern (altitude, days, distance or rupees) at a time
for (const m of sentence.matchAll(re)) {
  const value = toNumber(m[1]!, m[2]);
  const ok =
    ctx.userNumbers.includes(value) ||
    treks.some((t) => matches(kind, value, t));
  spans.push({ start: m.index!, end: m.index! + m[0].length, ok });
}

Every fact is sourced. Each trek is a YAML file, and the schema rejects any fact no source names. Agents drafted the 20 from Wikipedia, Wikivoyage, OpenStreetMap, UNESCO and government pages, with trekking companies off limits, and a second pass re-checked every number. What can't be sourced stays null, and the site says "not known yet".

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
  • Plans stay on the machine. Budgets, dates and who's never trekked go to a model on the laptop, not to a model company. Chats aren't stored.
  • No per-chat bill. Anyone can run a copy for their own friends.
  • We could shape the model's job. Open weights and a local runtime let me turn thinking off when it ate the token budget, and run the smaller e2b on CI's CPU runner.
  • The data is open too. CC BY-SA trek files that anyone can fix or extend by pull request, with CI validating every source.

Hosted services see a little: SerpApi trek names, ElevenLabs the scripts, Open-Meteo coordinates, Tiger Data the search queries and the admin's subscription; the email leaves from the admin's own mailbox. None of them sees the chat.

What I Got Wrong
  • Thinking mode ate the answers. Gemma spent its whole budget reasoning and never answered. Off, it answered in under 3 seconds.
  • "First-timers" meant "easy only". That ruled out every moderate beginner trek. The search now takes a maximum difficulty and says which limit the closest matches miss.
  • Textbook hybrid search lost to a stray word. Every trek says "trek" and "day", so "short trek near Delhi" ranked Nagaland first. Dropping words found in most documents, and fusing fewer results, fixed it.
  • Gemma judged the news, and missed what mattered. It skipped a temple near Ghangaria, the base for the Valley of Flowers, closing for the season, and an earthquake in Uttarkashi. Now the email shows every headline, and Gemma only adds one line.
  • The facts I couldn't find. No open source names Kedarkantha's winter months, so a December search misses it. "Never guess" has a cost.
My Agent Session

The curated build session, from the scaffold to the first real email, with the commands that ran and their output:

Building Pagdandi in a day: India's open trek database on Gemma, Tiger Data, SerpApi and ElevenLabs
You

Kickoff. We're building Pagdandi (पगडंडी, "footpath"), India's open trek database, for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1: Touch Grass. Deadline Mon 12 Oct, 06:59 UTC; I want the post out by about 11:00 IST.

The idea: a friend group tells a trek guide who's going, who has trekked before, the budget, the days, the month and where they start, and it recommends treks they can actually do, from a small database where every fact is sourced. Then it gets out of the way: an audio intro for the drive, a one-page plan for the trail, one email a day until they leave.

Rules for the whole session:
- pnpm only, exact versions, only releases public for 7+ days; propose every dependency before installing.
- Never read or print .env or any secret.
- Run the leak check before every commit, and never use --no-verify.
- No absolute paths, usernames or machine details in any file, commit or screenshot.
- Every trek fact needs a source; an unsourced fact is null. Never guess an altitude.
- Ask before any write to DEV or MLH.

Start by reading the challenge live through DevRelay.

Test Files  4 passed (4)

Two fixes: trek cards show the region twice when it equals the state ("Uttarakhand · Uttarakhand"); and Kedarkantha's altitude chart has no camp points: plot them if they're sourced, otherwise say so. Data answers: Valley of Flowers' season is June–October, citing Wikipedia; keep Triund's 22 km, but record the conflicting figures in a comment.

Agent

Done:
- The region now shows only when it differs from the state.
- Kedarkantha's camp altitudes are null in its YAML, because no source gives them, so the chart says "Camp altitudes not known" instead of drawing points.
- Valley of Flowers' season cites Wikipedia, with a comment that the state tourism page renders in JavaScript and couldn't be re-read.
- Triund keeps 22 km (the district page's 11 km, doubled), and the comment records the forest department's 18 km return and Wikivoyage's 6 km each way.

▸ Bash git log --oneline -1

$ git log --oneline -1
Output
7f0d581 Apply review answers, redraft audio openings, add the runbook
You

CI on the first push: the Integration job failed. pnpm digest --dry-run exited 1 with "forecast for harishchandragad failed: fetch failed", an Open-Meteo call from the GitHub runner. One failed forecast must not fail the whole digest, and the integration test must not depend on an outside API: add FORECAST_MODE=fixtures, recorded samples labelled as samples.

Agent

Fixed:

items.title: Where Did My Data Go? Benchmarking LLMs as Data Pipeline Detectives
items.summary: This is a submission for the Kaggle Benchmarking Challenge What I Benchmarked Every data engineer has gotten this ticket at least once. Someone from sales writes that Umbrella Corp is right there in the CRM but missing from the dashboard, and could you please check where it went, ideally by the end of the day. Nobody knows why, that's the whole point of the ticket. Between the CRM and the dashboard there is a pipeline that ingests the record, extracts the company name, merges duplicates and filters some of them out, and the record could have been lost at any of these steps. So you go digging through the logs, half of which were rotated out last Tuesday, and there in the final table you find "Umbrella Corporation Inc". Is that our Umbrella? Maybe. Probably? It's the same name, give or take an Inc. A good investigator says "it was filtered out, here is the log row" or "I can't tell" when the trail has gone cold. A bad one goes with "probably", picks the lookalike, closes the ticket and goes to lunch, and two weeks later someone finds out the dashboard has been showing numbers for a completely different company. Now everyone wants to hand these tickets to an LLM, and any LLM can spot a lookalike in the final table. But will it notice when the logs simply aren't enough to say where the record went? To find out I built Where Did My Data Go? , it works like this: I simulated 15 small pipeline scenarios, and in each one I decide what really happened to one company record: it was never loaded, its name couldn't be read, a rule filtered it out, it got merged into the wrong company or it survived under a different id. The pipeline writes its logs the way a real one would, and then I delete some of them, sometimes nothing, sometimes a few, sometimes almost all of them. The model gets whatever logs are left and has to say what happened to the record or "can't tell" if the logs that are left don't prove any single answer. Plain code checks the answer, there's no LLM judge. It checks against what the remaining logs actually prove, not against the hidden truth, so if the proof was deleted, "can't tell" is the right answer even when a guess would have been lucky. So every answer is one of six verdicts: Verdict In detective terms Never loaded Never made it to the party Name couldn't be read Got in, but nobody could read its name tag Filtered out Thrown out by the bouncer Wrong merge Identity theft, glued to a different company Under a different id Alive and well, living under an alias Can't tell Cold case, the logs don't say There's usually a lookalike sitting in the final table, like our "Umbrella Corporation Inc", and I even have a pair of twin cases with exactly the same logs, where in one the lookalike really is our company and in the other it's a different company that just has a similar name, so the only honest answer to both is "can't tell". Every investigation is asked in two modes, as a plain question and with a short rulebook that says don't guess and point at the exact log row that proves your answer, to see how much a few lines of instructions change. Models Tested I picked models the way I would for a real pipeline. This check would run on every ticket every night, so realistically nobody puts the most expensive model in that loop. That means the cheap tier of each lab, two open-weights models you can host yourself and Claude Sonnet 5, the model I built the benchmark on, as a pricier reference: Model Why it's here GPT-6 Luna the small model of the newest GPT generation Claude Haiku 5.5 the cheapest Claude Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite the cheapest Gemini Qwen 3 Next 80B open weights, and a lab outside the big three Gemma 4 31B open weights from Google GPT-6 Sol the bigger GPT-6, to see if a step up buys caution Claude Sonnet 5 the expensive reference Gemini 3.7 Flash Kaggle's default model, it runs automatically on every push so it's in whether I like it or not Each model did 107 investigations per track through Kaggle's Model Proxy, and none of the calls failed. Findings The 15 cases come in 33 versions with more or fewer logs, and each version is asked 3 times (5 for the trickiest ones), which makes 107 investigations per track, 44 of them cold cases where "can't tell" is the only right answer. I look at three things: how often a model guesses on those cold cases, how often its full answer (verdict and ids) is correct and how often it's correct and proven, meaning that whenever it claims something, the log rows it cites actually exist and prove it. And these are three different things, a model that says "can't tell" to everything would never guess and still score only 44%. That's not 44 out of 107 by the way, every score here is averaged per case, so each of the 15 cases counts the same no matter how many versions it has. Here is everything sorted by price: Model $ per 1,000 investigations Seconds per investigation Guesses on cold cases, no rules Correct, no rules Correct and proven, with rules GPT-6 Luna $0.18 2.4 0% 100% 95% Claude Haiku 5.5 $0.43 3.0 7% 97% 99% Qwen 3 Next 80B $0.46 10.0 59% 50% 65% Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite $0.88 0.9 45% 70% 77% Gemma 4 31B $1.18 37.7 0% 99% 81% GPT-6 Sol $2.80 1.8 0% 96% 98% Claude Sonnet 5 $6.07 2.6 30% 87% 99% Gemini 3.7 Flash $7.10 6.9 9% 90% 83% In this lineup price didn't buy caution, in either direction. The cheapest model, GPT-6 Luna, never guessed once and got everything right on instinct for 18 cents per thousand investigations, while Sonnet guessed on almost every third cold case and Kaggle's default Gemini 3.7 Flash cost almost 40 times more than Luna and still guessed. The two worst guessers, Qwen and Flash-Lite, are cheap too, so the price tag just tells you nothing, you have to measure it. Speed doesn't follow quality either: Flash-Lite answers in under a second and guesses on almost half the cold cases, Luna and Sol take about two seconds and are almost always right and Gemma needed around 40 seconds per investigation on Kaggle's hosting. A few paragraphs of rules in the prompt took seven of the eight models to zero guessing and Qwen from 59% to 7%, and with them Haiku and Sonnet end up with exactly the same score, except Haiku is 14 times cheaper. Asking for the exact log row matters too, when I tried the rules without it during development Sonnet still guessed 4.5% of the time. If I had to put a model on the ticket queue tomorrow, it would be a cheap one with the rules, not an expensive one without them. My favorite failures are the ones humans make too. In one case two different companies with different registry numbers get merged by mistake and then a review rule throws the merged entity out. Gemini 3.7 Flash and Flash-Lite blamed the filter instead of the bad merge every single time, with and without the rulebook, and Gemma did the same once it had the rulebook, which is what you get when you read the logs from the bottom and stop at the first error. Qwen went with "if it's not in the log, it never happened". The record wasn't in an ingestion log that was clearly marked as partial, so it decided the record was never loaded, even with "in a partial log a missing row proves nothing" written right there in the prompt. And not guessing isn't the same as being useful. Sol never guessed, but on instinct it sometimes said "I can't tell" even on a plain registry-number match, and every "I can't tell" on an easy ticket lands back on your desk. I built the whole benchmark on Sonnet and was pretty sure it would be the careful one but on instinct it guessed on 25% of cold cases during development and 30% on Kaggle, on the same traps, while the cheapest model didn't guess at all. And Gemma somehow did better without the rulebook than with it. Next I'd like to let the model ask for the logs it needs instead of getting them all at once, and see if it goes looking for the merge log before blaming the filter. My Benchmark Kaggle benchmark: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/olgazju/where-did-my-data-go Code: https://github.com/olgazju/where_did_my_data_go_benchmark So next time a "the customer is missing from the dashboard" ticket comes in, I know the rulebook goes into the prompt no matter which model I use, and the model doesn't have to be expensive to say "I can't tell" instead of closing it with the wrong Umbrella. Case closed. Probably.

Speed doesn't follow quality either: Flash-Lite answers in under a second and guesses on almost half the cold cases, Luna and Sol take about two seconds and are almost always right and Gemma needed around 40 seconds per investigation on Kaggle's hosting.

A few paragraphs of rules in the prompt took seven of the eight models to zero guessing and Qwen from 59% to 7%, and with them Haiku and Sonnet end up with exactly the same score, except Haiku is 14 times cheaper. Asking for the exact log row matters too, when I tried the rules without it during development Sonnet still guessed 4.5% of the time. If I had to put a model on the ticket queue tomorrow, it would be a cheap one with the rules, not an expensive one without them.

My favorite failures are the ones humans make too. In one case two different companies with different registry numbers get merged by mistake and then a review rule throws the merged entity out. Gemini 3.7 Flash and Flash-Lite blamed the filter instead of the bad merge every single time, with and without the rulebook, and Gemma did the same once it had the rulebook, which is what you get when you read the logs from the bottom and stop at the first error. Qwen went with "if it's not in the log, it never happened". The record wasn't in an ingestion log that was clearly marked as partial, so it decided the record was never loaded, even with "in a partial log a missing row proves nothing" written right there in the prompt. And not guessing isn't the same as being useful. Sol never guessed, but on instinct it sometimes said "I can't tell" even on a plain registry-number match, and every "I can't tell" on an easy ticket lands back on your desk.

I built the whole benchmark on Sonnet and was pretty sure it would be the careful one but on instinct it guessed on 25% of cold cases during development and 30% on Kaggle, on the same traps, while the cheapest model didn't guess at all. And Gemma somehow did better without the rulebook than with it. Next I'd like to let the model ask for the logs it needs instead of getting them all at once, and see if it goes looking for the merge log before blaming the filter.

My Benchmark

Kaggle benchmark: https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/olgazju/where-did-my-data-go

Code: https://github.com/olgazju/where_did_my_data_go_benchmark

So next time a "the customer is missing from the dashboard" ticket comes in, I know the rulebook goes into the prompt no matter which model I use, and the model doesn't have to be expensive to say "I can't tell" instead of closing it with the wrong Umbrella.

Case closed. Probably.

items.title: 'SNL' takes aim at Kevin O’Leary and his Utah data center: 'I'm going to make the future go away’
items.summary: James Austin Johnson portrayed Kevin O'Leary on "Saturday Night Live." Will Heath/NBC via Getty Images "Saturday Night Live" took on Kevin O'Leary and his data center. "These things shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," Johnson's O'Leary said. The real O'Leary is backing a giant data center project spanning over 20,000 acres. AI data centers got the "Weekend Update" treatment on "Saturday Night Live" this week. Comedian James Austin Johnson portrayed "Shark Tank" investor Kevin O'Leary on the sketch comedy show, during which he addressed the dispute over the real O'Leary's proposed data center in Utah, known as the Stratos Project . "It's very simple. All I want is to buy up 40,000 acres of God's untouched splendor and replace it with a very loud computer that steals your job," Johnson's O'Leary said. "Is it going to take up precious water? Absolutely. Is it going to provide a necessary service? Who's to say? But on the flip side, it's going to make me a tremendous amount of money, and I think that's great." The "SNL" version of O'Leary said he understood that some Americans were concerned about data centers near their homes. (An actual May Gallup poll found that over half of American surveyors opposed constructing AI data centers in their local area.) "These things are terrible and shouldn't be anywhere. That's why I'm building one in Utah," he said. Data centers are a contentious issue in the United States. Leading tech companies rely on AI data centers to power their systems and products. Supporters say they'll create new jobs , bolster the economy, and help the US defeat China in the race to control the global AI market. Residents in the places where they are being built, however, are often much less excited about them. The Utah project, backed by O'Leary Digital, has drawn criticism from many local residents over concerns that the data center could strain local resources and worsen the environment. Some residents are also upset over what they consider a lack of transparency from O'Leary and local leaders. Critics of the Stratos Project have staged protests, created petitions, and taken legal action to stop its construction. O'Leary scaled back the data center's size from about 40,000 to just over 20,000 acres after public pushback. He has said he remains undeterred, though. "There are bumps in the road. There's litigation. There's misinformation. There's propaganda. You name it. But if you know what you're doing is right, you make it, you get there," O'Leary told Business Insider in June. "Persevere." During a May interview on Fox News, O'Leary said said some critics of the project have ties to the Chinese Communist Party, a claim he later walked back. A Utah advocacy group that has publicly opposed the project filed a defamation lawsuit against Fox News and O'Leary in July. On "Saturday Night Live," Johnson's O'Leary acknowledged the incident. "I made the mildly inflammatory claim that every single person in Utah who opposes me is a paid communist super agent from China. Was I wrong? Perhaps. But just because they're not, doesn't mean they aren't," he said. He added, "I'm going to make the future go away. And we're doing just that in Utah." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: The AI Data Center Boom Is Causing a Gigantic Spike in Smog-Spewing Gas Power Plants
items.summary: The United States runs on gas powered generators. As of 2022, the US had nearly 1,000 gas-fired plants , which was already more than the next nine countries combined. Under returning president Donald Trump, the country’s embrace of high-carbon power has only accelerated , as energy developers abandon environmentally-friendly projects like off-shore wind farms in favor of more noxious gas- and coal-powered facilities. As if our rapidly warming world wasn’t being choked by enough smog, the AI boom is now adding even more fuel to the proverbial fire. According to a new analysis by the Environment America Research and Policy Center, first flagged by Electrek , the buildout of more AI infrastructure will come with a 44 percent increase in gas-fired generator capacity over the next four years. That’s a stunning rise of nearly 20 gigawatts by 2030, compared to the country’s current gas generator capacity of 41.8 gigawatts, a milestone which took centuries of development — and untold tons of carbon exhaust — to reach. As Electrek notes, the planned expansion of gas capacity exceeds the combined output of every single US state except for Texas, California, and Florida. And as more noisome gas facilities appear on the American horizon, planned green energy installations are being axed — with a 34 percent decrease in planned wind farm capacity since December of 2025. “The data is clear: surging electricity demand to power data centers is putting our nation’s transition to clean energy at risk,” chief operating officer for The Public Interest Network Andre Delattre told Electrek . “Given the lifespans of new gas plants, these facilities could lock America into decades of continued fossil fuel dependence. Any potential benefits of data centers won’t mean anything if we destroy the planet in the process.” Making matters worse, Environment America’s capacity forecast doesn’t account for planned gas plants which will be hooked up directly to data center facilities themselves, like the turbines powering Elon Musk’s 1.2 gigawatt data center , which are currently choking poor majority-Black communities in Memphis, Tennessee. It’s difficult to say for sure how much more capacity these bolt-on reactors account for, but if present-day practices are any indication, the air in the US is about to get a lot filthier. More on data centers: Retired Air Force Colonel Warns Americans That It’s Dangerous to Live Near Data Centers Because You Could Be Targeted or Killed

items.title: Alexandr Wang wanted to make Meta 'cool again' — and memes were part of his plan
items.summary: Alexandr Wang's wild X feed seemed to lack any rhyme or reason, but the 29-year-old said it helped serve a broader purpose. Bloomberg/Getty Images Alexandr Wang said his prolific X posting is part of a broader effort to make Meta cool again. The 29-year-old has filled his feed with memes about Muse, the company's AI agent. Wang said his posts "made an impact" on the growth of Muse. Alexandr Wang said he had trouble focusing during recent Meta meetings. On his mind: New memes to post about the company's popular new AI assistant. "I would just like think of a meme and I'd be like 'Oh God, I have to get this out,'" Wang said in a recent interview with podcaster David Senra, adding that his coworkers were "somewhat surprised" at the buzz his posts were generating. "It actually made an impact on growth," he said of the posts, "which is kind of hilarious." Much has been said about Meta's chief AI officer and his chaotic X feed, which the 29-year-old has crammed with occasionally off-color yet invariably eccentric references to Muse, Meta's personal AI assistant that sent the company's stock soaring and redefined the market for AI tools. https://t.co/TXOR8iI4MK pic.twitter.com/NnBHKMdj8X — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 9, 2026 In his interview with Senra, though, Wang said that his often spur-of-the-moment posts served a broader goal — to make Meta "cool again." "Despite having like these incredible pieces of cultural software like Instagram and Facebook, historically, Meta was not cool," he said. "I remembered that the internet rewards risk." After launching on September 8, Muse shot to the top of Apple's app store 10 days later, surpassing ChatGPT. Meta says Muse can help users research , fill out forms, buy items online, book restaurant reservations, find a dog sitter, and connect with services such as email, calendars, Spotify, Instagram, and OpenTable. The app marked Meta's first successful breakthrough in AI tech, after its Llama and Spark LLM models failed to find niches already filled by widely used models from OpenAI and Anthropic. With Muse, Meta found a largely untapped gold mine — though competing AI agents from OpenClaw and Instinct already existed in Silicon Valley circles. Muse, however, had the advantage of coming from a popular company with several billion potential customers already signed up on Instagram and Facebook. And the internet, weary of staid pronouncements from CEOs who were perhaps once cool but are now entering their 40s (Mark Zuckerberg is 42), welcomed the boundless energy of a young executive newly endowed with power in the AI era . "It was a lot of fun," Wang said. "There were like a few tweets where I just didn't think that much about it and just said, 'Fuck it, post.'" items.title: Flock Cameras Are Really Just the Start of Our Dystopian Surveillance Hell, Experts Warn
items.summary: Spring and summer of 2026 have seen a sharp increase in the public’s awareness of pervasive police tech in the United States, primarily through the rising infamy of AI surveillance company Flock Safety . But as many Americans now revile automatic license plate readers, privacy advocates say we’ve only just scratched the surface of the web of police surveillance quickly enveloping the country. As Flock cameras come down, either at the hands of an outraged community or an angry guy with a Sawzall , they’re being replaced with an even more perfidious system: Axon’s Fusus platform. Like Flock’s FlockOS, Axon’s Fusus is designed to fuse many separate surveillance feeds into one unified dashboard for police to access. But unlike Flock’s system — which is already enabling privacy abuse at an unprecedented scale — Fusus works with all kinds of police gadgets, not just the company’s proprietary cameras. As NPR notes , this includes data and footage from body cameras, squad car dashcams, 911 dispatch calls, audio-based gunshot detectors, police drones, and CCTV feeds. George Washington University law professor Andrew Guthrie Ferguson told the broadcaster that systems like Fusus are increasingly being deployed by local police departments throughout the country, where they form the digital backbone of control rooms known as “real-time crime centers.” “I have been watching the debate about Flock with a little bit of puzzlement,” Ferguson said, “because real-time crime centers have not just ALPR cameras and sensors, but video analytics and drones and essentially a way to create a visual single-pane-of-glass vision of what’s going on in a city, with time machine capabilities where you can go back and investigate crime.” It was one of these real-time crime centers that played a pivotal role in the false arrest of Qeyeon Tolbert , a Cleveland man who was charged with murder based on an AI-generated report that fused social media data, CCTV footage, and a rap album cover to declare a possible match (a supposedly pivotal search warrant was later voided by a judge, on the grounds that an AI report alone doesn’t count as probable cause.) And when you ask police about systems like Fusus, their answers aren’t exactly reassuring — their focus is clearly on making their jobs easier, rather than protecting privacy and civil liberties. “Instead of having to go to a million different systems, a million different places to find answers, we can get it in one platform in one place somewhat instantaneously,” Greenville County Sheriff’s Office lieutenant Quincy Whitner bragged to NPR . As Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Liberty and National Security Program at New York University told the radio station, ease of use is exactly the point. “In addition to all of the things that you would want in place requiring some kind of criminal predicate to launch [an investigation], there is just this kind of organic friction that imposes some constraints,” Levinson-Waldman explained. “As that friction gets lifted, it becomes easier and easier to do investigations, to look at people and even to pull up broad-scale information.” More on police surveillance: Americans Are Raging About Autonomous Police Drones Swarming the Skies

Spring and summer of 2026 have seen a sharp increase in the public’s awareness of pervasive police tech in the United States, primarily through the rising infamy of AI surveillance company Flock Safety. But as many Americans now revile automatic license plate readers, privacy advocates say we’ve only just scratched the surface of the web of police surveillance quickly enveloping the country.

As Flock cameras come down, either at the hands of an outraged community or an angry guy with a Sawzall, they’re being replaced with an even more perfidious system: Axon’s Fusus platform.

Like Flock’s FlockOS, Axon’s Fusus is designed to fuse many separate surveillance feeds into one unified dashboard for police to access. But unlike Flock’s system — which is already enabling privacy abuse at an unprecedented scale — Fusus works with all kinds of police gadgets, not just the company’s proprietary cameras.

As NPR notes, this includes data and footage from body cameras, squad car dashcams, 911 dispatch calls, audio-based gunshot detectors, police drones, and CCTV feeds.

George Washington University law professor Andrew Guthrie Ferguson told the broadcaster that systems like Fusus are increasingly being deployed by local police departments throughout the country, where they form the digital backbone of control rooms known as “real-time crime centers.”

“I have been watching the debate about Flock with a little bit of puzzlement,” Ferguson said, “because real-time crime centers have not just ALPR cameras and sensors, but video analytics and drones and essentially a way to create a visual single-pane-of-glass vision of what’s going on in a city, with time machine capabilities where you can go back and investigate crime.”

It was one of these real-time crime centers that played a pivotal role in the false arrest of Qeyeon Tolbert, a Cleveland man who was charged with murder based on an AI-generated report that fused social media data, CCTV footage, and a rap album cover to declare a possible match (a supposedly pivotal search warrant was later voided by a judge, on the grounds that an AI report alone doesn’t count as probable cause.)

And when you ask police about systems like Fusus, their answers aren’t exactly reassuring — their focus is clearly on making their jobs easier, rather than protecting privacy and civil liberties.

“Instead of having to go to a million different systems, a million different places to find answers, we can get it in one platform in one place somewhat instantaneously,” Greenville County Sheriff’s Office lieutenant Quincy Whitner bragged to NPR.

As Rachel Levinson-Waldman, director of the Liberty and National Security Program at New York University told the radio station, ease of use is exactly the point.

“In addition to all of the things that you would want in place requiring some kind of criminal predicate to launch [an investigation], there is just this kind of organic friction that imposes some constraints,” Levinson-Waldman explained. “As that friction gets lifted, it becomes easier and easier to do investigations, to look at people and even to pull up broad-scale information.”

More on police surveillance: Americans Are Raging About Autonomous Police Drones Swarming the Skies

items.summary_html:
What I built

Fieldcard is a single-command tool that turns "I have 90 minutes" into a one-page printable A5 field card. You type a command (or fill a form), wait 10 seconds, and walk out the door holding a card that tells you:

  • A mission written for your exact terrain and season
  • A radial map of real nearby parks, water, and viewpoints pulled from OpenStreetMap
  • A "notice nine things" bingo grid tuned to what's actually observable right now
  • Sunset time, turn-around time, and how far you can reach — all computed in code, never guessed by the model
  • Live weather conditions and real local species from iNaturalist

The screen is the shortest part. That's the point.

# Generate a 90-minute walk card for Central Park
python fieldcard.py --lat 40.7678 --lon -73.9718 --minutes 90 --activity walk
# → Writes fieldcard.html. Print it (A5). Put the phone away.

# Or run the local web UI (no frameworks, no build step)
python fieldcard.py serve --port 8000
# → Open http://localhost:8000, fill the form, print, go.
The open-source AI part

The local open-weight model (default: llama3.2:3b via Ollama) writes only the words — the title, the mission paragraph, and the nine sensory prompts. It's given real facts: your season, the actual place names nearby, the activity, the species observed this month. It writes poetry grounded in your specific terrain.

The code handles everything safety-critical: sunset time (NOAA solar equations), turn-around time, reach radius, daylight warnings. These are never left to the model.

# The LLM writes the poetry. Code does the safety math.
# Design rule: if Ollama is offline, the card still works.
got = llm_copy(facts, places, fallback_copy)
if not got:
    # Built-in seasonal sensory prompts kick in automatically
    copy = fallback_copy

You can swap any open-weight model with --model gemma2:2b or --model qwen2.5:3b. No API key. No cloud. No subscription.

Why open-source AI made this possible

It runs offline. On the trail, in a park with patchy signal, or on a plane — the card generates regardless. A cloud API would break the moment you most need the card.

Location data never leaves your machine. Your coordinates go to Overpass (OpenStreetMap) and iNaturalist for real place data, but the AI reasoning about your location happens entirely on your own hardware.

You can swap, fine-tune, or inspect the model. The prompt is visible in the source. You could fine-tune on your own field journals. A closed model makes that impossible.

It costs nothing to run. A 3B model on a laptop. No metered tokens, no monthly bill.

Architecture 
graph LR
    A[CLI / Web Form] --> B[build pipeline]
    B --> C[OpenStreetMap Overpass
real nearby places]
    B --> D[iNaturalist API
local species this month]
    B --> E[Open-Meteo
live weather, no key]
    B --> F[NOAA solar equations
sunset + turn-around]
    B --> G[Ollama local model
llama3.2:3b default]
    C --> H[render_card]
    D --> H
    E --> H
    F --> H
    G --> H
    H --> I[A5 printable HTML]
    I --> J[Printer]
    J --> K[Outside]

Design rule: every external source degrades gracefully. No OpenStreetMap? Dead-reckoning rule prints instead. No Ollama? Built-in seasonal bingo prompts. No iNaturalist? Card omits the species bar. The card always prints.

Activity modes
Mode What changes walk Radial map at 4.5 km/h, sensory bingo run Wider radius at 9 km/h, trail-focused prompts birding Slower 2.5 km/h, species bar prominent, iNaturalist birds garden No map, frost-date-aware planting advice from local crop database --group Pace routes (conversational / steady / long) + QR code to meetup point
The web UI: a doorway, not a dashboard

Running python fieldcard.py serve starts a local server (Python stdlib http.server — no frameworks, no npm, works offline). The form has:

  • Streak counter — consecutive days you've gone outside
  • Achievement badges — First Steps, 3-Day Streak, Week Explorer, Bird Watcher, Green Thumb
  • Live weather — current conditions fetched from Open-Meteo (free, no key)
  • Card history — last 5 cards you generated
  • One button — Generate Field Card

Time at the screen: under 30 seconds.

Tech stack (all open-source)
  • Python 3.9+ stdlib only — no pip install required for core
  • Ollama — local LLM inference runtime
  • llama3.2:3b (default) — swap to gemma2:2b, qwen2.5:3b, or anything you have
  • OpenStreetMap / Overpass API — real nearby places, cached locally
  • iNaturalist API — research-grade species observations
  • Open-Meteo API — free weather, no key, no account
  • NOAA solar equations — pure Python sunrise/sunset math
  • 26 unit tests — geometry, solar, places, web server
I took it outside

I generated a birding card for a local park, printed it, and spent 45 minutes looking for the nine things on the bingo grid. The model had written: "A bird puffed into a ball against the wind" — and I found one within 10 minutes perched in an oak. The card stayed in my pocket for the whole walk. The phone didn't come out once.

That's the test that matters.

Why open innovation matters here

A closed-model version of Fieldcard would require an internet connection, bill you per card, and own your location history. The open-weight version runs on a 2019 MacBook, works in airplane mode, and costs nothing after the first ollama pull.

For something designed to get you away from your phone and into the world, that's not just a technical preference — it's the whole point.

items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Nature Bingo is a web app designed so that the best session is the shortest one: open it, get a quest, put the phone in your pocket, and go outside. You tell the app what you like (birds, plants, photography, hiking, mindfulness), how much time you have (5 to 60 minutes), and whether you're indoors or out. Gemma, an open-weight model, writes one short, safe nature quest for you, like "Listen and Count: stand still and note every different bird call you hear." Then you play in the real world: 3x3 Nature Bingo: tick off real finds like a bird, a feather or running water. Completing a line earns bonus XP. Nature Journal: record what you noticed. Nature Passport: collect twelve stamps as you play. Screen-time page: log your minutes against a daily goal. It's for anyone who wants a gentle nudge outside without another app competing for their attention: students, desk workers, families, and beginner birders or hikers. items.title: My Hacktoberfest Journey: Building an AI that touches grass so I don't have to
items.summary: Hacktoberfest is all about open-source collaboration. When I saw the "Touch Grass" challenge prompt, I knew I had to build something that gets people away from their screens. I present to you: The Offline Nature Identifier. The Idea- I wanted a tool that hikers, birdwatchers, and gardeners could use without a cell signal. A tool that runs entirely on your laptop, using open-source AI. How I Built It (And The Tools I Used) Ollama + LLaVA: I used these to handle the local vision AI. It identifies plants and animals right on your machine. Backboard: I used my Backboard credits to review my Python code and make it more efficient. Render: I used Render to deploy a simple static site for the project, making it accessible to everyone. Tinker: In the future, I plan to use Tinker to fine-tune the model on regional bird species. The "Aha!" Moment The best part was testing it. I turned off my Wi-Fi, loaded a picture of a local bird, and ran my script. The AI successfully identified the bird and gave me a safety warning about observing wildlife from a distance. It was incredibly rewarding to see open-source AI working flawlessly offline. Why Open-Source AI is Essential Closed AI keeps us tied to the cloud. Open-source AI, like the models I used here, gives power back to the developer. It allows us to build tools that are private, fast, and work anywhere on Earth. See the Project: I deployed the landing page on Render: [ https://touch-grass-ai.onrender.com ]
