items.title: AirWindow: Turning an AQI Number into a Decision, Built on AWS
items.summary: Every morning in Indian cities, millions of people check the air quality and see a number like “AQI 168”. Then they are left guessing. Is it safe to open the window? Can my child go for a walk? Should my father with asthma stay in? I’m Nikhil, a third-year B.Tech student, and for the Air track I built AirWindow: a free web app that turns the air-quality forecast into an hour-by-hour plan for one person. What it does You enter a city and pick who the plan is for: a healthy adult, a child, an older adult, someone pregnant, someone with asthma, or an outdoor worker. AirWindow then shows: When to open your windows and when to keep them shut. If the whole day is bad, it finds the least-bad hour for a 10-minute air change. The best slot for a walk, run or commute. You breathe about 2.5x more air walking and 5x more running than at rest, so running has stricter limits. Whether to wear an N95 mask, and whether the air is getting better or worse. Tips in your language. English, Hindi and Telugu are pre-written, and Amazon Bedrock writes a short briefing in 11 Indian languages. Email alerts when the next few hours turn unhealthy. The same AQI affects people differently, so the bars in the chart are scaled for the person you pick. Fixing the forecast with TinyFish Air-quality forecasts are model estimates, and real monitoring stations are closer to the truth. But stations publish on web pages, not on a free API. So a scheduled job uses the TinyFish Web Agent. I give it a station page URL and a plain-English goal: “return the current AQI and main pollutant as JSON”. The result is cached, and the planner nudges the forecast toward it, fading the correction over 6 hours. It never lowers the risk by more than half the gap, because under-warning is worse than over-warning. How I used AWS The whole backend is serverless and defined in one AWS SAM template: API Gateway (HTTP API) is the public entry point, with throttling. Lambda has two functions: one serves the page and the plan API, and one runs on a schedule for TinyFish checks and alerts. EventBridge triggers the scheduled function every 3 hours. DynamoDB caches forecasts and station readings with TTL, so page loads never wait on slow web-agent work. SNS sends alert emails. Filter policies mean each person only gets alerts for their city and risk group. Bedrock writes the multilingual briefing from facts the planner has already calculated. If it is unavailable, the app falls back to pre-written tips. Systems Manager Parameter Store keeps the TinyFish API key encrypted. CloudWatch collects logs, and IAM gives each function only the permissions it needs. I also used boto3 and the AWS CLI for the code and setup. What I learned Separating the fast path (reading cached data) from the slow path (web-agent calls on a schedule) kept the app responsive and the cost low. I also kept the planning logic as pure Python with no network or AWS calls, so I could write 24 automated tests for it. There are honest limits. The forecast is a regional model, a station can be kilometres from your street, and the station pages use the US AQI scale rather than India’s CPCB scale. This is general guidance, not medical advice.
items.summary_html:
Every morning in Indian cities, millions of people check the air quality and see a number like “AQI 168”. Then they are left guessing. Is it safe to open the window? Can my child go for a walk? Should my father with asthma stay in?

I’m Nikhil, a third-year B.Tech student, and for the Air track I built AirWindow: a free web app that turns the air-quality forecast into an hour-by-hour plan for one person.

What it does

You enter a city and pick who the plan is for: a healthy adult, a child, an older adult, someone pregnant, someone with asthma, or an outdoor worker. AirWindow then shows:

When to open your windows and when to keep them shut. If the whole day is bad, it finds the least-bad hour for a 10-minute air change.
The best slot for a walk, run or commute. You breathe about 2.5x more air walking and 5x more running than at rest, so running has stricter limits.
Whether to wear an N95 mask, and whether the air is getting better or worse.
Tips in your language. English, Hindi and Telugu are pre-written, and Amazon Bedrock writes a short briefing in 11 Indian languages.
Email alerts when the next few hours turn unhealthy.

The same AQI affects people differently, so the bars in the chart are scaled for the person you pick.

Fixing the forecast with TinyFish

Air-quality forecasts are model estimates, and real monitoring stations are closer to the truth. But stations publish on web pages, not on a free API.

So a scheduled job uses the TinyFish Web Agent. I give it a station page URL and a plain-English goal: “return the current AQI and main pollutant as JSON”. The result is cached, and the planner nudges the forecast toward it, fading the correction over 6 hours. It never lowers the risk by more than half the gap, because under-warning is worse than over-warning.

How I used AWS

The whole backend is serverless and defined in one AWS SAM template:

API Gateway (HTTP API) is the public entry point, with throttling.
Lambda has two functions: one serves the page and the plan API, and one runs on a schedule for TinyFish checks and alerts.
EventBridge triggers the scheduled function every 3 hours.
DynamoDB caches forecasts and station readings with TTL, so page loads never wait on slow web-agent work.
SNS sends alert emails. Filter policies mean each person only gets alerts for their city and risk group.
Bedrock writes the multilingual briefing from facts the planner has already calculated. If it is unavailable, the app falls back to pre-written tips.
Systems Manager Parameter Store keeps the TinyFish API key encrypted.
CloudWatch collects logs, and IAM gives each function only the permissions it needs.

I also used boto3 and the AWS CLI for the code and setup.

What I learned

Separating the fast path (reading cached data) from the slow path (web-agent calls on a schedule) kept the app responsive and the cost low. I also kept the planning logic as pure Python with no network or AWS calls, so I could write 24 automated tests for it.

There are honest limits. The forecast is a regional model, a station can be kilometres from your street, and the station pages use the US AQI scale rather than India’s CPCB scale. This is general guidance, not medical advice.

items.title: Building Complex AI Infrastructure on AWS with HashiCorp Terraform
items.summary: AI applications are becoming more complex every day. A production-ready AI system may require GPU-powered compute, large-scale data pipelines, model endpoints, vector databases, secure networking, monitoring, and automated deployments. Setting up all these components manually in AWS can be time-consuming and difficult to maintain. What if we could define the entire infrastructure as code and provision it consistently whenever we need it? This is where HashiCorp Terraform meets AWS Cloud for AI infrastructure . In this article, let's explore how Terraform can help us design, provision, and manage a scalable infrastructure for AI applications on AWS. 🚀 1. Understanding the AI Infrastructure Challenge Imagine building an AI-powered document assistant that allows users to upload documents, generate embeddings, store them in a vector database, and retrieve relevant context for a Large Language Model (LLM). Behind this simple application, several AWS services may work together: Amazon S3 for storing documents and model artifacts. AWS Lambda for event-driven processing. AWS Glue for large-scale data preparation. Amazon SageMaker AI for model training and deployment. Amazon Bedrock for accessing supported foundation models through managed APIs. Amazon OpenSearch Service for vector search. Amazon EKS for containerized AI workloads. Amazon VPC and IAM for networking and access control. Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and logging. AWS Step Functions for orchestrating multi-step workflows. The challenge is not just creating these resources. It is connecting them securely, managing dependencies, controlling costs, and keeping development, testing, and production environments consistent. 🏗️ 2. Where Does Terraform Fit In? HashiCorp Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that lets us define AWS resources using declarative configuration files written in HCL. Instead of creating resources individually through the AWS Console, we describe the infrastructure we want. Terraform uses the AWS provider to manage supported resources and compare the desired configuration with its state. For AI infrastructure, this means we can manage networking, storage, IAM permissions, compute resources, model endpoints, and supporting services through version-controlled code. Terraform does not train an AI model or generate embeddings by itself. It provisions and manages the infrastructure that enables those workloads to run. 🧠 3. Example: AI Infrastructure Architecture on AWS Consider a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application. The architecture could look like this: Users / Applications | Application API | Amazon API Gateway | AWS Lambda | +------------------+------------------+ | | Amazon Bedrock Vector Search Foundation Model Amazon OpenSearch Service | | +---------------+---------------------+ | Retrieved Context Document Ingestion: Amazon S3 → Lambda / Step Functions → Embedding Generation → Vector Database Infrastructure Management: HashiCorp Terraform | +-- VPC, Subnets, Security Groups +-- IAM Roles and Policies +-- S3 and Processing Resources +-- Model Access and Search Resources +-- CloudWatch Monitoring This is a conceptual architecture. The exact services and connections depend on the application's requirements, and the Terraform configuration must define the required permissions, integrations, and networking. ⚙️ 4. Provisioning AWS AI Infrastructure with Terraform Let's look at a simplified example of how Terraform can define an S3 bucket for storing AI documents. terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 6.0" } } } provider "aws" { region = var . aws_region } variable "aws_region" { type = string default = "ap-south-1" } variable "environment" { type = string default = "dev" } resource "aws_s3_bucket" "ai_documents" { bucket = var . ai_bucket_name tags = { Project = "AI-Platform" Environment = var . environment ManagedBy = "Terraform" } } variable "ai_bucket_name" { type = string description = "Globally unique S3 bucket name" } This example defines a storage resource for AI documents. The bucket name must be globally unique, and the example intentionally leaves it as a required variable. For production, we should also configure encryption, public-access blocking, appropriate bucket policies, and any required lifecycle rules. We can extend this configuration with additional Terraform resources for networking, processing, vector search, model endpoints, and monitoring. 🧩 5. Managing Complex Infrastructure with Terraform Modules As the AI platform grows, putting everything into one large Terraform file becomes difficult to maintain. We can separate the infrastructure into reusable modules. ai-infrastructure/ │ ├── main.tf ├── variables.tf ├── outputs.tf ├── providers.tf │ ├── modules/ │ ├── networking/ │ ├── storage/ │ ├── data-processing/ │ ├── model-serving/ │ ├── vector-search/ │ ├── security/ │ └── monitoring/ │ └── environments/ ├── dev/ ├── staging/ └── production/ Each module has a clear responsibility. Networking module: Creates VPCs, subnets, routing, and security groups. Data-processing module: Provisions S3, Lambda, and other required data-processing resources. Model-serving module: Manages supported SageMaker AI endpoints or other model-serving infrastructure. Vector-search module: Provisions the required OpenSearch resources and associated access controls. Security module: Manages IAM roles, policies, and encryption-related resources. Monitoring module: Defines CloudWatch log groups, metrics, alarms, and dashboards where supported. Modules make it easier to reuse infrastructure patterns across multiple AI projects. 🔄 6. Automating AI Infrastructure Deployment Terraform can also be integrated into a CI/CD pipeline. A typical workflow looks like this: A developer updates Terraform code and creates a pull request. Automated checks validate formatting and configuration. Terraform generates a plan showing the proposed infrastructure changes. The team reviews and approves the plan. The deployment pipeline applies the approved changes. Monitoring checks help identify infrastructure or application issues. Example commands: terraform fmt -check terraform init terraform validate terraform plan terraform apply In a production pipeline, the apply step should follow the organization's approval process. Remote state, state locking where supported, secure credentials, and restricted deployment permissions are essential. This workflow makes infrastructure changes easier to review and track. 🤖 7. Terraform and MLOps: Beyond Infrastructure Creation AI infrastructure requires more than compute resources. A complete MLOps workflow may include: Data ingestion and preprocessing. Model training and evaluation. Model artifact storage. Model endpoint deployment. Embedding generation and vector indexing. Monitoring and alerting. Controlled model and infrastructure updates. Terraform can provision the AWS resources that support these stages. Other tools and application workflows perform the actual training, inference, data processing, and model lifecycle operations. For example, Terraform can create a SageMaker endpoint and the required execution roles, while a separate deployment pipeline manages model artifacts and endpoint updates. Similarly, Terraform can provision the infrastructure for an EKS-based inference service, while Kubernetes and its deployment tools manage application workloads and pod scaling. Understanding this separation helps avoid treating Terraform as an AI orchestration engine. 🔐 8. Security and Cost Optimization for AI Workloads AI infrastructure can become expensive, especially when GPU instances, continuously running endpoints, and large search clusters are involved. Terraform can help establish consistent controls, but cost optimization still requires monitoring and operational decisions. Security considerations: Apply least-privilege IAM policies. Encrypt data at rest and in transit. Keep sensitive credentials out of Terraform files. Store Terraform state securely because it can contain sensitive values. Restrict network access to databases and model-serving resources. Review permissions and infrastructure plans before deployment. Cost considerations: Choose appropriate instance types for the workload. Avoid leaving unused GPU instances and model endpoints running. Use autoscaling where supported and appropriate. Set CloudWatch alarms and AWS Budgets. Apply lifecycle policies to data and artifacts where appropriate. Review resource changes before applying them. Terraform helps define these controls as code, making them easier to review and reproduce. 🎯 Final Thoughts Building production-ready AI infrastructure involves much more than deploying a model. It requires networking, security, storage, compute, data processing, model serving, monitoring, and reliable deployment practices. HashiCorp Terraform helps bring these components together through Infrastructure as Code. By combining Terraform with AWS services such as Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon EKS, and CloudWatch, teams can create infrastructure that is more consistent, maintainable, and easier to scale. The real advantage is not simply creating more cloud resources. It is making complex AI infrastructure repeatable, reviewable, and manageable throughout its lifecycle. I'm exploring how Terraform and AWS can be combined to build reliable AI platforms, and I'd love to learn from others working in this space. Let's discuss: Would you use Terraform to manage your entire AI infrastructure, or would you combine it with tools such as Kubernetes, Helm, and dedicated MLOps pipelines?
items.summary_html:
AI applications are becoming more complex every day. A production-ready AI system may require GPU-powered compute, large-scale data pipelines, model endpoints, vector databases, secure networking, monitoring, and automated deployments.

Setting up all these components manually in AWS can be time-consuming and difficult to maintain.

What if we could define the entire infrastructure as code and provision it consistently whenever we need it?

This is where HashiCorp Terraform meets AWS Cloud for AI infrastructure.

In this article, let's explore how Terraform can help us design, provision, and manage a scalable infrastructure for AI applications on AWS.

🚀 1. Understanding the AI Infrastructure Challenge

Imagine building an AI-powered document assistant that allows users to upload documents, generate embeddings, store them in a vector database, and retrieve relevant context for a Large Language Model (LLM).

Behind this simple application, several AWS services may work together:

  • Amazon S3 for storing documents and model artifacts.
  • AWS Lambda for event-driven processing.
  • AWS Glue for large-scale data preparation.
  • Amazon SageMaker AI for model training and deployment.
  • Amazon Bedrock for accessing supported foundation models through managed APIs.
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service for vector search.
  • Amazon EKS for containerized AI workloads.
  • Amazon VPC and IAM for networking and access control.
  • Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and logging.
  • AWS Step Functions for orchestrating multi-step workflows.

The challenge is not just creating these resources. It is connecting them securely, managing dependencies, controlling costs, and keeping development, testing, and production environments consistent.

🏗️ 2. Where Does Terraform Fit In?

HashiCorp Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code tool that lets us define AWS resources using declarative configuration files written in HCL.

Instead of creating resources individually through the AWS Console, we describe the infrastructure we want.

Terraform uses the AWS provider to manage supported resources and compare the desired configuration with its state.

For AI infrastructure, this means we can manage networking, storage, IAM permissions, compute resources, model endpoints, and supporting services through version-controlled code.

Terraform does not train an AI model or generate embeddings by itself. It provisions and manages the infrastructure that enables those workloads to run.

🧠 3. Example: AI Infrastructure Architecture on AWS

Consider a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) application.

The architecture could look like this:

                    Users / Applications
                             |
                    Application API
                             |
                    Amazon API Gateway
                             |
                      AWS Lambda
                             |
          +------------------+------------------+
          |                                     |
    Amazon Bedrock                       Vector Search
    Foundation Model                Amazon OpenSearch Service
          |                                     |
          +---------------+---------------------+
                          |
                    Retrieved Context

Document Ingestion:
Amazon S3 → Lambda / Step Functions
          → Embedding Generation
          → Vector Database

Infrastructure Management:
HashiCorp Terraform
          |
          +-- VPC, Subnets, Security Groups
          +-- IAM Roles and Policies
          +-- S3 and Processing Resources
          +-- Model Access and Search Resources
          +-- CloudWatch Monitoring

This is a conceptual architecture. The exact services and connections depend on the application's requirements, and the Terraform configuration must define the required permissions, integrations, and networking.

⚙️ 4. Provisioning AWS AI Infrastructure with Terraform

Let's look at a simplified example of how Terraform can define an S3 bucket for storing AI documents.

terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = var.aws_region
}

variable "aws_region" {
  type    = string
  default = "ap-south-1"
}

variable "environment" {
  type    = string
  default = "dev"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "ai_documents" {
  bucket = var.ai_bucket_name

  tags = {
    Project     = "AI-Platform"
    Environment = var.environment
    ManagedBy   = "Terraform"
  }
}

variable "ai_bucket_name" {
  type        = string
  description = "Globally unique S3 bucket name"
}

This example defines a storage resource for AI documents. The bucket name must be globally unique, and the example intentionally leaves it as a required variable.

For production, we should also configure encryption, public-access blocking, appropriate bucket policies, and any required lifecycle rules.

We can extend this configuration with additional Terraform resources for networking, processing, vector search, model endpoints, and monitoring.

🧩 5. Managing Complex Infrastructure with Terraform Modules

As the AI platform grows, putting everything into one large Terraform file becomes difficult to maintain.

We can separate the infrastructure into reusable modules.

ai-infrastructure/
│
├── main.tf
├── variables.tf
├── outputs.tf
├── providers.tf
│
├── modules/
│   ├── networking/
│   ├── storage/
│   ├── data-processing/
│   ├── model-serving/
│   ├── vector-search/
│   ├── security/
│   └── monitoring/
│
└── environments/
    ├── dev/
    ├── staging/
    └── production/

Each module has a clear responsibility.

Networking module: Creates VPCs, subnets, routing, and security groups.

Data-processing module: Provisions S3, Lambda, and other required data-processing resources.

Model-serving module: Manages supported SageMaker AI endpoints or other model-serving infrastructure.

Vector-search module: Provisions the required OpenSearch resources and associated access controls.

Security module: Manages IAM roles, policies, and encryption-related resources.

Monitoring module: Defines CloudWatch log groups, metrics, alarms, and dashboards where supported.

Modules make it easier to reuse infrastructure patterns across multiple AI projects.

🔄 6. Automating AI Infrastructure Deployment

Terraform can also be integrated into a CI/CD pipeline.

A typical workflow looks like this:

  1. A developer updates Terraform code and creates a pull request.
  2. Automated checks validate formatting and configuration.
  3. Terraform generates a plan showing the proposed infrastructure changes.
  4. The team reviews and approves the plan.
  5. The deployment pipeline applies the approved changes.
  6. Monitoring checks help identify infrastructure or application issues.

Example commands:

terraform fmt -check
terraform init
terraform validate
terraform plan
terraform apply

In a production pipeline, the apply step should follow the organization's approval process. Remote state, state locking where supported, secure credentials, and restricted deployment permissions are essential.

This workflow makes infrastructure changes easier to review and track.

🤖 7. Terraform and MLOps: Beyond Infrastructure Creation

AI infrastructure requires more than compute resources.

A complete MLOps workflow may include:

  • Data ingestion and preprocessing.
  • Model training and evaluation.
  • Model artifact storage.
  • Model endpoint deployment.
  • Embedding generation and vector indexing.
  • Monitoring and alerting.
  • Controlled model and infrastructure updates.

Terraform can provision the AWS resources that support these stages. Other tools and application workflows perform the actual training, inference, data processing, and model lifecycle operations.

For example, Terraform can create a SageMaker endpoint and the required execution roles, while a separate deployment pipeline manages model artifacts and endpoint updates.

Similarly, Terraform can provision the infrastructure for an EKS-based inference service, while Kubernetes and its deployment tools manage application workloads and pod scaling.

Understanding this separation helps avoid treating Terraform as an AI orchestration engine.

🔐 8. Security and Cost Optimization for AI Workloads

AI infrastructure can become expensive, especially when GPU instances, continuously running endpoints, and large search clusters are involved.

Terraform can help establish consistent controls, but cost optimization still requires monitoring and operational decisions.

Security considerations:

  • Apply least-privilege IAM policies.
  • Encrypt data at rest and in transit.
  • Keep sensitive credentials out of Terraform files.
  • Store Terraform state securely because it can contain sensitive values.
  • Restrict network access to databases and model-serving resources.
  • Review permissions and infrastructure plans before deployment.

Cost considerations:

  • Choose appropriate instance types for the workload.
  • Avoid leaving unused GPU instances and model endpoints running.
  • Use autoscaling where supported and appropriate.
  • Set CloudWatch alarms and AWS Budgets.
  • Apply lifecycle policies to data and artifacts where appropriate.
  • Review resource changes before applying them.

Terraform helps define these controls as code, making them easier to review and reproduce.

🎯 Final Thoughts

Building production-ready AI infrastructure involves much more than deploying a model. It requires networking, security, storage, compute, data processing, model serving, monitoring, and reliable deployment practices.

HashiCorp Terraform helps bring these components together through Infrastructure as Code.

By combining Terraform with AWS services such as Amazon S3, AWS Lambda, Amazon SageMaker AI, Amazon Bedrock, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Amazon EKS, and CloudWatch, teams can create infrastructure that is more consistent, maintainable, and easier to scale.

The real advantage is not simply creating more cloud resources. It is making complex AI infrastructure repeatable, reviewable, and manageable throughout its lifecycle.

I'm exploring how Terraform and AWS can be combined to build reliable AI platforms, and I'd love to learn from others working in this space.

Let's discuss:

Would you use Terraform to manage your entire AI infrastructure, or would you combine it with tools such as Kubernetes, Helm, and dedicated MLOps pipelines?

items.title: Errand Walker: a 1B open model that turns your to-do list into a walk
items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass What I Built Most short errands happen by default in a car or on a scooter, not because walking is worse, but because planning a walk takes effort. Which shop is closest? In what order? Is it really 40 minutes on foot, or does it just feel like a lot? Errand Walker removes that effort. You type the list the way you'd type it into a notes app: pharmacy, post office, buy rice A small open-weight model turns that into structured errands. OpenStreetMap finds the nearest matching places, a routing API computes one loop, and the app answers in a single line: how many stops, how long on foot, how long by car, and whether you can skip the car. The screen is the shortest part of the experience. Planning takes about six seconds, and then the phone goes back in your pocket. It's a phone-first web app (PWA) for anyone with a handful of small errands in a place with decent OpenStreetMap coverage. It also understands some Indonesian input ("beli obat, kirim paket"), which I evaluated separately from English. Demo In the video I ask for an ATM, a pharmacy and a meal. The app parses the three errands, picks the nearest candidate for each, orders them into a loop and shows the verdict and route on the map. The live demo uses a fixed public landmark as its start point, so it never needs or reveals my real location. You can also tap the map to set your own start. Taking it outside I tested the app on my phone in demo mode, but I did not complete a timed walk to compare predicted and real minutes. That comparison is the next thing I'd do. Code derbyps / errand-walker Errand Walker Type a messy errand list ("pharmacy, post office, buy rice, return parcel"). Get one loop you can walk or bike, with times for walking, cycling and driving, and a one-line verdict such as "3 stops, 17 min on foot (4 min by car). Skip the car." A small open-weight model (Gemma 3 1B, run by llama.cpp) turns the text into structured errands OpenStreetMap data (via Overpass) finds the nearest matching places. OpenRouteService routes the loop It is a phone-first PWA built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1 "Touch Grass". The model needs no API key and no per-call cost, and with the bundled model no AI vendor sees your text. Built with an AI coding agent (OpenCode, model claude-sonnet-5-5) from a human-written product spec ( PRD.md ). How it works Phone (PWA, Leaflet) | POST /api/plan {text, lat, lng} v FastAPI |- parser: LLM (llama-server, … View on GitHub MIT licensed. The README covers running it locally (Ollama or llama.cpp), the Docker and Render deployment, the privacy data flow, the full eval tables and the known limitations. The project was started on October 11, inside the challenge window, and any commits after the deadline are listed in the README. How I Built It The open pieces Model: Gemma 3 1B instruction-tuned, 4-bit GGUF (Q4_K_M, about 806 MB, an ungated build, so no token is needed anywhere). Runtime: llama.cpp's llama-server in production, Ollama on my laptop. The app talks to either through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the model is a set of environment variables, not a dependency. Data and routing: OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API, and OpenRouteService for foot, bike and car routes. App: FastAPI backend and a vanilla JS + Leaflet frontend with no build step. Hosted in one Docker container on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB). One job for the model. The LLM does exactly one thing: map each errand to one of ten fixed categories (pharmacy, post office, groceries, ATM, bakery, hardware, laundry, cafe, clinic, market) or other . The output is constrained to a JSON schema, so a 1B model can't wander. On the first attempt, 100% of its outputs were valid JSON in every run. Categories map to OSM tags, so the model never invents a place. It only picks a type of place, and the real places come from map data. Three layers around the model. A small model is not trustworthy by itself, so I put deterministic code around it: A keyword parser (with fuzzy matching for typos and some Indonesian words) that overrides the model when a keyword clearly matches. A grounding check that drops any model errand sharing no word with what you actually typed. A fallback to the keyword parser alone if the model is down or returns something unusable. The app degrades, it doesn't crash. How accurate is it? I wrote a dev set of 26 cases (57 expected errands, English and Indonesian) and later added a held-out set of 15 cases (26 errands) that I wrote after freezing the prompt and keyword list. A test pins a hash of the frozen config, so I couldn't tune against the held-out set by accident. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals, because these samples are small. Set Parser Accuracy Dev (57 errands) raw model, Ollama 82.5% [71-90] Dev raw model, deployed container 82.5% Held-out (26 errands) raw model, Ollama 96.2% [81-99] Held-out model + keyword merge, container 92.3% Held-out + grounding check ‡, container 96.2% ‡ I built the grounding check after seeing a held-out failure, so that row only shows it fixes the case that motivated it. It is not an independent result. Some things I'd rather say than hide: I set a 90% bar for English accuracy up front. The dev set missed it (86.8% on Ollama, 89.5% in the container), with intervals far too wide to separate either figure from 90%. I did not switch to a 4B model, because the larger Render tier costs several times more and I couldn't show it would help. The held-out score is higher mostly because those cases are shorter and simpler, not because the model generalizes better. The failure that mattered was a hallucination. Given "main game" (no real errand), the model invented a pharmacy, an ATM and a laundry stop. In daily use, that would send someone to a pharmacy they never asked for. The grounding check dropped all three in each run. "potong rambut" (haircut) is still mislabeled as a clinic in the container. Two runtimes with nominally the same model did not give identical outputs. Three dev cases differed between Ollama and llama-server , in opposite directions. Latency on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB, demo point, three errands, Overpass cache pre-warmed at startup): Request Total Model call First after deploy 6083 ms 5348 ms Warm 5896 ms 5172 ms Warm 5811 ms 5061 ms This is n=3 with one input. The first request is the first after a fresh deploy, not a cold boot from suspend, and I did not measure cold boot, a six-errand list, or a location the cache hasn't seen. Those will be slower, since an uncached location needs a live Overpass query. Things that went wrong along the way In a container limited to 1 CPU, llama-server with 4 threads ran at about 2 tokens/s, and with threads matched to the CPU quota it ran at about 19 tokens/s. start.sh now sizes threads to the quota. The llama.cpp binary needed a newer glibc than the default slim Python image, so the final image is based on Debian trixie. Public Overpass servers are flaky. I tested six mirrors with the real query: one answered 6 of 6, one returned a 504 about a third of the time, and three failed most requests. The app retries and falls back across two mirrors. A first request on a fresh container took about 19 seconds in the model alone, so startup now runs one throwaway model call in the background. OpenStreetMap quality is the real ceiling. In one smoke test, "buy rice" resolved to a batik shop that is tagged as a general goods store. Privacy, honestly. Errand text never goes to an LLM vendor, because the model runs inside my own container. But location does leave your device: the server sends your start point rounded to three decimals to Overpass, and the exact start to OpenRouteService. The server doesn't store or log coordinates or errand text (I grepped the container logs to check), and the app has no analytics and no cookies. AI use. I built this with Claude Code. That tool is not open source, and I don't count it as the open-source AI in this project. The open-source parts are the model, the runtime and the map data. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Here is what open weights gave me that a closed API wouldn't have: Cost per call is zero. I pay for the instance (about $25/month, billed by the second), not for tokens, so a week of hosting is a few dollars whether the app gets ten requests or ten thousand. A tool meant for daily use shouldn't have a meter running on every errand list. The model is a setting. Because the app speaks an OpenAI-compatible protocol, the same code ran on my laptop's GPU through Ollama (about one second per call) and inside a 1-CPU container (about five seconds). Comparing them showed that the same nominal model behaves slightly differently in two runtimes. I could only find that out because I controlled the runtime. The text stays with me. What you type into a to-do list can be personal ("pharmacy" says something). Here it is handled by a model running in a container I control, with no third-party model provider involved. Open data is part of this too. Places and routes come from OpenStreetMap and OpenRouteService, which is why the app needs no credit card and no map-vendor contract. It is also why the app inherits OSM's gaps. The honest cost is accuracy. A larger hosted model would probably handle messy Indonesian better and would not have invented a pharmacy errand out of "main game." With a 1B model, you have to build the guardrails yourself: the schema, the keyword layer, the grounding check and the fallback. For a narrow task like this one, I think that trade is worth it. It's also the part of the build I learned the most from. Prize Categories Best Use of Render: the whole app, including the model server, runs in one Docker web service on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB), with the model baked in at build time. Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 1B, self-hosted and run through llama.cpp (and Ollama locally), with schema-constrained output and a measured eval.
items.summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 1: Touch Grass

What I Built

Most short errands happen by default in a car or on a scooter, not because walking is worse, but because planning a walk takes effort. Which shop is closest? In what order? Is it really 40 minutes on foot, or does it just feel like a lot?

Errand Walker removes that effort. You type the list the way you'd type it into a notes app:

pharmacy, post office, buy rice

A small open-weight model turns that into structured errands. OpenStreetMap finds the nearest matching places, a routing API computes one loop, and the app answers in a single line: how many stops, how long on foot, how long by car, and whether you can skip the car.

The screen is the shortest part of the experience. Planning takes about six seconds, and then the phone goes back in your pocket. It's a phone-first web app (PWA) for anyone with a handful of small errands in a place with decent OpenStreetMap coverage. It also understands some Indonesian input ("beli obat, kirim paket"), which I evaluated separately from English.

Demo

In the video I ask for an ATM, a pharmacy and a meal. The app parses the three errands, picks the nearest candidate for each, orders them into a loop and shows the verdict and route on the map.

The live demo uses a fixed public landmark as its start point, so it never needs or reveals my real location. You can also tap the map to set your own start.

Taking it outside

I tested the app on my phone in demo mode, but I did not complete a timed walk to compare predicted and real minutes. That comparison is the next thing I'd do.

Code

derbyps / errand-walker
Errand Walker

Type a messy errand list ("pharmacy, post office, buy rice, return parcel"). Get one loop you can walk or bike, with times for walking, cycling and driving, and a one-line verdict such as "3 stops, 17 min on foot (4 min by car). Skip the car."

A small open-weight model (Gemma 3 1B, run by llama.cpp) turns the text into structured errands OpenStreetMap data (via Overpass) finds the nearest matching places. OpenRouteService routes the loop It is a phone-first PWA built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 1 "Touch Grass". The model needs no API key and no per-call cost, and with the bundled model no AI vendor sees your text.

Built with an AI coding agent (OpenCode, model claude-sonnet-5-5) from a human-written product spec (PRD.md).

How it works 
Phone (PWA, Leaflet)
  | POST /api/plan {text, lat, lng}
  v
FastAPI
  |- parser:  LLM (llama-server,
…
View on GitHub

MIT licensed. The README covers running it locally (Ollama or llama.cpp), the Docker and Render deployment, the privacy data flow, the full eval tables and the known limitations. The project was started on October 11, inside the challenge window, and any commits after the deadline are listed in the README.

How I Built It

The open pieces

  • Model: Gemma 3 1B instruction-tuned, 4-bit GGUF (Q4_K_M, about 806 MB, an ungated build, so no token is needed anywhere).
  • Runtime: llama.cpp's llama-server in production, Ollama on my laptop. The app talks to either through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, so the model is a set of environment variables, not a dependency.
  • Data and routing: OpenStreetMap through the Overpass API, and OpenRouteService for foot, bike and car routes.
  • App: FastAPI backend and a vanilla JS + Leaflet frontend with no build step. Hosted in one Docker container on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB).

One job for the model. The LLM does exactly one thing: map each errand to one of ten fixed categories (pharmacy, post office, groceries, ATM, bakery, hardware, laundry, cafe, clinic, market) or other. The output is constrained to a JSON schema, so a 1B model can't wander. On the first attempt, 100% of its outputs were valid JSON in every run. Categories map to OSM tags, so the model never invents a place. It only picks a type of place, and the real places come from map data.

Three layers around the model. A small model is not trustworthy by itself, so I put deterministic code around it:

  1. A keyword parser (with fuzzy matching for typos and some Indonesian words) that overrides the model when a keyword clearly matches.
  2. A grounding check that drops any model errand sharing no word with what you actually typed.
  3. A fallback to the keyword parser alone if the model is down or returns something unusable. The app degrades, it doesn't crash.

How accurate is it? I wrote a dev set of 26 cases (57 expected errands, English and Indonesian) and later added a held-out set of 15 cases (26 errands) that I wrote after freezing the prompt and keyword list. A test pins a hash of the frozen config, so I couldn't tune against the held-out set by accident. Intervals are 95% Wilson intervals, because these samples are small.

Set Parser Accuracy Dev (57 errands) raw model, Ollama 82.5% [71-90] Dev raw model, deployed container 82.5% Held-out (26 errands) raw model, Ollama 96.2% [81-99] Held-out model + keyword merge, container 92.3% Held-out + grounding check ‡, container 96.2%

‡ I built the grounding check after seeing a held-out failure, so that row only shows it fixes the case that motivated it. It is not an independent result.

Some things I'd rather say than hide:

  • I set a 90% bar for English accuracy up front. The dev set missed it (86.8% on Ollama, 89.5% in the container), with intervals far too wide to separate either figure from 90%. I did not switch to a 4B model, because the larger Render tier costs several times more and I couldn't show it would help.
  • The held-out score is higher mostly because those cases are shorter and simpler, not because the model generalizes better.
  • The failure that mattered was a hallucination. Given "main game" (no real errand), the model invented a pharmacy, an ATM and a laundry stop. In daily use, that would send someone to a pharmacy they never asked for. The grounding check dropped all three in each run.
  • "potong rambut" (haircut) is still mislabeled as a clinic in the container.
  • Two runtimes with nominally the same model did not give identical outputs. Three dev cases differed between Ollama and llama-server, in opposite directions.

Latency on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB, demo point, three errands, Overpass cache pre-warmed at startup):

Request Total Model call First after deploy 6083 ms 5348 ms Warm 5896 ms 5172 ms Warm 5811 ms 5061 ms

This is n=3 with one input. The first request is the first after a fresh deploy, not a cold boot from suspend, and I did not measure cold boot, a six-errand list, or a location the cache hasn't seen. Those will be slower, since an uncached location needs a live Overpass query.

Things that went wrong along the way

  • In a container limited to 1 CPU, llama-server with 4 threads ran at about 2 tokens/s, and with threads matched to the CPU quota it ran at about 19 tokens/s. start.sh now sizes threads to the quota.
  • The llama.cpp binary needed a newer glibc than the default slim Python image, so the final image is based on Debian trixie.
  • Public Overpass servers are flaky. I tested six mirrors with the real query: one answered 6 of 6, one returned a 504 about a third of the time, and three failed most requests. The app retries and falls back across two mirrors.
  • A first request on a fresh container took about 19 seconds in the model alone, so startup now runs one throwaway model call in the background.
  • OpenStreetMap quality is the real ceiling. In one smoke test, "buy rice" resolved to a batik shop that is tagged as a general goods store.

Privacy, honestly. Errand text never goes to an LLM vendor, because the model runs inside my own container. But location does leave your device: the server sends your start point rounded to three decimals to Overpass, and the exact start to OpenRouteService. The server doesn't store or log coordinates or errand text (I grepped the container logs to check), and the app has no analytics and no cookies.

AI use. I built this with Claude Code. That tool is not open source, and I don't count it as the open-source AI in this project. The open-source parts are the model, the runtime and the map data.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Here is what open weights gave me that a closed API wouldn't have:

  • Cost per call is zero. I pay for the instance (about $25/month, billed by the second), not for tokens, so a week of hosting is a few dollars whether the app gets ten requests or ten thousand. A tool meant for daily use shouldn't have a meter running on every errand list.
  • The model is a setting. Because the app speaks an OpenAI-compatible protocol, the same code ran on my laptop's GPU through Ollama (about one second per call) and inside a 1-CPU container (about five seconds). Comparing them showed that the same nominal model behaves slightly differently in two runtimes. I could only find that out because I controlled the runtime.
  • The text stays with me. What you type into a to-do list can be personal ("pharmacy" says something). Here it is handled by a model running in a container I control, with no third-party model provider involved.
  • Open data is part of this too. Places and routes come from OpenStreetMap and OpenRouteService, which is why the app needs no credit card and no map-vendor contract. It is also why the app inherits OSM's gaps.

The honest cost is accuracy. A larger hosted model would probably handle messy Indonesian better and would not have invented a pharmacy errand out of "main game." With a 1B model, you have to build the guardrails yourself: the schema, the keyword layer, the grounding check and the fallback. For a narrow task like this one, I think that trade is worth it. It's also the part of the build I learned the most from.

Prize Categories
  • Best Use of Render: the whole app, including the model server, runs in one Docker web service on Render (1 CPU / 2 GB), with the model baked in at build time.
  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 3 1B, self-hosted and run through llama.cpp (and Ollama locally), with schema-constrained output and a measured eval.

items.title: Add an AI chatbot with sources to a WordPress site on AWS (Amazon Bedrock)
items.summary: This guide sets up AI Chatbot, Agents & MCP for Amazon Bedrock so a WordPress site answers visitors from its own pages, with links to the pages it used, on Claude or another model in Amazon Bedrock. To see it first without an AWS account, open the Live Preview on the plugin's WordPress.org page. It runs a small bakery site in your browser, and the chat quotes the best-matching passage of the site's pages. Before you start An AWS account that can use Amazon Bedrock. Check your account's plan and Bedrock access. AWS's newer sign-up experience , which AWS is releasing to a limited number of customers, includes it in the Free Tier without multi-Region or cross-Region features. A new AWS Free Tier account gets $100 in credits when it is created and can earn up to $100 more, up to $200 over six months; remaining credits apply to AWS bills after upgrading to the Paid plan. WordPress 6.4 or later and PHP 7.4 or later. Bedrock bills per use. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing and set an AWS Budget before opening the chat to the public. 1. Install the plugin In WordPress, open Plugins > Add New , search for Amazon Bedrock , then install and activate AI Chatbot, Agents & MCP for Amazon Bedrock . 2. Choose a Region and a model Open AI Chat Bedrock > Settings , choose the AWS Region, such as Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and pick a model. Enable access to that model in the same Region in the Amazon Bedrock console if your account requires it. 3. Connect to Bedrock Choose one: The server's IAM role (recommended on EC2, ECS or EKS). Leave the credentials empty. Attach an IAM role to the instance or task that may invoke only the models the site uses. Diagnostics shows the least-privilege policy for your settings. An Amazon Bedrock API key (anywhere else, including Amazon Lightsail or other hosting). In the Bedrock console, open API keys in the same Region, generate a long-term key with an expiry, and paste it under AI Chat Bedrock > Settings > AWS authentication . It is stored encrypted. On WordPress 7.1 and later you can paste it under Settings > Connectors > Amazon Bedrock instead. To keep it out of the database, define AI_CHAT_BEDROCK_API_KEY in wp-config.php . Never give a WordPress site broad AWS administrator permissions. 4. Check it Save the settings and run Diagnostics while signed in. It sends one short question to the model and reports the answer, or what to fix. 5. Add the chat Insert the chat block, add [ai_chat_bedrock] to a page, or turn on the floating chat for every page. Answers come from your published pages in the visitor's language, with their sources. Guest chat stays off until you turn it on, and requests are rate limited; set a daily request limit under the settings as well. Optional The official WordPress AI plugin. On WordPress 7.0 and later, Bedrock is a provider for core's AI Client, so the WordPress AI plugin's features run on Bedrock. Its image generation and editing need an image model chosen under AI Chat Bedrock > Settings > Model ; image requests go to US West (Oregon), where Bedrock offers the Stability models. AI agents. Under Settings > Agents and tools you can turn on the site description for agents, an llms.txt file, site content abilities and a WordPress MCP server. Diagnostics lists what is turned on for agents. Only published, public content is described. More answers: FAQ · Support Disclosure: I maintain this plugin.
items.summary_html:
This guide sets up AI Chatbot, Agents & MCP for Amazon Bedrock so a WordPress site answers visitors from its own pages, with links to the pages it used, on Claude or another model in Amazon Bedrock.

To see it first without an AWS account, open the Live Preview on the plugin's WordPress.org page. It runs a small bakery site in your browser, and the chat quotes the best-matching passage of the site's pages.

Before you start
  • An AWS account that can use Amazon Bedrock. Check your account's plan and Bedrock access. AWS's newer sign-up experience, which AWS is releasing to a limited number of customers, includes it in the Free Tier without multi-Region or cross-Region features. A new AWS Free Tier account gets $100 in credits when it is created and can earn up to $100 more, up to $200 over six months; remaining credits apply to AWS bills after upgrading to the Paid plan.
  • WordPress 6.4 or later and PHP 7.4 or later.
  • Bedrock bills per use. Review Amazon Bedrock pricing and set an AWS Budget before opening the chat to the public.
1. Install the plugin

In WordPress, open Plugins > Add New, search for Amazon Bedrock, then install and activate AI Chatbot, Agents & MCP for Amazon Bedrock.

2. Choose a Region and a model

Open AI Chat Bedrock > Settings, choose the AWS Region, such as Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and pick a model. Enable access to that model in the same Region in the Amazon Bedrock console if your account requires it.

3. Connect to Bedrock

Choose one:

  • The server's IAM role (recommended on EC2, ECS or EKS). Leave the credentials empty. Attach an IAM role to the instance or task that may invoke only the models the site uses. Diagnostics shows the least-privilege policy for your settings.
  • An Amazon Bedrock API key (anywhere else, including Amazon Lightsail or other hosting). In the Bedrock console, open API keys in the same Region, generate a long-term key with an expiry, and paste it under AI Chat Bedrock > Settings > AWS authentication. It is stored encrypted. On WordPress 7.1 and later you can paste it under Settings > Connectors > Amazon Bedrock instead. To keep it out of the database, define AI_CHAT_BEDROCK_API_KEY in wp-config.php.

Never give a WordPress site broad AWS administrator permissions.

4. Check it

Save the settings and run Diagnostics while signed in. It sends one short question to the model and reports the answer, or what to fix.

5. Add the chat

Insert the chat block, add [ai_chat_bedrock] to a page, or turn on the floating chat for every page. Answers come from your published pages in the visitor's language, with their sources. Guest chat stays off until you turn it on, and requests are rate limited; set a daily request limit under the settings as well.

Optional
  • The official WordPress AI plugin. On WordPress 7.0 and later, Bedrock is a provider for core's AI Client, so the WordPress AI plugin's features run on Bedrock. Its image generation and editing need an image model chosen under AI Chat Bedrock > Settings > Model; image requests go to US West (Oregon), where Bedrock offers the Stability models.
  • AI agents. Under Settings > Agents and tools you can turn on the site description for agents, an llms.txt file, site content abilities and a WordPress MCP server. Diagnostics lists what is turned on for agents. Only published, public content is described.

More answers: FAQ · Support

Disclosure: I maintain this plugin.

items.title: 10 Ready-to-Run DeepResearch Workflows for Finance, Life Sciences, and Supply Chain
items.summary: Day 11 of 30 Days of Search Quick summary Valyu Workflows are prebuilt, versioned DeepResearch templates. Each defines a research task, typed inputs, a research strategy, and expected deliverables. This guide covers four finance workflows, three life-sciences workflows, and three supply-chain workflows , verified against Valyu's workflow catalogue. You can run them from the Valyu platform or programmatically with one VALYU_API_KEY . No separate model-provider account is required. Preview first: template previews do not spend research credits. Starting a DeepResearch task does. The code below previews by default and only starts research when you pass --run . Workflows are in Beta . Pin a template version for repeatable configuration, check source access, and review the cited report and generated files before using the findings. A company profile, a clinical-trial tracker, and a supplier-risk assessment need different research instructions. You could write and maintain a prompt for each. Or you could start with a template that already defines the scope, source priorities, and output structure. A Valyu DeepResearch workflow packages those instructions into a reusable research template. You supply the inputs such as a company, disease area, product, or policy question and Valyu starts an asynchronous research task. Depending on the template, the outputs include a cited report and Excel, Word, or PowerPoint files. This is not a list of hypothetical agents. The ten entries below are actual curated, battle-tested deepresearch workflows , with their real workflow IDs and variable names. The 10 workflows at a glance # Workflow Category Required input Requested deliverables 1 Company Profile Finance company Excel + Word 2 Comparable Companies Finance target Excel 3 Earnings Preview Finance ticker , period Excel 4 Commercial Due Diligence Finance target Word + Excel + PowerPoint 5 Drug Competitive Landscape Life sciences indication Excel + Word 6 Clinical Trial Tracker Life sciences disease Excel 7 Company Pipeline Analysis Life sciences company Excel + Word 8 Supplier & Geo-Risk Map Supply chain product Excel + PowerPoint 9 Commodity Deep Dive Supply chain commodity Excel + Word 10 Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact Supply chain policy_and_scope Excel + Word These are the templates' requested deliverables, not a guarantee that every file will succeed on every run. Check the task status and each deliverable's status separately. Run a workflow from the platform Open Workflows in the Valyu platform , choose a template, and fill in its inputs. Review the resolved research scope, mode, and deliverables before starting the run. For a developer integration, the same workflow runs through valyu.deepresearch.create() using workflowId and workflowParams . You do not need to construct your own search loop or connect another language-model provider. Set up the TypeScript examples once Use Node.js 22 or newer. In a new working directory: npm init -y npm install valyu-js@2.10.3 npm install --save-dev tsx@4.23.15 Create .env and keep it out of version control: VALYU_API_KEY=replace-with-your-valyu-key Add .env , .env.* , and research-output/ to .gitignore . Saved task results can contain sensitive research and temporary, signed download links. The following helper handles the parts shared by all ten examples: previewing, explicit paid-run opt-in, checking task creation, waiting for completion, and saving the result. Save it as run-workflow.mts : import { mkdir , writeFile } from " node:fs/promises " ; import { Valyu } from " valyu-js " ; type WorkflowParams = Record < string , string | number > ; export async function runWorkflow ( workflowId : string , workflowParams : WorkflowParams , workflowVersion = 1 , ): Promise < void > { const apiKey = process . env . VALYU_API_KEY ; if ( ! apiKey ) throw new Error ( " Set VALYU_API_KEY in .env. " ); const valyu = new Valyu ( apiKey ); const preview = await valyu . workflows . preview ( workflowId , { workflowParams , workflowVersion , }); if ( ! preview . success || ! preview . resolved ) { throw new Error ( `Could not preview workflow ${ workflowId } . Check its inputs and version.` ); } console . log ( JSON . stringify ({ workflow : preview . workflow , resolved : preview . resolved , estimatedCredits : preview . estimated_credits , }, null , 2 )); if ( ! process . argv . includes ( " --run " )) { console . log ( " Preview only. Add --run to create a paid DeepResearch task. " ); return ; } const task = await valyu . deepresearch . create ({ workflowId , workflowParams , workflowVersion , tools : { code_execution : { enabled : true } }, }); if ( ! task . success || ! task . deepresearch_id ) { throw new Error ( `Could not start workflow ${ workflowId } . No task ID was returned.` ); } const taskId = task . deepresearch_id ; console . log ( `Started task ${ taskId } . Keep this ID to resume monitoring later.` ); const result = await valyu . deepresearch . wait ( taskId , { pollInterval : 10 _000 , maxWaitTime : 2 * 60 * 60 * 1 _000 , }); if ( ! result . success || result . status !== " completed " ) { throw new Error ( `Task ${ taskId } did not complete successfully. Check its status in the platform.` ); } // Use only a safe server-issued identifier as the local filename. if ( ! /^ [ A-Za-z0-9_- ] +$/ . test ( taskId )) throw new Error ( " Unexpected task ID format. " ); await mkdir ( " research-output " , { recursive : true }); const filename = `research-output/ ${ taskId } .json` ; await writeFile ( filename , JSON . stringify ( result , null , 2 ), { flag : " wx " }); console . log ( `Saved report, sources, and task metadata to ${ filename } .` ); for ( const file of result . deliverables ?? []) { if ( file . status === " completed " && file . url ) { console . log ( ` ${ file . type } : download link saved in ${ filename } .` ); } else { console . warn ( `A ${ file . type } deliverable did not complete. Review the saved task result.` ); } } } Save one of the workflow snippets below as example.mts beside this helper. Do not concatenate all ten: each is a separate example. Preview it without starting research: npx tsx --env-file = .env example.mts Start that workflow when you are ready: npx tsx --env-file = .env example.mts --run The preview is a template-resolution and input-validation step; it does not test whether every requested source or deliverable will be available during research. A local wait timeout also does not cancel the remote task. Use the printed task ID to check its status before starting another run. Finance workflows 1. Company Profile Use it when: you need a company overview and financial summary before a meeting, diligence review, or deeper analysis. The Company Profile workflow organizes company research into a financial-summary workbook and a short Word profile. Its source strategy prioritizes filings, investor materials, and earnings commentary; for private companies, it also draws on public company information and relevant coverage. Workflow ID: ib-company-profile Input: company Recommended mode in version 1: standard Requested files: Excel financial summary and Word company profile. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " ib-company-profile " , { company : " NVIDIA (NVDA) " , }); Check that financial figures use the intended currency and reporting period. A company profile is a research starting point, not an investment recommendation. 2. Comparable Companies Use it when: you want a peer-comparison workbook rather than a collection of disconnected company summaries. The Comparable Companies workflow researches a target and builds trading comparables. Its template combines market information with filings and investor materials. The useful review questions are whether the peers really match the business, and whether the financial periods and metric definitions are comparable. Workflow ID: ib-comps-analysis Input: target —not company . Recommended mode in version 1: standard Requested files: Excel trading-comparables workbook. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " ib-comps-analysis " , { target : " Palantir (PLTR) " , }); Review the peer selection, data timestamps, and any unavailable estimates before using the workbook. 3. Earnings Preview Use it when: you want the questions and evidence to investigate ahead of a company's earnings release. The Earnings Preview workflow brings together prior disclosures, management commentary, and business-specific indicators. Supply both the ticker and the reporting period so the task does not have to infer which release you mean. Workflow ID: hf-earnings-preview Inputs: ticker , period Recommended mode in version 1: standard Requested files: Excel earnings-preview workbook. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " hf-earnings-preview " , { ticker : " AMD " , period : " Q4 2026 " , }); Choose a period that is still ahead of the release when you run this example. Separate reported facts from expectations; a preview is not a prediction of the earnings result. 4. Commercial Due Diligence Use it when: you need to test a specific commercial thesis, such as whether a company can move upmarket or defend its pricing. The Commercial Due Diligence workflow asks a broader question than a company profile. Its template investigates the market, customers, competitors, and the thesis being tested, with a report, workbook, and presentation as requested outputs. Workflow ID: pe-commercial-dd Required input: target Optional input: thesis_question Recommended mode in version 1: heavy Requested files: Word report, Excel workbook, and PowerPoint deck. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " pe-commercial-dd " , { target : " Rippling " , thesis_question : " Can they win upmarket vs Workday? " , }); Public-source diligence cannot establish everything you would learn from customer interviews or a confidential data room. Treat missing information as a gap, not evidence in favor of the thesis. Life-sciences workflows 5. Drug Competitive Landscape Use it when: you need to understand the therapies and development programs competing within an indication or treatment class. The Drug Competitive Landscape workflow builds an overview of assets, trials, reported results, and upcoming readouts. Its strategy includes trial registries, sponsor releases, conference material, and regulatory information. Workflow ID: ls-drug-competitive-landscape Input: indication Recommended mode in version 1: heavy Requested files: Excel landscape workbook and Word report. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " ls-drug-competitive-landscape " , { indication : " KRAS G12C inhibitors in NSCLC " , }); Cross-trial comparisons need care: different populations, endpoints, and follow-up periods can make headline results incomparable. This is a research landscape, not treatment guidance. 6. Clinical Trial Tracker Use it when: you want a structured view of relevant studies in a disease area. The Clinical Trial Tracker workflow uses ClinicalTrials.gov as a primary source and cross-checks with sponsor announcements and conference material. Its Excel tracker helps you inspect the study landscape without manually rebuilding a table for every research question. Workflow ID: ls-clinical-trial-tracker Input: disease —not indication . Recommended mode in version 1: standard Requested files: Excel trial-tracker workbook. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " ls-clinical-trial-tracker " , { disease : " Alzheimer's disease - anti-amyloid and anti-tau " , }); Check registry identifiers, record-update dates, recruitment status, and the distinction between estimated and actual completion dates. One run produces a research snapshot; ongoing monitoring requires repeated runs and explicit change detection. 7. Company Pipeline Analysis Use it when: you need a company-level view of drug-development programs and upcoming catalysts. The Company Pipeline Analysis workflow combines company pipeline pages, presentations, disclosures, and trial-registry evidence. Its requested workbook separates pipeline, catalysts, commercial context, and deal information, alongside a Word analysis. Workflow ID: ls-pipeline-analysis Input: company Recommended mode in version 1: heavy Requested files: Excel pipeline-analysis workbook and Word report. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " ls-pipeline-analysis " , { company : " Vertex Pharmaceuticals " , }); Keep announced milestones separate from observed trial events. Any commercial or peak-sales assumptions require their own evidence and uncertainty labels. Supply-chain workflows 8. Supplier & Geo-Risk Map Use it when: you want to identify supplier concentration and geographic exposure for a product or component. The Supplier & Geo-Risk Map workflow researches the supplier landscape, production footprint, and trade-policy context. Its requested workbook and slide deck provide a starting point for reviewing dependencies and investigating alternatives. Workflow ID: sc-supplier-map Input: product Recommended mode in version 1: heavy Requested files: Excel supplier-map workbook and PowerPoint risk readout. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " sc-supplier-map " , { product : " High-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators " , }); Do not treat a research-derived supplier map as an exhaustive bill of materials or verified procurement record. Confirm supplier relationships, capacity claims, and locations before making operational decisions. 9. Commodity Deep Dive Use it when: you need a research brief on the supply, demand, inventories, and production context of a commodity. The Commodity Deep Dive workflow prioritizes government and industry sources alongside producer disclosures and relevant market information. It requests a workbook and Word report rather than only a price summary. Workflow ID: sc-commodity-deep-dive Input: commodity Recommended mode in version 1: heavy Requested files: Excel commodity workbook and Word report. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " sc-commodity-deep-dive " , { commodity : " Copper " , }); Check units, geography, time periods, and the distinction between spot prices and futures. An inventory observation or supply forecast is not a guaranteed price outcome. 10. Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact Use it when: you want to investigate a particular policy scenario and its consequences for a defined industry or supply chain. The Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact workflow considers policy documents, notices, trade information, and affected-company disclosures. The input needs both the policy question and the scope of the analysis. Workflow ID: sc-tariff-impact Input: policy_and_scope Recommended mode in version 1: standard Requested files: Excel impact workbook and Word memo. import { runWorkflow } from " ./run-workflow.mts " ; await runWorkflow ( " sc-tariff-impact " , { policy_and_scope : " Assess current US tariffs on EV batteries and battery cells imported " + " from China, and their implications for US auto OEMs. Distinguish " + " effective rules from proposals and state the effective dates " , }); This example deliberately asks the task to establish the current rules instead of assuming a particular tariff rate. Check product classifications, effective dates, exemptions, and the primary policy documents. The report is research, not legal or customs advice. Discover workflows instead of guessing their inputs The catalogue can change. Before integrating another template, inspect its variables rather than assuming that every workflow takes a company field. In this list alone, the input keys include target , ticker , disease , indication , and policy_and_scope .
