items.summary_html:
Day 11 of 30 Days of Search

Quick summary
  • Valyu Workflows are prebuilt, versioned DeepResearch templates. Each defines a research task, typed inputs, a research strategy, and expected deliverables.
  • This guide covers four finance workflows, three life-sciences workflows, and three supply-chain workflows, verified against Valyu's workflow catalogue.
  • You can run them from the Valyu platform or programmatically with one VALYU_API_KEY. No separate model-provider account is required.
  • Preview first: template previews do not spend research credits. Starting a DeepResearch task does. The code below previews by default and only starts research when you pass --run.
  • Workflows are in Beta. Pin a template version for repeatable configuration, check source access, and review the cited report and generated files before using the findings.

A company profile, a clinical-trial tracker, and a supplier-risk assessment need different research instructions. You could write and maintain a prompt for each. Or you could start with a template that already defines the scope, source priorities, and output structure.

A Valyu DeepResearch workflow packages those instructions into a reusable research template. You supply the inputs such as a company, disease area, product, or policy question and Valyu starts an asynchronous research task. Depending on the template, the outputs include a cited report and Excel, Word, or PowerPoint files.

This is not a list of hypothetical agents. The ten entries below are actual curated, battle-tested deepresearch workflows, with their real workflow IDs and variable names.

The 10 workflows at a glance
# Workflow Category Required input Requested deliverables 1 Company Profile Finance company Excel + Word 2 Comparable Companies Finance target Excel 3 Earnings Preview Finance ticker, period Excel 4 Commercial Due Diligence Finance target Word + Excel + PowerPoint 5 Drug Competitive Landscape Life sciences indication Excel + Word 6 Clinical Trial Tracker Life sciences disease Excel 7 Company Pipeline Analysis Life sciences company Excel + Word 8 Supplier & Geo-Risk Map Supply chain product Excel + PowerPoint 9 Commodity Deep Dive Supply chain commodity Excel + Word 10 Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact Supply chain policy_and_scope Excel + Word

These are the templates' requested deliverables, not a guarantee that every file will succeed on every run. Check the task status and each deliverable's status separately.

Run a workflow from the platform

Open Workflows in the Valyu platform, choose a template, and fill in its inputs. Review the resolved research scope, mode, and deliverables before starting the run.

For a developer integration, the same workflow runs through valyu.deepresearch.create() using workflowId and workflowParams. You do not need to construct your own search loop or connect another language-model provider.

Set up the TypeScript examples once

Use Node.js 22 or newer. In a new working directory:

npm init -y
npm install valyu-js@2.10.3
npm install --save-dev tsx@4.23.15

Create .env and keep it out of version control:

VALYU_API_KEY=replace-with-your-valyu-key

Add .env, .env.*, and research-output/ to .gitignore. Saved task results can contain sensitive research and temporary, signed download links.

The following helper handles the parts shared by all ten examples: previewing, explicit paid-run opt-in, checking task creation, waiting for completion, and saving the result. Save it as run-workflow.mts:

import { mkdir, writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

type WorkflowParams = Record<string, string | number>;

export async function runWorkflow(
  workflowId: string,
  workflowParams: WorkflowParams,
  workflowVersion = 1,
): Promise<void> {
  const apiKey = process.env.VALYU_API_KEY;
  if (!apiKey) throw new Error("Set VALYU_API_KEY in .env.");

  const valyu = new Valyu(apiKey);
  const preview = await valyu.workflows.preview(workflowId, {
    workflowParams,
    workflowVersion,
  });
  if (!preview.success || !preview.resolved) {
    throw new Error(`Could not preview workflow ${workflowId}. Check its inputs and version.`);
  }

  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    workflow: preview.workflow,
    resolved: preview.resolved,
    estimatedCredits: preview.estimated_credits,
  }, null, 2));

  if (!process.argv.includes("--run")) {
    console.log("Preview only. Add --run to create a paid DeepResearch task.");
    return;
  }

  const task = await valyu.deepresearch.create({
    workflowId,
    workflowParams,
    workflowVersion,
    tools: { code_execution: { enabled: true } },
  });
  if (!task.success || !task.deepresearch_id) {
    throw new Error(`Could not start workflow ${workflowId}. No task ID was returned.`);
  }

  const taskId = task.deepresearch_id;
  console.log(`Started task ${taskId}. Keep this ID to resume monitoring later.`);

  const result = await valyu.deepresearch.wait(taskId, {
    pollInterval: 10_000,
    maxWaitTime: 2 * 60 * 60 * 1_000,
  });
  if (!result.success || result.status !== "completed") {
    throw new Error(`Task ${taskId} did not complete successfully. Check its status in the platform.`);
  }

  // Use only a safe server-issued identifier as the local filename.
  if (!/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/.test(taskId)) throw new Error("Unexpected task ID format.");
  await mkdir("research-output", { recursive: true });
  const filename = `research-output/${taskId}.json`;
  await writeFile(filename, JSON.stringify(result, null, 2), { flag: "wx" });
  console.log(`Saved report, sources, and task metadata to ${filename}.`);

  for (const file of result.deliverables ?? []) {
    if (file.status === "completed" && file.url) {
      console.log(`${file.type}: download link saved in ${filename}.`);
    } else {
      console.warn(`A ${file.type} deliverable did not complete. Review the saved task result.`);
    }
  }
}

Save one of the workflow snippets below as example.mts beside this helper. Do not concatenate all ten: each is a separate example.

Preview it without starting research:

npx tsx --env-file=.env example.mts

Start that workflow when you are ready:

npx tsx --env-file=.env example.mts --run

The preview is a template-resolution and input-validation step; it does not test whether every requested source or deliverable will be available during research. A local wait timeout also does not cancel the remote task. Use the printed task ID to check its status before starting another run.

Finance workflows 1. Company Profile

Use it when: you need a company overview and financial summary before a meeting, diligence review, or deeper analysis.

The Company Profile workflow organizes company research into a financial-summary workbook and a short Word profile. Its source strategy prioritizes filings, investor materials, and earnings commentary; for private companies, it also draws on public company information and relevant coverage.

  • Workflow ID: ib-company-profile
  • Input: company
  • Recommended mode in version 1: standard
  • Requested files: Excel financial summary and Word company profile.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("ib-company-profile", {
  company: "NVIDIA (NVDA)",
});

Check that financial figures use the intended currency and reporting period. A company profile is a research starting point, not an investment recommendation.

2. Comparable Companies

Use it when: you want a peer-comparison workbook rather than a collection of disconnected company summaries.

The Comparable Companies workflow researches a target and builds trading comparables. Its template combines market information with filings and investor materials. The useful review questions are whether the peers really match the business, and whether the financial periods and metric definitions are comparable.

  • Workflow ID: ib-comps-analysis
  • Input: target—not company.
  • Recommended mode in version 1: standard
  • Requested files: Excel trading-comparables workbook.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("ib-comps-analysis", {
  target: "Palantir (PLTR)",
});

Review the peer selection, data timestamps, and any unavailable estimates before using the workbook.

3. Earnings Preview

Use it when: you want the questions and evidence to investigate ahead of a company's earnings release.

The Earnings Preview workflow brings together prior disclosures, management commentary, and business-specific indicators. Supply both the ticker and the reporting period so the task does not have to infer which release you mean.

  • Workflow ID: hf-earnings-preview
  • Inputs: ticker, period
  • Recommended mode in version 1: standard
  • Requested files: Excel earnings-preview workbook.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("hf-earnings-preview", {
  ticker: "AMD",
  period: "Q4 2026",
});

Choose a period that is still ahead of the release when you run this example. Separate reported facts from expectations; a preview is not a prediction of the earnings result.

4. Commercial Due Diligence

Use it when: you need to test a specific commercial thesis, such as whether a company can move upmarket or defend its pricing.

The Commercial Due Diligence workflow asks a broader question than a company profile. Its template investigates the market, customers, competitors, and the thesis being tested, with a report, workbook, and presentation as requested outputs.

  • Workflow ID: pe-commercial-dd
  • Required input: target
  • Optional input: thesis_question
  • Recommended mode in version 1: heavy
  • Requested files: Word report, Excel workbook, and PowerPoint deck.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("pe-commercial-dd", {
  target: "Rippling",
  thesis_question: "Can they win upmarket vs Workday?",
});

Public-source diligence cannot establish everything you would learn from customer interviews or a confidential data room. Treat missing information as a gap, not evidence in favor of the thesis.

Life-sciences workflows 5. Drug Competitive Landscape

Use it when: you need to understand the therapies and development programs competing within an indication or treatment class.

The Drug Competitive Landscape workflow builds an overview of assets, trials, reported results, and upcoming readouts. Its strategy includes trial registries, sponsor releases, conference material, and regulatory information.

  • Workflow ID: ls-drug-competitive-landscape
  • Input: indication
  • Recommended mode in version 1: heavy
  • Requested files: Excel landscape workbook and Word report.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("ls-drug-competitive-landscape", {
  indication: "KRAS G12C inhibitors in NSCLC",
});

Cross-trial comparisons need care: different populations, endpoints, and follow-up periods can make headline results incomparable. This is a research landscape, not treatment guidance.

6. Clinical Trial Tracker

Use it when: you want a structured view of relevant studies in a disease area.

The Clinical Trial Tracker workflow uses ClinicalTrials.gov as a primary source and cross-checks with sponsor announcements and conference material. Its Excel tracker helps you inspect the study landscape without manually rebuilding a table for every research question.

  • Workflow ID: ls-clinical-trial-tracker
  • Input: disease—not indication.
  • Recommended mode in version 1: standard
  • Requested files: Excel trial-tracker workbook.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("ls-clinical-trial-tracker", {
  disease: "Alzheimer's disease - anti-amyloid and anti-tau",
});

Check registry identifiers, record-update dates, recruitment status, and the distinction between estimated and actual completion dates. One run produces a research snapshot; ongoing monitoring requires repeated runs and explicit change detection.

7. Company Pipeline Analysis

Use it when: you need a company-level view of drug-development programs and upcoming catalysts.

The Company Pipeline Analysis workflow combines company pipeline pages, presentations, disclosures, and trial-registry evidence. Its requested workbook separates pipeline, catalysts, commercial context, and deal information, alongside a Word analysis.

  • Workflow ID: ls-pipeline-analysis
  • Input: company
  • Recommended mode in version 1: heavy
  • Requested files: Excel pipeline-analysis workbook and Word report.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("ls-pipeline-analysis", {
  company: "Vertex Pharmaceuticals",
});

Keep announced milestones separate from observed trial events. Any commercial or peak-sales assumptions require their own evidence and uncertainty labels.

Supply-chain workflows 8. Supplier & Geo-Risk Map

Use it when: you want to identify supplier concentration and geographic exposure for a product or component.

The Supplier & Geo-Risk Map workflow researches the supplier landscape, production footprint, and trade-policy context. Its requested workbook and slide deck provide a starting point for reviewing dependencies and investigating alternatives.

  • Workflow ID: sc-supplier-map
  • Input: product
  • Recommended mode in version 1: heavy
  • Requested files: Excel supplier-map workbook and PowerPoint risk readout.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("sc-supplier-map", {
  product: "High-bandwidth memory (HBM) for AI accelerators",
});

Do not treat a research-derived supplier map as an exhaustive bill of materials or verified procurement record. Confirm supplier relationships, capacity claims, and locations before making operational decisions.

9. Commodity Deep Dive

Use it when: you need a research brief on the supply, demand, inventories, and production context of a commodity.

The Commodity Deep Dive workflow prioritizes government and industry sources alongside producer disclosures and relevant market information. It requests a workbook and Word report rather than only a price summary.

  • Workflow ID: sc-commodity-deep-dive
  • Input: commodity
  • Recommended mode in version 1: heavy
  • Requested files: Excel commodity workbook and Word report.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("sc-commodity-deep-dive", {
  commodity: "Copper",
});

Check units, geography, time periods, and the distinction between spot prices and futures. An inventory observation or supply forecast is not a guaranteed price outcome.

10. Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact

Use it when: you want to investigate a particular policy scenario and its consequences for a defined industry or supply chain.

The Tariff & Trade-Policy Impact workflow considers policy documents, notices, trade information, and affected-company disclosures. The input needs both the policy question and the scope of the analysis.

  • Workflow ID: sc-tariff-impact
  • Input: policy_and_scope
  • Recommended mode in version 1: standard
  • Requested files: Excel impact workbook and Word memo.


import { runWorkflow } from "./run-workflow.mts";

await runWorkflow("sc-tariff-impact", {
  policy_and_scope:
    "Assess current US tariffs on EV batteries and battery cells imported " +
    "from China, and their implications for US auto OEMs. Distinguish " +
    "effective rules from proposals and state the effective dates",
});

This example deliberately asks the task to establish the current rules instead of assuming a particular tariff rate. Check product classifications, effective dates, exemptions, and the primary policy documents. The report is research, not legal or customs advice.

Discover workflows instead of guessing their inputs

The catalogue can change. Before integrating another template, inspect its variables rather than assuming that every workflow takes a company field. In this list alone, the input keys include target, ticker, disease, indication, and policy_and_scope.

Save this separate discovery example as discover.mts:

import { Valyu } from "valyu-js";

if (!process.env.VALYU_API_KEY) throw new Error("Set VALYU_API_KEY in .env.");
const valyu = new Valyu();

const listing = await valyu.workflows.list({
  scope: "valyu",
  vertical: "life-sciences",
  limit: 100,
});
if (!listing.success) throw new Error("Could not list workflows.");

for (const workflow of listing.workflows ?? []) {
  console.log(workflow.slug, workflow.title, workflow.version);
}

const detail = await valyu.workflows.get("ls-clinical-trial-tracker", 1);
if (!detail.success || !detail.workflow) throw new Error("Could not inspect workflow.");
console.log(detail.workflow.variables);
console.log(detail.workflow.deliverables);

Run discovery with npx tsx --env-file=.env discover.mts. Listing and inspecting templates do not start research tasks.

What to know before running these in production

Pin versions. workflowVersion: 1 pins template configuration—not the underlying facts or live data. Different dates can produce different findings even with the same template version.

Use workflow fields, not a second freeform prompt. A workflow run uses workflowId and workflowParams. Do not combine those with query, input, researchStrategy, or reportFormat; those freeform fields are mutually exclusive with a workflow run. Supported run-level overrides include mode, deliverables, search configuration, and human-review checkpoints. Tools merge with the template's tools rather than replacing the entire configuration.

Check source access and costs. Template discovery and preview are not proof of dataset access. Specialized sources depend on your account and plan. DeepResearch runs consume credits; enabled tools and deliverables can add charges. Check the current pricing and the resolved template before execution.

Enable the tools the files need. Excel, Word, and PowerPoint deliverables require code execution. The checked template previews returned empty tool settings, so the helper explicitly enables tools.code_execution. Do not assume that requesting a file also enables the tool needed to generate it.

Separate research completion from file completion. Read the report's citations and the status of each requested deliverable. Preserve the task ID and handle failed or cancelled runs. For a server integration, use signed completion webhooks rather than keeping a request open for the duration of research.

Add human review where it matters. Workflows can use DeepResearch review checkpoints for plans, source domains, or outlines. If you enable them, implement the interaction-response flow; unattended polling alone will not approve a checkpoint.

FAQ What is the difference between a DeepResearch workflow and a research prompt?

A prompt is one instruction. A Valyu workflow is a versioned template that also defines typed inputs, a research strategy, output structure, requested deliverables, and recommended mode and tools.

Do I need an external model API key?

No. These examples use the Valyu TypeScript SDK and VALYU_API_KEY. Valyu DeepResearch handles the research and report generation.

Can I preview a workflow before spending credits?

Yes. valyu.workflows.preview() resolves the template with your inputs without starting a research run. The helper in this article previews by default; adding --run explicitly starts a paid task.

Can the workflows produce spreadsheets and presentations?

Yes. Templates can request Excel, Word, PowerPoint, PDF, and CSV deliverables. The ten examples above show the files requested by their checked version-1 templates. Verify individual file statuses after the run.

Are these workflows customizable?

Valyu-curated templates are read-only. You can use supported per-run overrides, or create and version your own private organization workflows. Inspect the template and Workflows documentation before changing configuration.

Try one workflow before building ten integrations

Choose the output you actually need: a company profile, trial tracker, supplier map, or policy memo. Inspect its inputs, preview the resolved task, and run one example. Review the sources and generated files before wiring the result into a dashboard or recurring process.

Browse the prebuilt workflows in the Valyu platform or follow the Workflows API guide to run them from your application.

items.title: Which CVEs to patch first this week (KEV + EPSS, 27 Sep 2026)
items.summary: There are more than 380,000 CVEs with an EPSS score and no team patches them all. The two free signals that cut the list down fastest are CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog (confirmed exploitation in the wild) and FIRST's EPSS (the probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days). This week's list, and a repeatable way to build it. This week: 17 new exploited CVEs, 3-day deadlines Between 14 and 25 September 2026 CISA added 17 CVEs to KEV (catalog version 2026.09.25, 1,726 CVEs in total). All 17 carry a federal due date three days after they were added (the latest due date is 28 September). Sorted by EPSS: CVE Vendor / product Added Federal due EPSS CVE-2026-71362 Adobe Commerce and Magento 24 Sep 27 Sep 87.5% CVE-2026-76461 Cisco Secure Email Gateway 14 Sep 17 Sep 28.3% CVE-2026-93616 Check Point (multiple products) 22 Sep 25 Sep 19.7% CVE-2026-87902 WordPress Core (remote file inclusion) 25 Sep 28 Sep 18.2% CVE-2026-76460 Cisco Identity Services Engine 16 Sep 19 Sep 14.0% CVE-2025-39682 Linux Kernel 18 Sep 21 Sep 2.9% CVE-2026-7273 Zyxel GS1900 switches 21 Sep 24 Sep 2.5% CVE-2026-94127 F5 BIG-IP APM 22 Sep 25 Sep 2.2% CVE-2026-65660 Microsoft SharePoint 25 Sep 28 Sep 2.1% CVE-2026-67279 MikroTik RouterOS 25 Sep 28 Sep 1.0% The other seven (Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator, a second Check Point CVE, two more Linux kernel CVEs, WSO2, Acronis Backup and Google Pixel) score under 1.1%. They are still exploited; EPSS only tells you where mass exploitation is most likely. EPSS of the CVEs CISA added 14–25 Sep 2026 Adobe Commerce 87.5% Cisco Email Gateway 28.3% Check Point 19.7% WordPress Core 18.2% Cisco ISE 14.0% Linux Kernel 2.9% Zyxel GS1900 2.5% F5 BIG-IP APM 2.2% FIRST EPSS scores dated 27 Sep 2026: the estimated chance of exploitation activity in the next 30 days. Top 8 of the 17 additions. The order to patch in In KEV and internet-facing: Adobe Commerce/Magento, WordPress core, Cisco Secure Email Gateway, Check Point gateways, F5 BIG-IP APM, SharePoint. Exploitation is confirmed and the systems are reachable by anyone. In KEV, inside the network: Cisco ISE, the Linux kernel CVEs, Zyxel switches, MikroTik routers, Acronis Backup. Not in KEV but EPSS above 10%: the early-warning list. 17,267 CVEs have an EPSS of 10% or more today, and only 1,274 of them are in KEV. Run your scanner output through both signals and the gap is where the next KEV entries usually come from. Everything else by CVSS and exposure , on your normal patch cycle. Try it: CVEs added to KEV in the last 14 days (free, no key): curl 'https://kevscope-api.cybermaxtools.com/api/kev/recent?days=14' Why KEV plus EPSS beats CVSS alone CVSS rates how bad a flaw could be. It does not say whether anyone is using it. Of the 1,726 KEV entries, 361 are known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Vendor pages show how concentrated the risk is: Microsoft has 389 CVEs in KEV, Cisco 99, Apple 94 and Ivanti 35. See every vendor. Automate it: one call per 20 CVEs Paste your scanner's CVE list into Kevscope and every CVE comes back with a verdict ( act_now , high , medium , low ) and the evidence behind it: KEV status, due date and ransomware use, EPSS score and percentile, CVSS and CISA's SSVC decision points. The rules are public: act_now means it is in KEV or SSVC says exploitation is active; high means EPSS of 10% or more, or an automatable CVSS 9+ flaw with a public exploit. curl "https://kevscope-api.cybermaxtools.com/api/priority?cve=CVE-2026-71362,CVE-2026-65660" The same key works as a remote MCP server, so an AI agent can triage a scan for you. Kevscope : CVE priority API: up to 20 CVEs per call, each with a verdict and the KEV, EPSS, CVSS and SSVC evidence. Free: 200 calls a day, no key and no card. Paid keys from $19/month (10,000 calls), or $5 pay as you go (2,000, no expiry). See Kevscope plans and pricing Published prices on 27 September 2026: OpenCVE Starter is €19/month and Pro €49/month; Vulners Basic is $600/month. Kevscope is free for 200 calls a day, then $19/month for 10,000 calls. Prefer a report to an API? The Exploited Vulnerabilities Brief lands every Monday. Sources: CISA KEV catalog , FIRST EPSS scores dated 27 Sep 2026, NIST NVD . Published automatically by CyberMax. Every number above comes from the linked public data; nothing is estimated.

  3. Not in KEV but EPSS above 10%: the early-warning list. 17,267 CVEs have an EPSS of 10% or more today, and only 1,274 of them are in KEV. Run your scanner output through both signals and the gap is where the next KEV entries usually come from.

CVSS rates how bad a flaw could be. It does not say whether anyone is using it. Of the 1,726 KEV entries, 361 are known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Vendor pages show how concentrated the risk is: Microsoft has 389 CVEs in KEV, Cisco 99, Apple 94 and Ivanti 35. See every vendor.

Paste your scanner's CVE list into Kevscope and every CVE comes back with a verdict (act_now, high, medium, low) and the evidence behind it: KEV status, due date and ransomware use, EPSS score and percentile, CVSS and CISA's SSVC decision points. The same key works as a remote MCP server, so an AI agent can triage a scan for you.

items.title: Trump's AI rebrand is catching on with tech leaders like Elon Musk and Satya Nadella
items.summary: Marc Benioff said Salesforce's AIForce platform will be renamed SIForce. Bloomberg/Getty Images Trump called those who don't adopt the term Super Intelligence "the enemy." Marc Benioff said Salesforce's AIForce platform is becoming SIForce. Elon Musk also pledged to rename SpaceXAI as SpaceXSI. Donald Trump wants two letters scrubbed from the tech industry’s vocabulary, and some executives are already reaching for replacements. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said Friday that his company’s AIForce platform is getting a new name. “The era of Super Intelligence is here. AIForce is officially SIForce,” Benioff wrote on X. The announcement follows Elon Musk’s pledge Sunday to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, giving Trump’s campaign to replace “artificial intelligence” with “ super intelligence ” traction beyond Washington. The company's X account has already been changed. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella has also made the switch, referring to the tech as "Super Intelligence" in an X post about AI model containment and governance on Saturday. While Nadella has used the term "superintelligence" in the past, this was the first time he used it as two words — and capitalized. Salesforce’s change concerns its agent platform, rather than the company’s corporate name. Trump, meanwhile, is turning his terminology preference into a test. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. The warning escalates a push Trump formalized in a September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to substitute “Super Intelligence” and “SI” for “ Artificial Intelligence ” and “AI” in official communications, websites, reports, and policy documents, to the extent permitted by law. Private companies aren’t required by the order to follow suit. But Benioff’s announcement and Musk’s proposed rebrand show how the president’s preferred language is making its way into corporate branding. The administration’s argument is that AI has outgrown its name. The executive order says today’s systems increasingly amplify human creativity and that “Super Intelligence” better captures their potential. The rebranding push complicates matters for companies whose names include AI, and raises questions over what counts as superintelligence. The term generally describes systems far more capable than humans across a broad range of tasks, and renaming existing products doesn’t establish that they meet that threshold. OpenAI, Scale AI, Character AI, and Resolve AI did not respond to requests for comment. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: This Graph of Data Center Spending Compared to All Other Construction Will Give You Chills
items.summary: Against all odds, the US economy continues to grow at a record-setting pace. Yet as new economic data shows, that growth is anything but healthy, and predicated almost entirely on the AI boom. A new essay by podcaster and writer Derek Thompson takes a look at key economic metrics surrounding AI in 2026. Among the most striking is a bar graph showing growth in construction spending, a key indicator of economic stability. Using data from Harvard Kennedy School economist Jason Furman, Thompson shows that growth in data center construction has exploded this year, while all but one other category has regressed. By the numbers, data center construction has grown at a rate of 64.5 percent in the most recent year, while new energy infrastructure has grown by 4.1 percent to keep pace — since demand is growing for electricity to power the AI boom. Everything else has collapsed: multi-family home building fell by 5.6 percent, while healthcare and commercial retail construction both tumbled by 10.1 percent. New educational construction tumbled by 12.6 percent, while manufacturing — supposedly a key target for the Trump administration — has collapsed, shrinking nearly 24 percent from 2025 to 2026. Thompson is perhaps best known for his “abundance” theory, a deregulation-brained policy agenda with roots in neoliberal economic thought. But if there’s any abundance to be had in the US economy at the moment, it’s clearly coming on the back of AI — and with investors growing increasingly skeptical over the sustainability of AI spending, it could only be a matter of time before data center spending tumbles back down to Earth. More on data centers: Retired Air Force Colonel Warns Americans That It’s Dangerous to Live Near Data Centers Because You Could Be Targeted or Killed

items.title: Claude Code found my app’s shared contract in two MCP calls. Then the records ran out.
items.summary: Every Claude Code user has watched a new session start from zero. You open it on a system you built last week, ask for a small feature, and the agent begins by rediscovering your own architecture: which service owns the data, which frontend calls it, which type the two of them share. The conversation that explained all of that is gone or compressed into a summary, and the source files show what exists without saying what depends on what. So far, the main answer is memory. Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md instructions and its own auto-memory notes at the start of every session, and since September 17, the redesigned Projects, in beta in Claude Code cloud sessions, keep a shared memory across threads, so Claude can recall that “the release moved to Friday” or “who to check in with before touching the billing service.” I wanted to test a different source of context: the dependency records a build platform writes when it creates each version of a component. Disclosure: I’m an engineer at Bit Cloud, a platform that builds, hosts, and deploys even a single app from its first component, with coding agents working on it over MCP. I asked Claude to build on it to see what an agent can do when the platform records each part and its dependencies as they are versioned. The project and its build records are public. What can a fresh session recover without memory? The system was a small support console I had built with Claude Code earlier, and I wrote up how I built and deployed it separately. The prompt that started that build mentioned tooling in two words, “using Bit”, and otherwise described the product. It has four components: a React app, an Express service backed by MongoDB, a shared ticket entity, and a platform component that puts the app and the service behind one gateway. All four are versioned in a public scope , bit-oss.support, and the console runs in production over HTTPS. To test what the records alone could carry, I opened a fresh Claude Code session in an empty workspace, with no conversation history and no local code, and asked: Add filtering by ticket status and assignee to the support console in bit-oss.support. Claude checked the workspace and found no local components. Its next message was: “The workspace is empty, so the support console lives remotely. Let me read the bit-oss.support scope through the MCP.” It called `read_scope` for `bit-oss.support`. That returned the four components and their dependencies. It then called `read_components` for the app, service, and ticket entity, retrieving API references and file inventories before importing source or editing code. The app and service both depended on the same version of the ticket entity. Its class documentation read, “shared between the support service and the agent-facing app,” and the API reference included that sentence. The project could supply this context without the original conversation. Claude imported all four components with `bit import`, inspected the source, and implemented client-side filtering within the app. Validation reported 41 passing tests, including nine new filtering tests. MCP helped it discover the system; source inspection and tests established how to change it. The change stayed inside the app, leaving the shared ticket entity and the service alone. Knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch. Where did the records run out? They ran out at behavior. The app’s API reference does list the routes it calls, `GET /tickets`, `POST /tickets`, `PATCH /tickets/:id` and `POST /tickets/:id/comments`, in the documentation for a fake service it uses in tests, but nothing checks that list against the real service. The records told Claude which components shared the ticket contract; whether the routes on each side still matched had to be read by hand and tested. A green build also proves less than it seems to. The MongoDB integration tests skip when their temporary database cannot start on the CI runner, so a passing build doesn’t show they ran. I checked persistence by hand: create a ticket, add a comment, restart the platform against the same database, and see that both are still there. And this is a demo, with a predefined demo account and a public signing secret. Concurrency control, migrations, recovery procedures, and mandatory database tests are all still to do. That is ordinary engineering work, and it is where I want an engineer’s time to go. Memory files or dependency records? Memory holds what someone chose to write down. In Claude Code, that means CLAUDE.md (or AGENTS.md) instructions a person writes, and auto-memory notes Claude writes from corrections and preferences, and the redesigned Projects add decisions, such as why an export was dropped, which no build system will ever record. Each note is accurate as of the moment it was written. Claude Code records each memory file’s write time, and its documentation explains why: “the timestamp shows how current the fact is.” The build system writes a dependency record when it creates a component version, and it is part of that version. When the support app was versioned, the build system recorded its dependency on one specific version of the ticket entity, without anyone deciding it was worth noting, and the record cannot drift from the version it describes. And because `read_scope` returns each component at its latest version, the records Claude read were current. A memory note carries the time it was written, but nothing ties it to a code version. In the test, the session had no conversation and no local code. The only memory in the workspace was the generic AGENTS.md that `bit new` writes, which tells the agent to look things up on the platform, and the records did the rest: they were enough to find the shared contract. The two cover different ground and work best together: memory for intent, such as the release date, the person to ask, or why a feature was cut, and records for structure and meaning, which version of what depends on which. Nx serves its project graph to agents over MCP, and Sourcegraph serves code search and navigation across repositories; both do that well. For this test, I wanted something narrower: a record per component, written when its version was created, that still holds when the other side of a dependency lives somewhere the agent hasn’t indexed. When should a team start? At the first component. The records in this test cost nothing extra, because they were written as each version was made, starting on day one. I had created the workspace with `bit new`, which supplied the Bit Cloud MCP connection in `.mcp.json` and an AGENTS.md with instructions for the agent, and at the start of the original build Claude used that connection to look through an existing design-system scope for parts it could reuse; the four components now depend on 16 that already existed, ten of them from that design system. Rebuilding that map later, after one team renames a shared field and another finds out from its error logs, is the expensive version of the same work. None of it requires our product; it just needs dependencies recorded wherever the work happens. Agents can already reach production, and what they still lack, on every request after the first, is a view of the system they are about to change. That view is cheapest to build before the second component exists.

items.title: Crypto Gurus Concerned AI Is Poised to Crack Blockchain Math, Allowing Hackers to Steal Funds With Impunity
items.summary: As tech companies continue to claim their AI models are capable of cracking some of the toughest problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades , the crypto community is starting to become uneasy. As Business Insider reports , certain luminaries of the scene are concerned that AI could unlock blockchain wallets, whose public keys are currently protected by nearly ironclad mathematical computation. “Yesterday’s OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us,” Ethereum researcher Justin Drake tweeted this week. “They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen.” As a result, Drake called “upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for ‘bunker mode,'” recommending crypto holders to move their assets to “fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash,” or a cryptographic mathematical function that acts like a digital fingerprint. While the precise threat of an AI model capable of cracking causing crypto armageddon remains unclear, the community has already been wary of a separate threat in the form of quantum computers, which experts warn could eventually break current encryption algorithms by drawing on a qubit-based architecture. While Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin took a less alarmist tone when discussing these threats, he still argued that AI could eventually overtake quantum computers as the biggest threat to the crypto community. “I don’t recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today,” he wrote in his own lengthy commentary on X . “But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.” Even hashes may not hold and could “theoretically” be “broken too,” Buterin argued. If AI were to ever achieve such capabilities, the stakes could be considerable. As CoinDesk reports , millions of Bitcoin sit in address with public keys that are visible to all on the blockchain. Yet how much of a problem AI will actually pose remains debatable. Despite plenty of breathless media coverage about AI companies’ claims of a mathematical revolution thanks to AI, many experts have since cried foul, arguing that they have yet to actually provide sufficient and legible evidence . “OpenAI is flooding us with claimed revolutionary breakthroughs,” University of Milan associate professor Valerio Capraro tweeted . “Yet nobody knows whether the proofs are correct or whether they prove what they claim to be proving.” In a statement this week, the Association for Human Mathematics also undermined OpenAI’s recent claims. “We reject OpenAI’s assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism,” they wrote. In other words, the crypto community may be panicking over a distant or nonexistent threat. At the same time, there have already been instances of AI-assisted attacks on crypto wallets, according to CoinDesk . However, instead of brute forcing their way in through mathematical computation, AI allowed the attackers to identify and exploit years-old firmware bugs that left certain wallets vulnerable. If there’s one thing Buterin and Drake can agreed on, it’s that the community shouldn’t act recklessly. Buterin warned that crypto holders should “be careful” about migrating wallets from address to address for additional layers of security. “I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined,” he admitted. items.summary_html:
As tech companies continue to claim their AI models are capable of cracking some of the toughest problems that have stumped mathematicians for decades, the crypto community is starting to become uneasy.

As Business Insider reports, certain luminaries of the scene are concerned that AI could unlock blockchain wallets, whose public keys are currently protected by nearly ironclad mathematical computation.

“Yesterday’s OpenAI drop made it clear that mathematical superintelligence is upon us,” Ethereum researcher Justin Drake tweeted this week. “They say there are weeks where decades happen. We are about to live through weeks where centuries of mathematical progress happen.”

As a result, Drake called “upon the blockchain industry to calmly begin planning for ‘bunker mode,'” recommending crypto holders to move their assets to “fresh addresses, i.e. addresses whose pubkeys remain hidden behind a hash,” or a cryptographic mathematical function that acts like a digital fingerprint.

While the precise threat of an AI model capable of cracking causing crypto armageddon remains unclear, the community has already been wary of a separate threat in the form of quantum computers, which experts warn could eventually break current encryption algorithms by drawing on a qubit-based architecture.

While Ethereum creator Vitalik Buterin took a less alarmist tone when discussing these threats, he still argued that AI could eventually overtake quantum computers as the biggest threat to the crypto community.

“I don’t recommend anyone scramble to move their funds to new wallets today,” he wrote in his own lengthy commentary on X. “But we should take the risks to cryptography from AI-accelerated math seriously, and minimize our exposure to not just quantum-vulnerable cryptography, but also potentially AI-vulnerable cryptography.”

Even hashes may not hold and could “theoretically” be “broken too,” Buterin argued.

If AI were to ever achieve such capabilities, the stakes could be considerable. As CoinDesk reports, millions of Bitcoin sit in address with public keys that are visible to all on the blockchain.

Yet how much of a problem AI will actually pose remains debatable. Despite plenty of breathless media coverage about AI companies’ claims of a mathematical revolution thanks to AI, many experts have since cried foul, arguing that they have yet to actually provide sufficient and legible evidence.

“OpenAI is flooding us with claimed revolutionary breakthroughs,” University of Milan associate professor Valerio Capraro tweeted. “Yet nobody knows whether the proofs are correct or whether they prove what they claim to be proving.”

In a statement this week, the Association for Human Mathematics also undermined OpenAI’s recent claims.

“We reject OpenAI’s assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism,” they wrote.

In other words, the crypto community may be panicking over a distant or nonexistent threat.

At the same time, there have already been instances of AI-assisted attacks on crypto wallets, according to CoinDesk. However, instead of brute forcing their way in through mathematical computation, AI allowed the attackers to identify and exploit years-old firmware bugs that left certain wallets vulnerable.

If there’s one thing Buterin and Drake can agreed on, it’s that the community shouldn’t act recklessly. Buterin warned that crypto holders should “be careful” about migrating wallets from address to address for additional layers of security.

“I personally have lost more money in botched migrations than I have lost in all hacks combined,” he admitted.

More on AI and math: Mathematicians React With Fury as OpenAI Releases Hundreds of New AI-Generated Proofs

items.title: Claude found 29,000 possible bugs in open source. Only 516 have been fixed.
items.summary: Anthropic’s new OSS Scanner, launched last week as part of its broader Cyber Mission, exposes a problem inside the company’s security research operation. Claude is finding potential vulnerabilities faster than human researchers can verify them. Over six months of scanning some of the world’s most widely used open source projects, Anthropic’s models surfaced more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities . Its human review pipeline, which relies on six external security research firms to reproduce and triage findings, has worked through only about 6,000. A disclosure dashboard puts some numbers behind the problem. As of October 2, outside security firms had confirmed 5,674 of the 6,123 findings they reviewed as valid, but only 516 vulnerabilities had been patched upstream. The company sent 6,157 findings to maintainers, and 584 CVE and GitHub Security Advisory identifiers were issued, though some findings received both. Roughly 23,000 candidates remain unreviewed. Claude is finding potential vulnerabilities faster than human researchers can verify them. How the fast track works Instead of making maintainers wait for its researchers to work through the backlog, Anthropic is giving eligible projects free, periodic scans powered by its top models, including Claude Mythos. The findings go directly to maintainers, without anyone at Anthropic validating them first. Anthropic says projects that received its first reports increasingly asked for everything else it had, and it has already sent nearly 5,000 unvalidated reports to maintainers who requested them. The company now calls the arrangement an “optional fast-track.” Bypassing the backlog Expert penetration testers who vet its coordinated disclosures were asked to check 97 critical and high-severity findings that an early version of the scanner produced across 48 projects. Eighty-five cleared the bar for disclosure, while 11 of the remaining 12 were real bugs that duplicated known issues or other findings from the scan. Only one was a false positive. Those figures describe the scanner’s early output, but not the 29,000 candidates from Anthropic’s separate disclosure program. The sample says little about lower-severity findings or how the scanner will perform at scale. In its technical announcement , Anthropic acknowledged that maintainers have reported inflated severity ratings and cases where the scanner misunderstood a project’s threat model. What maintainers are reporting What separates these reports from a SAST alert queue is how they are packaged. Anthropic says reports include a self-contained reproducer, an explanation that, when possible, identifies where the bug was introduced through bisection, and a candidate patch when the model can produce one. Anton Arapov , director of OpenSSL Corporation, said the reports Anthropic sent , raw model output included, matched and sometimes beat what the project gets from human researchers. He added that a report with a working exploit attached is “basically job done for an engineer as you can verify it right away.” Todd Ouska , founder of wolfSSL, reported that 72 of the 74 reports his team received were valid and five became CVEs. PostgreSQL committer Noah Misch said several reports arrived with fixes the project could use “nearly as-is.” Misch also credited fast-track access with letting PostgreSQL address the newest issues before they shipped in a GA release. But the most pointed endorsement came from The cURL Project founder Daniel Stenberg, who spent last year publicly complaining about the flood of AI-generated slop hitting his project’s bug bounty, which curl shut down in January. He now says OSS Scanner found multiple issues in curl, including one of the worst vulnerabilities the project has seen reported in the last few years. Anthropic builds each project in an isolated VM and cuts off internet access before scanning begins. Reports go directly to maintainers by email, and they can pause or opt out at any time. The GitHub repository contains the enrollment and configuration tools, but not the scanner itself. Finding bugs versus fixing them A reproducer and a proposed patch can save time, but maintainers still have to test the fix, handle backports, and ship it, sometimes knowing the change will break behavior users rely on, which is the tradeoff OpenSSH’s maintainers made when they deliberately broke two features in the name of security . Anthropic is restricting access to established open source projects that have the resources to handle more vulnerability reports. Anthropic is restricting access to established open-source projects with the resources to handle more vulnerability reports. Projects must meet OSS-Fuzz-style eligibility criteria , and Anthropic checks that the person signing up is a core maintainer. The company also expects participating projects to be keeping up with the high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities already reported to them. Who gets OSS Scanner access? The service targets projects equipped to handle that work. Eligibility follows OSS-Fuzz-style criteria for widely used, security-critical open source software. Anthropic verifies that applicants are core maintainers, and its FAQ says participating projects should already be keeping up with verified high- and critical-severity reports. The disclosure terms give participating maintainers room to work at their own pace. Unvalidated scanner findings carry no 90-day clock. However, a report the company later validates through its standard program can be disclosed 90 days after maintainers learn a human has confirmed it. Anthropic says it may eventually attach a disclosure period to some high-severity scanner findings after giving projects notice and a chance to opt out. Eligible maintainers can get free Claude Max 20x subscriptions through Claude for OSS . The idea is to help projects keep up with the growing number of findings, but free access to Claude doesn’t give maintainers more time to review and ship fixes. And as other AI-assisted coding efforts have shown , code that compiles cleanly can still contain problems that human reviewers need to catch.

items.title: There’s Even a Pay Gap Between Male and Female AI Agents
items.summary: Even female AI agents appear to get paid less than their male counterparts. Researchers from the University of Limerick in Ireland found that gender bias in the workplace still persists in how people interact with AI models, leading to female presenting chatbots to receive less pay, they report in a study published in the journal Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction which will be presented at an upcoming conference. In experiments, the researchers had 189 participants work in a virtual reality office place and instructed them to complete work-related tasks with a variety of AI assistants, including those that were either male or female-presenting. To make the stakes more real, the participants were given real money to divide between themselves and the AI assistants. The result: Johan, the male AI, was paid markedly better than “Johanna,” the female AI. In all, Johanna received 10.25 percent less for completing the same work, and it was also perceived as less human-like than its male counterpart, the study found. “What is striking about our findings is that the technology behind these AI agents was exactly the same, but people did not treat them in the same way,” coauthor Mary Hausfeld, an assistant professor UL’s Kemmy Business School, said in a statement about the work. “We often think of AI as being neutral, but the way we design and present these systems can activate those same assumptions and biases that exist in our interactions with other people,” she continued. “We don’t want to inadvertently reproduce existing inequalities in a new technological setting.” The study was intended to investigate how an AI is presented or embodied influences how humans perceive and interact with it, with the researchers noting how these tools are increasingly being framed as “ digital coworkers .” They tested three different AI representations inside the virtual office environment: as a traditional chatbot; as a desktop robot lacking a face or movement, or as either a male or human avatar that sat next to them in the virtual environment. Overall, the human-like assistants were trusted more than the traditional chatbot and robot representations, and were compensated accordingly. The humans gave them more money and more credit for their contribution to the work. Strangely, though, the participants denied that their behavior was being swayed by the anthropomorphic AIs. In interviews, many participants insisted they preferred non-human-like assistants and that the gender of the AI assistant was irrelevant. Going forward, Haesfeld argues, we need to be a lot more careful about how AI agents are presented. Their appearance, or how they’re embodied, shouldn’t be treated only as an aesthetic decision. “Such choices may affect how much people trust AI, how they judge its contribution, and even how they financially reward it,” she said. More on AI: Workers Are Spending An Astonishing Amount of Their Own Money On AI for Their Jobs

items.title: My friends use AI regularly, but I refuse to. I'm learning to keep my beliefs and opinions about it to myself.
items.summary: The author refuses to use AI. Courtesy of Ashley Archambault I decided early on that I don't want to use AI; I can't see any practical ways it could help me. My friends, however, love using AI in their daily lives. It has created some uncomfortable situations, but I try not to share my opinions. My first true encounter with AI was at a teacher training about two years ago, where the objective was to show the different ways AI could save teachers' time. My reaction to using AI to design my next lesson plan was not positive. I admittedly saw the ease in stating your lesson's objective and yielding a full lesson plan in seconds. It was tempting to give it a try, but all I could think about was how I wouldn't even know how to teach without designing my own lesson plans. I then decided to ask AI for an age-appropriate chore chart for my 10-year-old son at the time. It was the one thing in my life that I could think of that I really needed help with. The list AI gave me was adequate, but I knew I would never reference it. It felt cold and generic. I decided then not to use AI anymore; I wish I could say the same for my friends. I feel peer pressure to start using AI All my close friends use AI regularly to do everything from designing their weekly meal plans to scheduling out their entire weeks. They rave about how brilliant and helpful it is. Getting on board with AI is almost starting to feel like peer pressure. I do realize that I cannot entirely resist technological change, but choosing to do my own thing instead of using AI is my choice right now. What makes me most uncomfortable is feeling like I'm being interrogated about why I'm choosing not to use it. I'd love to stand on the rooftops and yell about why I don't want to use AI, but because I love my friends, I don't want to criticize them and their choices. Because of a good friend, AI did me a big favor once One of my friends talked me out of a poor haircut decision by asking ChatGPT to alter a photo she had of me with the haircut. It was not a good look, and in this instance, a friend used AI to save me from regretting a rash haircut decision and many years of awkwardly growing my hair out. Still, this one experiment wasn't enough to lure me to AI use in my everyday life. While I do my best to support and hype up my friends, I make a point of telling my girlfriends that I prefer their untouched, original photos. And it's the truth. I explain that I love seeing all the imperfections, and that the unfiltered version of them is the one I find more beautiful. In this way, I feel like I can still express my opinions about AI while showing my love and respect for them simultaneously. I now want to be more thoughtful when sharing my opinions I think it's been a blessing in disguise to be so close to people utilizing AI because it's forced me to learn how to communicate my feelings about it in a nonconfrontational way. I might have strong opinions regarding the technology, but that doesn't mean one of my best friends needs a lecture from me for asking ChatGPT to show her how to add more protein to her diet. I'd rather listen to her tell me excitedly about the week of dinners she's looking forward to because I just love listening to her. Whether or not I'm using AI in my day-to-day life is irrelevant to our friendship unless she asks for my direct opinion on it. What's more, not wanting to disrespect my friends' decisions to use AI has helped me communicate my own feelings more thoughtfully, taking everyone's feelings into account. It doesn't mean I agree with it or that I'm going to start using it. I'm still pretty resistant to the technology, but I'm even more resistant to making anyone who uses it feel bad about it. items.title: I got divorced abroad and decided to stay in Europe. My $900 pension goes so much further in a tiny French village.
items.summary: Karen Anderson moved to a small village in Northwestern France. Courtesy of Karen Anderson/ Getty Images After divorcing her European husband, Karen Anderson decided to remain in France. She says she'd love to move back to the US, but the higher cost of living makes that unrealistic. She says affordable housing and healthcare have made life in France far less stressful. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Karen Anderson, 57, a Californian who moved to the UK in 2011 and now lives in a small village in northwestern France. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity. I was working as a 911 dispatcher for a California police department when I met my ex-husband, who is English. After dating for a year, we got married in 2011 and eventually moved to his home country, the United Kingdom. I wanted a different life and the chance to experience more of the world. For years, we split our time between the UK, where he worked, and France. And in 2016, we bought a house in France for €45,000 ($50,450), far less than anything we could have afforded in the UK. At closing, I remember being handed more than 100 pages of paperwork. We were foreigners buying a home in a language we didn't understand, so it was very scary. But our hands were held during the process. After my divorce, I decided to remain in France In 2021, I returned to the US to care for my mom, who had been diagnosed with cancer. After getting screened myself, I was also diagnosed, so I ended up staying in the States for about a year while undergoing treatment. During that time, I got a job at Amazon , which helped me get health coverage. I eventually returned to Europe, but by 2023, my ex-husband and I decided to divorce. Although we were married in California, we had to divorce under French law. The process was difficult and took three years to finalize. While the divorce was still underway, I returned to the US to see whether I could make a life there again. It took me about six months to find work, and I eventually became a flight attendant with Frontier Airlines. Unfortunately, I could only afford a twin bed in a house I shared with 13 other women, so I decided to move back to Europe. Once our divorce was finalized, my ex-husband bought out my share of the house. This year, I bought a home of my own in France for €59,100 ($66,159). The process couldn't have been more different from the first time around. I only had to sign three documents electronically, and that was it. The system has changed so much in less than 10 years. For me, staying in France is really about affordability. My $900 monthly pension from my former job as a dispatcher is enough to cover my mortgage, utilities, home insurance, and car insurance. If I were living in the US, I would still need to work just to support myself, but there aren't many job opportunities at my age. I live in a small, idyllic village in northwestern France I live in Saint-Servais, a village of about 400 people in Brittany, in northwestern France , mostly known as the birthplace of crêpes. Breton has a distinct identity, and its people have their own language and traditions. What I love most about living here is that there just aren't as many temptations. You don't feel the same pressure to buy material things. The lifestyle is easy and tranquil. Saint-Servais is surrounded by farmland, with fields of maize grown for cattle feed, as well as sheep, pigs, and chickens. Despite being so small, the village has a restaurant and a church dating back to the 14th or 15th century. There aren't many everyday conveniences. There's no bakery, butcher, or grocery store, so I drive about two and a half miles whenever I need to pick up groceries or fresh bread, which is important to me. A village in Brittany, France. Andrea Pistolesi/Getty Images There's no light pollution or traffic noise in Saint-Servais. I can look outside and see the stars every night of the year, which amazes me. There aren't police sirens or much crime, either. Like many homes in the village, mine is made of stone and, to be honest, it's been a bit of a money pit. It's about 732 square feet. It's small but very cute. The ground floor is underground, and the two bedrooms are upstairs, one of which has an ensuite bathroom. Altogether, I have three bathrooms, which is very unusual for a house this size. Because the ground floor is underground, I have a great deal of humidity. Dampness is a real problem across Europe because of the cool, rainy climate. We get about six months of rain each year, which is very different from California. There isn't central heating or air conditioning in most homes here. I heat mine with a wood-burning stove, and I cut my own firewood. I could install a heat pump, which also provides cool air; it's still relatively new. France is behind the times in some ways — we only got fiber internet in my area in the last few years. My quality of life is better in France In America, we live to work. In France, people work to live. The standard workweek is 35 hours, and many businesses close from noon to 2 p.m. for lunch — they take it very seriously. I came from the US, where I worked 80 to 100 hours a week at the police department. I absolutely loved my job, but it owned me. I recently got a job as a real estate agent. I'm relatively new, and right now my hours are scattered. I'm not quite there yet on understanding how to curtail self-employment. A town in Brittany, France. Clement LEONARD/Getty Images Europe has great healthcare . In the UK, our healthcare was covered regardless of whether you worked because of the National Health Service. France is a little different. Everyone — citizens and legal residents alike — is reimbursed for about 70% of most healthcare costs. Then you buy a top-up, or what the French call a "mutuelle," to cover the rest. How much you pay depends on the coverage you choose. Because I previously had cancer, I receive full coverage, and I've always been looked after. The challenge, though, is access. Doctors and dentists are few and far between. My doctor is two hours away, but my local pharmacy now has a Telebox where I can have a video consultation and get advice or a prescription. I don't see myself moving back to the US Living in France on my own has been a big transition — it's not exactly the life I envisioned. It may look like a dream to other people, but Americans don't always see the sacrifices you make to live abroad. I don't have my children or grandchildren nearby, and I really miss that. At this point, I can't imagine moving back to America. I wouldn't be able to afford the healthcare or housing. I'd love to have a partner again someday. Will some man whisk me away? Maybe. Maybe not. But I don't pin my hopes on that. For now, I have a great circle of friends, and I'm happy with the life I've built. France has given me the ability to enjoy life without worrying about the next paycheck or what it will afford me. Read the original article on Business Insider
items.summary_html:
Karen Anderson moved to a small village in Northwestern France.

Courtesy of Karen Anderson/ Getty Images

  • After divorcing her European husband, Karen Anderson decided to remain in France.
  • She says she'd love to move back to the US, but the higher cost of living makes that unrealistic.
  • She says affordable housing and healthcare have made life in France far less stressful.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Karen Anderson, 57, a Californian who moved to the UK in 2011 and now lives in a small village in northwestern France. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

I was working as a 911 dispatcher for a California police department when I met my ex-husband, who is English. After dating for a year, we got married in 2011 and eventually moved to his home country, the United Kingdom.

I wanted a different life and the chance to experience more of the world. For years, we split our time between the UK, where he worked, and France. And in 2016, we bought a house in France for €45,000 ($50,450), far less than anything we could have afforded in the UK.

At closing, I remember being handed more than 100 pages of paperwork. We were foreigners buying a home in a language we didn't understand, so it was very scary. But our hands were held during the process.

After my divorce, I decided to remain in France

In 2021, I returned to the US to care for my mom, who had been diagnosed with cancer. After getting screened myself, I was also diagnosed, so I ended up staying in the States for about a year while undergoing treatment. During that time, I got a job at Amazon, which helped me get health coverage.

I eventually returned to Europe, but by 2023, my ex-husband and I decided to divorce. Although we were married in California, we had to divorce under French law. The process was difficult and took three years to finalize.

While the divorce was still underway, I returned to the US to see whether I could make a life there again. It took me about six months to find work, and I eventually became a flight attendant with Frontier Airlines. Unfortunately, I could only afford a twin bed in a house I shared with 13 other women, so I decided to move back to Europe.

Once our divorce was finalized, my ex-husband bought out my share of the house. This year, I bought a home of my own in France for €59,100 ($66,159). The process couldn't have been more different from the first time around. I only had to sign three documents electronically, and that was it. The system has changed so much in less than 10 years.

For me, staying in France is really about affordability. My $900 monthly pension from my former job as a dispatcher is enough to cover my mortgage, utilities, home insurance, and car insurance.

If I were living in the US, I would still need to work just to support myself, but there aren't many job opportunities at my age.

I live in a small, idyllic village in northwestern France

I live in Saint-Servais, a village of about 400 people in Brittany, in northwestern France, mostly known as the birthplace of crêpes. Breton has a distinct identity, and its people have their own language and traditions.

What I love most about living here is that there just aren't as many temptations. You don't feel the same pressure to buy material things. The lifestyle is easy and tranquil.

Saint-Servais is surrounded by farmland, with fields of maize grown for cattle feed, as well as sheep, pigs, and chickens. Despite being so small, the village has a restaurant and a church dating back to the 14th or 15th century.

There aren't many everyday conveniences. There's no bakery, butcher, or grocery store, so I drive about two and a half miles whenever I need to pick up groceries or fresh bread, which is important to me.

A village in Brittany, France.

Andrea Pistolesi/Getty Images

There's no light pollution or traffic noise in Saint-Servais. I can look outside and see the stars every night of the year, which amazes me. There aren't police sirens or much crime, either.

Like many homes in the village, mine is made of stone and, to be honest, it's been a bit of a money pit. It's about 732 square feet. It's small but very cute. The ground floor is underground, and the two bedrooms are upstairs, one of which has an ensuite bathroom. Altogether, I have three bathrooms, which is very unusual for a house this size.

Because the ground floor is underground, I have a great deal of humidity. Dampness is a real problem across Europe because of the cool, rainy climate. We get about six months of rain each year, which is very different from California.

There isn't central heating or air conditioning in most homes here. I heat mine with a wood-burning stove, and I cut my own firewood. I could install a heat pump, which also provides cool air; it's still relatively new. France is behind the times in some ways — we only got fiber internet in my area in the last few years.

My quality of life is better in France

In America, we live to work. In France, people work to live. The standard workweek is 35 hours, and many businesses close from noon to 2 p.m. for lunch — they take it very seriously. I came from the US, where I worked 80 to 100 hours a week at the police department. I absolutely loved my job, but it owned me.

I recently got a job as a real estate agent. I'm relatively new, and right now my hours are scattered. I'm not quite there yet on understanding how to curtail self-employment.

A town in Brittany, France.

Clement LEONARD/Getty Images

Europe has great healthcare. In the UK, our healthcare was covered regardless of whether you worked because of the National Health Service. France is a little different. Everyone — citizens and legal residents alike — is reimbursed for about 70% of most healthcare costs. Then you buy a top-up, or what the French call a "mutuelle," to cover the rest.

How much you pay depends on the coverage you choose. Because I previously had cancer, I receive full coverage, and I've always been looked after.

The challenge, though, is access. Doctors and dentists are few and far between. My doctor is two hours away, but my local pharmacy now has a Telebox where I can have a video consultation and get advice or a prescription.

I don't see myself moving back to the US

Living in France on my own has been a big transition — it's not exactly the life I envisioned.

It may look like a dream to other people, but Americans don't always see the sacrifices you make to live abroad. I don't have my children or grandchildren nearby, and I really miss that.

At this point, I can't imagine moving back to America. I wouldn't be able to afford the healthcare or housing.

I'd love to have a partner again someday. Will some man whisk me away? Maybe. Maybe not. But I don't pin my hopes on that.

For now, I have a great circle of friends, and I'm happy with the life I've built. France has given me the ability to enjoy life without worrying about the next paycheck or what it will afford me.
